We all know that Rome wasn't built in a day, but we would like to know how many homes will be built in Wales in a year.

Minister, following alongside those aims to get people into social housing as soon as possible, I was wondering whether the pots of money currently given to registered social landlords to adapt old stock—current old stock—to meet the demand and needs of those on current waiting lists will continue.

speaker: John Clark AS
text: Will the Welsh Government follow in the footsteps of the Scottish Government and develop a strategic action plan to address escalating wildfire threats in Wales?

speaker: Catherine Cullen  AS
text: As a former teacher, I know first-hand the challenges facing our schools and the immense commitment shown by teachers and school leaders across Wales, and I'd like to thank Lynne Neagle for bringing forward this question. Of course, supporting teachers is vital, and fair pay is an important part of that, but we must also recognise that the pressures facing the profession go far beyond pay alone. There is workload, recruitment and retention, additional learning needs provision and the increasing demands placed on schools all requiring attention. I note that the NAHT, the school leaders' union, and the Association of School and College Leaders have now written to the education Minister, herself a former leader of the NAHT, to formally register a dispute with the Welsh Government over the pay settlement, alongside concerns with ALN funding. What makes this particularly significant is that neither union has previously been in a formal dispute with the Welsh Government; these are unprecedented circumstances. Therefore, can the Minister outline how the Welsh Government intends to rebuild consensus with these unions, resolve the issues that have led to this dispute, and what further action can be taken to support teachers and school leaders across Wales?

speaker: Llŷr Powell AS
text:
Diolch, Lywydd. I was sad and shocked on the weekend to find out about the passing of the Rt Hon Ann Widdecombe. I'm not going to comment today on the circumstances, but will celebrate the person that she was.

Ann was the MP for Maidstone for 23 years. She served in Government, serving the country that she loved as Minister of State for employment and Minister of State for prisons. Ann became a Member of the European Parliament for South West England in 2019. Her words were that she was there to ensure that the largest democratic vote the United Kingdom has had is fulfilled, and she pushed it through. She became an unlikely national treasure through her appearances on Strictly Come Dancing. She was on Big Brother. She appeared in several pantomimes across the country during the seasons, and even appeared in a production at the Royal Opera House.

She was a dedicated campaigner for animal causes. Ann went against her own party and friends when she was outspoken in supporting the ban on fox hunting, claiming it was immoral not to do so. She stood up for animals like donkeys and their welfare. She fought for the end of the use of animals in circuses. Ann showed us that you could be a true Conservative, a 'small c' conservative, but you can also stand up for your principles, you can go against your party. In tributes, we've heard that Ann was a maverick; she was. She was fearless in debate, she was kind-hearted, she was true to her faith at all times.

I had the pleasure of meeting Ann in 2019. It was a friendship that I cherish more than anything. I walked the streets of Ebbw Vale with her, where I saw women leaving a hair salon and nail bar quickly to have a selfie with the Strictly Come Dancing star that was Ann Widdecombe. She looked perplexed at how she was a star—she just saw herself as Ann. That's the person I knew every time I met her. She's a loss to this country, to our party and to Britain as a whole. We on these benches, and, I hope, across the Chamber, will pay tribute to her family and to the person whom we will long miss. Rest in peace, Ann.

speaker: Jason O'Connell AS
debate: 6. Member Debate under Standing Order 11.21(iv): Young people and employment
text:
I'd also like to declare an interest. It might surprise a few people to know that I'm a former young person myself. It was a while ago now, but—. I will say, I think when you think about the journey that young people go through, for too long, they've been kind of mis-sold a promise that if you go to university, then on the other side awaits a golden nirvana, a good job and big success, but the reality is that it hasn't—. Instead, thousands of young people across Wales, and indeed the UK, go into that process and they leave having to go for unpaid or low-paid jobs at the end of it in an unrelated field, because the degree that they had isn't valued by employers or wanted by the economy. They leave with debt. And the harsh reality is that the dreams of those young people going into those university courses have often been broken, and there's a lot of disappointment on the other side. And on both sides of the M4, young people have been mis-sold degrees, pushed through the system and leave with tens of thousands of pounds-worth of debt that they carry with them for decades. An economy of skilled workers that those employers have to go out to the world to look for to fill that—we could be filling right here in Wales. And many people in that generation are really paying the price for the decisions that we, as the older generation, have been making, and, certainly, in this Chamber.

Now, as has already been mentioned, 17 per cent of Welsh young people in Wales are NEET, and that, for a supposed advanced economy, is not an acceptable position to be in. Unlike many of them, I actually started my career with an apprenticeship, and I would say it was easily one of the best decisions I ever made. I would actually like to take the opportunity to pay tribute to those men and women at the civilian technical training school that I went on to work with. They've gone on throughout the world to achieve some remarkable things. It's just a shame that we couldn't keep them employed here in Wales, and that's what we have to look to do. I was able to earn and learn at the same time, and it led to a long and successful 30-year career across aerospace and defence. First of all with the Ministry of Defence at St Athan—a three-year apprenticeship that taught me and my colleagues the fundamentals of aerospace engineering. I then went on to the defence sector at another Welsh success story at General Dynamics, and various senior management positions soon after. So, apprenticeships may well be vocational in nature, but they can lead to some really exciting places for young people.

I know first-hand what apprenticeships can achieve. I understand the power of apprenticeships, for employers and for young people. They have dual value, and it's important that we consider that. Now, I want every young person in Wales to have those same opportunities. I think we can all agree to that premise. I think there will be consensus around the Chamber on that. I think there's power in that. That means shifting our focus away from low-value degrees and putting skilled trades back at the heart of where they belong, which is at the heart of Welsh education, so that people are aware of what those trades mean to the economy as they're coming through school and making those choices.

Now, today, young people who want to become electricians, engineers, plumbers and technicians are fighting over a handful of apprenticeship places. Despite skyrocketing demand, apprenticeship starts in Wales have actually fallen by around 37 per cent over the last decade. The last Government claimed they delivered 100,000 apprenticeships over the last term, but as we all now know, the figures were fiddled and the public were misled on that, and that's a terrible legacy to leave. Terrible delivery and a misrepresentation of data. But we need to turn that around.

Now, this debate today is an attempt to reclaim that narrative; we understand that. But I do think that we can all come together to recognise that programmes like Jobs Growth Wales and ReAct aren't enough to get our students through the process into producing high-quality jobs for employers. Too often these programmes have become a revolving door of courses, placements and paperwork, rather than a genuine route into secure employment and training. Now, of course it's not enough for me to say what we wouldn't do; we are the party that tells the public exactly what we would do. Reform Wales would expand high-quality degree apprenticeships, work with employers and make vocational skills just as respected as academic qualifications.

We also need to have an honest conversation about the impact of uncontrolled immigration on our jobs market. To not acknowledge the direct correlation is not to acknowledge the reality of the pressures that people face. Four hundred Welsh nurses, for example, paramedics and midwives who were trained here in Wales, ready, willing and able to work in our NHS, are unable to find work, while we import staff from abroad. Now, that's completely unacceptable to the men and women who are looking for jobs in our NHS. But that's what happens when Welsh workers aren't put first. Now, we appreciate anyone that wants to work in our NHS and contribute, but it can't be to the detriment of our own Welsh young people. Warm words aren't enough. We need better than the young person's guarantee. That's why—

speaker: Jason O'Connell AS
debate: 6. Member Debate under Standing Order 11.21(iv): Young people and employment
text: —we'll be abstaining today. Last point, and I will skip over.

speaker: Jason O'Connell AS
debate: 6. Member Debate under Standing Order 11.21(iv): Young people and employment
text: All parties have fallen short when it comes to prioritising the needs of our youngest. They deserve better. Restore will be abstaining. Thank you.

speaker: Tom Montgomery AS
debate: 6. Member Debate under Standing Order 11.21(iv): Young people and employment
text:
Thank you to the Member for bringing forward this debate, and to all those who have contributed so far. Creating pathways into employment for young people is critically important, as detailed in the motion. Given this, I truly welcome the spirit of this motion. It is incumbent upon all of us to find solutions to this issue. However, I do feel that there is more room for us to cover. We need more focus on vocational apprenticeships, particularly in relation to the building and construction industry. At this point, I must declare an interest, as my younger brother is currently completing one such vocational apprenticeship.

Trades and construction are a significant employer across our country. However, from the experience of my brother, I can tell this Chamber that the cuts to apprenticeship funding dealt a huge blow to the success of these vocational apprenticeships. I recall months of worry and concern as my brother's apprenticeship hung in the balance. He struggled to find a qualified trade to take him on as an apprentice. We must recognise that the vast majority of trades are sole traders or small in size, people that lack the financial reserves to employ an apprentice and all the costs that can come with that.

Previously, funding was available to help meet these costs. Apprentices could find stable work placements, essential to them completing their courses, and employers were supported. We had a pathway for young people to learn a trade, gain valuable work experience and move into full-time work. However, when cuts to funding came, this pathway was restricted. If you are serious about creating avenues into employment for every young person, then I believe this motion should be calling for those pathways to be re-established.

This leads me on to my next point. In my previous role, I worked in a charity, which, along with a number of other services, ran a successful back-to-work programme. I helped lead a project that took 16 individuals over a cohort of three months, mostly young people who were long-term unemployed, and we would pay them to work with us. Over three months, we gave them real work experience. We also set aside one day where we upskilled the participants in cv writing, interview skills, job search support, manual handling training, first aid, mental health and well-being support, to name just some of the skills we helped our participants receive. Over the two years that this project ran, we helped more than 40 young people back into full-time work.

I took away two key points from my time with this project. Firstly, like I already believed, Government cannot do it alone. We can create all the Government agencies, projects and schemes we want, but unless the Welsh Government is willing to financially support the private sector, and, importantly, the third sector, to provide job opportunities for long-term unemployed people, we will fail to create those pathways into employment.

Secondly, one of the largest barriers to getting people into work is experience. Without real work experience, many young people struggle to have the confidence to apply for jobs. They fail to make it through interview processes or simply don't know where to start when it comes to job hunting. I cannot tell you enough about the number of young people I worked with directly on this project who were able and willing to work, they just didn't know where to start. To see the transition that they went through in that short three-month window with us was remarkable.

So, this brings me on to my final point. We must recognise the importance of a young person's first part-time job, working as a pot wash or waiting tables. Whilst this is not a lifelong career for some, the workplace experience and skills that they gain are invaluable when it comes to moving to other work. This is exactly the point that I was trying to make last week in this place. The tourism and hospitality industry is a vital piece of the puzzle on this issue. I, like many others across Wales, worked in the hospitality sector. I held down a little part-time job from the age of 15, working around school, on weekends and in the evenings. And I recognised that my experience in this sector, working in pubs, restaurants, cafes in a variety of roles, gave me skills that no classroom could teach. It taught me the value of hard work. It helped me develop my interpersonal skills and gave me references for my cv. These are all vital components if we're serious about tackling youth unemployment. So, if we're serious about this issue, I truly believe we must engage with the tourism and hospitality sector, because I tell you they have been supporting young people into work and upskilling them for decades.

So, in conclusion, I do truly welcome the spirit of this motion, but I do believe that we have some more components that we need to consider if we're going to be successful in tackling youth unemployment in the future.

speaker: Benjamin Hodge Mckenna AS
debate: 6. Member Debate under Standing Order 11.21(iv): Young people and employment
text: Thank you, Shav, for tabling the debate today, and thank you to everyone for their contributions so far. I'd like to start on some points of agreement, firstly with my Reform colleague about the fact that we cannot ignore the pressures of immigration on the employment market for young people. The Migration Observatory at the University of Oxford notes that currently 10 per cent of jobs in Wales are occupied by people who are not UK citizens. That's up from 6 per cent in 2021, showing an increased trend of competition amongst the job market that will impact young people.

speaker: Benjamin Hodge Mckenna AS
debate: 6. Member Debate under Standing Order 11.21(iv): Young people and employment
text: Yes.

speaker: Benjamin Hodge Mckenna AS
debate: 6. Member Debate under Standing Order 11.21(iv): Young people and employment
text:
Well, you're going to have to take that up with the University of Oxford, because these are their statistics, Janet, but there we are.

I also agree with what Jane Dodds said about the crisis of opportunity that we have in the country at the moment. Previous generations, as has been mentioned, had a social contract in which if you went to work, you worked hard and you did everything that you could, your life would get better year upon year. But, increasingly, young people feel as though that social contract is not in place for them at the moment, and that no matter how hard they try or how much effort they put into the economy, it's not returning the dividends based on the effort that they've put in.

On that note, we can look to China for some symptoms of what has occurred in their economy, which is similar to what has happened here. In China, a social phenomenon occurred called tang ping, which translates roughly to 'lie flat', which was essentially the mass revolt of young people to disengage with the economy as much as possible, refuse to engage in the oppressive working structure, the 996—working nine till nine, six days a week—refusing to engage in social activities, to start families, or engage in society. This ended up getting so severe that the President of China had to do a televised public address, effectively begging young people, for the good of the country, to accept jobs that they were overqualified for, to beg university graduates to do things like work in food delivery. I fear that if we allow things to continue in this country, we could end up in a similar situation for young people. We already saw reports of quiet quitting a couple of years ago. People don't quiet quit from a job because they're lazy; you quiet quit because you're completely disengaged with the system and don't feel that it's delivering for you.

I'll finish with a couple of statistics from the labour market survey that the Welsh Government published in April, and there are two that are really striking. First, the economic inactivity rate amongst young people is at 26 per cent, and that was up 8.1 per cent. But in combination with that, the youth unemployment rate is also at 15.4 per cent. When you take those two stats together, economic activity excluding people in education and youth unemployment, that's about 40 per cent of young people who are not in work, whether they're looking for it or not, and that is a fundamentally shocking statistic for me to read, so I'll finish on that one. We do need to do everything possible to improve young people's prospects in this country. But unfortunately, I don't think the young people's guarantee is the answer, because it was launched in 2021 as the first phase, and we still see how shocking the statistics are today. Diolch yn fawr.

speaker: Laura Anne Jones AC
text:
We also recognise in our motion that wildlife is a source of infection, and that's what's been the missing action. Along with higher standards and everything else that farmers accept, it is a significant part of the problem that now, finally, needs to be addressed. Too often, farmers are falsely portrayed as if they do not care about animal welfare or the environment; nothing could be further from the truth. Welsh farmers are amongst our greatest animal lovers and environmental custodians. They do not want to see any animal killed unnecessarily. Our motion recognises the complexity of bovine TB, with the multiple routes of transmission, as well as the infection from wildlife, but we must recognise and accept that wildlife is a source of infection.

We need to incorporate culling in our plan, but, unlike England, we want to see a more targeted, science-led approach that will identify only wildlife and sets that have TB, not a blanket approach, targeting all sets. This, of course, will save wildlife and save unnecessary killing, and also it will help eradicate the disease arguably better than with the approach in England. If the technical advisory group recommends it, that recommendation must be given full consideration—it just must. The evidence already out there shows that this is likely to be a key element for success in ridding Wales of this cruel disease once and for all.

I'm sure you'd agree, Minister, that we need to look at, firstly, focusing these wildlife control efforts in areas with the highest level of bovine TB disease—in Monmouthshire, Pembrokeshire, Ceredigion and so forth. Local evidence showing us where this disease is prevalent should be used to identify those sets and show us where the action is necessary. This will, in turn, protect healthy badger populations, safeguard and save healthy cattle and give farmers in the worst affected areas and communities a chance to break that cycle of infection.

For years, after successive Labour Governments, farmers were given strategies, consultation reviews and warm words, and Labour's amendment today shows that they have still not learned that lesson. After 27 years in Government, nearly three decades of failure in tackling this disease, they want the Chamber to congratulate them for a so-called partnership approach and point to statistics suggesting it's improving. But I invite those who feel this way to attend livestock farms, to visit farms and actually listen to farmers, as everyone across Wales wants bovine TB gone for good, recognising the devastation it causes and the urgency to tackle this.

Farmers living through repeated breakdowns, restrictions and slaughter of healthy cattle will not recognise the rosy picture that you present. We are calling for a targeted, evidence-led approach in areas where bovine TB is most severe. Farmers have already paid too high a price for previous Governments not taking that action. They need a plan that works, they need a timetable. Let's be bold with our aims. Let's try to stop cattle, badgers and wildlife having to die unnecessary and painful deaths from TB.

We now have a Minister that agrees that we can no longer skirt around what we all know to be true—that wildlife is part of that problem. We now have a Minister who has said in this Chamber that he would not be afraid to take those difficult decisions if that's what the science points to. We now, finally, have consensus and an agreement across this Chamber that an urgent, different approach needs to be taken to rid Wales of bovine TB. The majority of us agree now that we need a targeted approach and that we need to take these difficult decisions to protect wildlife, save healthy badgers, healthy cattle, and save our farmers from further mental torture.

This is it. This is the time. This is the Senedd to make a significant difference to our farmers and our rural communities. Minister, if you back our motion today and you heed the cry from our rural communities who need real action, Reform, and other parties in this Chamber, I know, will back you, and we will be behind you 100 per cent. We have a responsibility to do this for future generations, and the ultimate responsibility, of course, lies on your shoulders. I hope today that you'll use this opportunity to state your clear intentions, to make an announcement with firm, clear plans and a timetable for action. We are grateful for your warm words to date on this, Minister, but now is that time for action. Let us be the Senedd and you be the Government to change this. I urge you to all come together across the Chamber today, ahead of the Royal Welsh Show next week, and the local shows in your constituencies this summer, and vote collectively for a motion that will send a strong, reassuring message to our agricultural industry that we are ready to take those tough, grown-up decisions, based in reality and science, that will mean we can finally support our farmers, save animals and rid Wales of this cruel disease once and for all. Diolch.

speaker: Laura Anne Jones AC
text:
Diolch, Lywydd. I move our Reform motion today in the name of Llŷr Powell.

This has been a long time coming. I believe that, finally, we have the consensus across this Chamber on how we need to and why we need to tackle this cruel bovine TB disease once and for all. I do so in the spirit of seriousness and responsibility, having seen grown men and women, farmers, on their knees crying due to their cattle being slaughtered by previous Governments' failure to tackle this devastating disease.

Bovine TB is not a party political problem. It is one of the top and one of the most pressing and painful issues facing our agricultural communities still today—not according to just me or my party, but according to the entire rural communities across Wales. When I was first elected to this place in 2003, bovine TB was already devastating Welsh farms and had cast a dark cloud over the industry. Over two decades later, farmers are still living under that same dark cloud, watching healthy cattle taken away, enduring endless restrictions and seeing family businesses and family members pushed to breaking point. I think we can all agree across this Chamber that the present strategy and past strategies have not worked. We cannot keep doing the same thing and expecting different results. We all know what needs doing. Our farmers are calling for a fresh start on this, and a bolder, targeted approach led by science.

This disease causes enormous financial damage, but the emotional toll is harder to measure. Coming from a farming family and community in Monmouthshire, I have seen the reality. I've seen the pain and the hardship it causes—watching cattle they have bred, reared and cared for being taken away to be slaughtered, in many cases unnecessarily. And on that, tests have to be improved. They have to be clearer. They have to be more accurate. For those who haven't seen it in their own communities, they may have seen the recent Clarkson's Farm episode of a cow being taken away for slaughter that was carrying twin calves, which were also killed, because of a test that came back as inconclusive, not definitive.

This is the cruel reality of what our farmers are having to deal with. And this isn't a stand-alone case. The toll that this has taken on some of our Welsh farmers has led them to take their own lives. It is not only the cost to human lives, but the cost to animal lives that must be considered. We must also account for the enormous cost to the public purse. Minister, how much has bovine TB cost Wales every year? How much has decades of failure to tackle this disease already cost the Welsh taxpayer, and how much more will it cost Wales if your Government follows in the previous footsteps of past Governments by failing to do what's necessary?

speaker: James Evans AS
text: Will the Member take an intervention?

speaker: James Evans AS
text: Do you not recognise that, actually, where badger culling took place in England, reinfection and incidence rates actually went down? So, it actually does prove that, where you do remove infected wildlife, it actually does improve the overall situation with regard to TB.

speaker: Helen Jenner AS
text:
I think everybody in the Siambr agrees on one thing: nobody wants bovine TB to be a part of Welsh farming in another 10 or 20 years' time. Whatever our views on how we get there, we all want to see this disease managed more effectively, not only in cattle, but in the general wildlife population as well. The difficulty is that farmers have been hearing that ambition for a very long time, yet, if you speak to them today, the majority don't feel like we're getting any closer to the long-term goal of eradicating the disease. Farmers still live with the same uncertainty, the same movement restrictions and the same crippling anxiety every time a test comes around. They still see healthy, productive cattle being slaughtered. I can't put into words just how distressing it is for me to read the latest data. Over 10,000 cattle were slaughtered in Wales last year alone, with 479 new herd incidents detected—479. My heart goes out to every person doing their best to cope with the mental strain caused by bovine TB. That is why Reform has brought this debate forward today, because we don't think it's good enough to simply carry on with the same conversation we've been having for years and expect farmers to believe that something is about to change.

One thing that has struck me over the last few weeks, and, indeed, during the election campaign, is that I've listened to Plaid Cymru say that they will follow the science. I don't disagree with that. In fact, that's exactly what the Government should be doing. But I keep coming back to the same question: follow the science to where? This isn't a new disease. We're not starting from scratch. Welsh Governments have had years of evidence available to them. They've had scientific advice. They've had the technical advisory group. They've had veterinary expertise, years of surveillance data and years of lived experience from the farmers themselves. Farmers in my constituency aren't asking whether the Government has enough evidence yet. They're asking what the Government has actually concluded from the scientific evidence it already has. Evidence doesn't make decisions; Ministers do. And this current Minister has years of experience in opposition. He knows better than anyone exactly what the science is telling him. At some point, this Government has to demonstrate what it has learned from the evidence it has spent years collecting, and that it's ready to harness that data and take meaningful, tangible steps to manage bovine TB in Wales.

I find myself thinking back to what Plaid Cymru used to say when they sat on the opposition benches. Llyr Gruffydd spoke passionately about bovine TB, he challenged Labour's approach, he spoke about the pressure on farming families and questioned whether the existing strategy was delivering what farmers had been promised. He spoke about the need to listen to the evidence and to the industry. Those were perfectly legitimate questions to ask and they're just as legitimate now that Plaid Cymru is in Government.

Farmers don’t see politics in the way we do. They don’t look at which benches people are sitting on; they simply want to know whether anything is going to actually change. What is this Senedd doing to help them, to make their lives easier and to give the next generation of farmers a future? If the answer is that we need more time, I suspect many farmers will say they've already given successive Governments enough time. If the answer is another review, they'll say that we've had reviews before. If the answer is more evidence, they'll quite reasonably ask what happened to all the evidence that we've already gathered. That isn't an argument against science—quite the opposite; it's an argument for having the confidence to act on the science.

I've never accepted that this debate should be reduced to people choosing sides before they've even discussed the evidence. Whether it's cattle controls, biosecurity, vaccination or a controlled wildlife cull, surely the starting point has to be an honest assessment of what is and isn't working. Because if we can't ask those questions now, after everything farmers have lived through, when can we?

The uncomfortable reality is that, after decades of increasingly stringent cattle controls, Wales is still recording thousands of reactor cattle every year and hundreds of new herd incidents. It is entirely reasonable to ask whether the strategy, taken as a whole, is getting us where we all want to be. I don't think that it's a criticism of farmers—quite the opposite; farmers have done what successive Governments have asked of them. They have accepted tighter controls, greater costs and more bureaucracy, because they believed they were contributing towards better management of the disease. Government now has to show the same willingness to examine its own approach, because—[Interruption.] No, I'd like to make progress. Behind every statistic is a family trying to make a living; behind every breakdown are years of breeding, investment and hard work. I don't believe farmers expect miracles, they know that this is one of the most difficult animal health challenges we face, but they do expect leadership, especially when the Minister talked such a good game in opposition.

With all due respect—and I say this as constructively as possible—does the Minister want his legacy in Government to be that of a doer, or does he want to be remembered as a talker or a promiser? Talk is cheap, farmers are clear: they don't want hope, they want action. Diolch yn fawr.

speaker: Andrew Griffin AS
text:
As one of the Members for Gwynedd Maldwyn, I have the privilege of representing one of the largest and most rural constituencies in Wales, where agriculture is the backbone of our economy and our communities, and I'm therefore grateful to speak in support of this motion. Before today's debate, I wanted to hear not from officials or policy papers, but from people living with bovine TB every day. So, over the weekend, I met with farmers from across Montgomeryshire. What those farmers told me was not just about cattle—it was about the emotional, financial and human cost of living under the constant shadow of bovine TB.

According to the latest NFU statistics, in the year to December 2024, there were 500 new bovine TB herd incidents across Wales, and more than 10,000 cattle were slaughtered as part of TB control. They're not just statistics. They represent hundreds of farming businesses, and thousands of difficult conversations around kitchen tables across rural Wales. When we debate bovine TB, it is easy to become consumed by statistics, testing regimes and policy arguments. Those things matter, but we should never lose sight of the people living through the disease every single day.

The farmers I met were not asking for sympathy. They were asking for certainty. They were asking for leadership. Farmers from across the Tanat, Vyrnwy and Severn valleys described living with the constant worry that the next routine test could change everything. Some also told me they had reduced their cattle numbers or moved away from keeping cattle altogether, because they simply could not continue living with the uncertainty and risk of prolonged TB restrictions. That should concern every Member of this Senedd. If farmers are changing the very nature of their business because of the fear of bovine TB, then the impact of this disease extends far beyond the individual farm.

When TB is detected, beef farmers can no longer sell their cattle freely. Dairy farmers continue producing milk, but movement restrictions still disrupt their businesses and make it difficult to plan for the future. The impact, however, goes far beyond the balance sheet. Farmers can prepare for bad weather. They can prepare for difficult markets. What they cannot prepare for is the uncertainty of not knowing whether the next routine test will change everything. Every TB test brings back the same question, 'What if this one comes back positive?' That uncertainty affects mental well-being, family life and confidence in the future. It creates sleepless nights and constant anxiety over whether the business will withstand another breakdown.

One of the most difficult conversations I had was with a farmer who described the reality of having to slaughter a recently-calved cow on the farm because of bovine TB restrictions. That is something no livestock keeper ever wants to experience. It is a stark reminder that behind every policy and every statistic are real people making heartbreaking decisions about animals they have cared for every day.

The farmers also made another point that struck me: whilst vets and testers are rightly paid for carrying out the testing regime, farmers themselves receive nothing for the considerable time spent gathering the livestock, handling the cattle and dealing with the disruption. That time has a financial cost.

The effects don't stop at the farm gate, either. Agriculture sustains livestock markets, feed merchants, agriculture suppliers, contractors, hauliers, machinery dealers and many other rural businesses. When a farm suffers a prolonged TB breakdown, the effects ripple through the whole rural economy. Llywydd, if our shared objective is the eradication of bovine TB—and I believe that is something every Member in this Chamber shares—then we have a duty to ask a simple question: is the current approach delivering that objective? If not, we have a responsibility to examine every source of infection, and every scientifically validated control method available to us. Whatever recommendations are ultimately made by the TB technical advisory group, I believe the Welsh Government has a duty to consider them objectively, proportionately, and on the basis of the available evidence. That's not ideology; it's good policy.

Behind every herd restriction is a farming family carrying an enormous emotional and financial burden. Behind every positive test is another difficult conversation around the kitchen table. Behind every statistic is a farming family trying to plan for the future. Some are now questioning whether they continue keeping cattle, and that should concern every one of us. Because, if cattle leave our farms, the effects are felt throughout the wider rural economy. Our decisions today don't just affect cattle. They affect people, they affect families, they affect livelihoods, and they affect the future of our rural communities.

Llywydd, farmers can live with many challenges: bad weather, volatile markets and rising costs. What they cannot live with is indefinite uncertainty. They deserve confidence that Wales is serious about eradicating bovine TB and prepared to follow the evidence wherever it leads. For the sake of our farmers, their families, and the generations that will follow, I urge Members across this Chamber to support this motion. Diolch.

speaker: Stephen Senior AS
text:
Thank you, Presiding Officer. Now, for some, this is handkerchiefs out time, because we need to talk about badgers and deer, both of which feature on the cuddly part of the animal spectrum, though I do notice that we have quite a few empty seats.

I looked at some of the data on this, and I have to say, initially, when I looked at England and Wales, the data looked remarkably similar, and I thought, what's the issue? But then I looked at Scotland, and Scotland's really, really interesting. And then I looked at the regions of England, and I looked at the regions of Wales, and a light came on. I could see myself directly what the problem was.

It's strange that some matters have become bizarrely and wrongly a matter of left and right, for example, bin collections and speed limits. For some reason, badgers fall into that category. It shouldn't be the case. Those in this Chamber who are perhaps vegans have a perfectly valid argument to deploy: there should be no cattle in the countryside, as they exist only for our benefit as consumers. No cattle, no badger problem. But for those of us who enjoy dairy products and meat and use leather, we know that there is a trade-off between our wishes and wildlife. The countryside that gives us a delight to be in is rarely natural. It has been created by our farmers over hundreds of years. They do a remarkable job, and we should listen to them.

In a perfect world, we'd have a reliable test for bovine TB. We'd have a proven vaccination for bovine TB, which we'd use in cattle, relatively easily, and in wildlife, which is a bit more difficult to achieve. But we don't have any of that yet, so we have to deal with the situation as we find it. The facts are that in some parts of Wales bovine TB is explosive. It is true that cattle are more likely to catch it from other members of the herd, but it's also true that the first infected in the herd is likely to become infected from wildlife, and there's a clear link between the number of badgers and infection. Scotland is largely clear of bovine TB and has a very low badger population. There's evidence from England that culling badgers in those TB reservoir areas substantially reduces cases after four years.

Food security should be at the forefront of all our minds, not to mention the risk of losing rare bloodlines and losing farmers with extensive knowledge and skills in dairy and beef. We should be working with farmers and vets to ensure that all diseased animals are culled early, but no matter what your view or how you came to it, the fact remains that bovines and badgers cohabit. Much effort and paperwork goes into testing cattle pre and post movement. Unfortunately, somebody forgot to send the badgers the memorandum about not moving around. In the real world, strategic culling within these wildlife reservoirs has to form part of TB management, at least for now.

This is a Reform UK motion, but it's a motion to help Welsh farmers. It is an example how this expanded Senedd can work together for the good of Wales. Please support it.

speaker: James Evans AS
text:
Diolch, Lywydd. I'd like to declare a relevant interest: I have close family who keep cattle. I'd like to thank all Members for their contribution to the debate today, and anyone who is involved in the industry who is watching this and looking for change here, and all those Members who talked about the financial, emotional and human pressures that bovine TB places on our farming families across Wales.

Laura Anne Jones opened the debate saying we finally have a consensus in this Chamber that something needs to be changed. You raised the stress and anxiety that farmers face, but also the economic damage to the industry. But you also talked about the human cost, and the cost it has in lives in the industry as well. And you also highlighted the infected wildlife and that we need a step change here. As the Minister highlighted as well, the programme board has said we do need to have a step change here in Wales. You did also reinforce about previous Governments failing to address the disease, with numerous projects that really didn't get us anywhere, just got us in the mess that we're in now.

Vikki Howells, it was good that you recognised the pressures that the disease placed on farmers. You also say that cattle-to-cattle transmission is high. I don't dispute that, but they've got to get infected from somewhere in the first place, and that tends to be from the wildlife population. You also mentioned the number of incidents going down, but I'd just like to quietly remind you that the herd of cattle across Wales has dropped by 40 per cent, so there's naturally going to be a drop in the numbers of herds getting infected when fewer and fewer people across this country are keeping cattle, for a number of the reasons that Members highlighted today.

You also said that the TAG needed more science and we needed more science again, but we've heard that from previous Labour Governments for a number of years. They know what the science is, but then when they don't like the science advice they're given, they say we need more, and then we need more again. You can't keep asking for more science until you get the answer you want. If the answer is clear from a number of studies, something needs to be done about it.

Andrew Griffin raised the 500 new outbreaks and 10,000 cattle lost every year. That's already at breaking point. The critical numbers of cattle across the country are so low now, that's putting huge pressure on the wider system, like our abattoirs. Other Members talked about the economic elements of that, especially the jobs that we're seeing lost in some of the abattoirs across the country. It all feeds into the reason why people are not keeping more cattle, because of the human impact of this disease. Having continuous testing of cattle all the time puts huge stress on our farmers, but also puts huge stress on the animals, which makes them very dangerous when you're handling them all the time. That is why we're seeing a rise in people getting injured by cattle with continuous TB testing.

Elwyn Vaughan, thank you for your contribution. I know you've talked on this a number of times when we both sat in the chamber of Powys County Council together. You highlighted the mental impacts that this places on families, and also the work that the young farmers clubs are doing across the country, an organisation that really made me come here a lot of the time. You talked about the work that they're doing to support people with their mental health across the country. And I would just say to anybody watching this debate, if you are struggling with your mental health and well-being in the industry, there are a number of charities in the rural sphere who will step in and help you, because no-one should have to suffer alone.

Helen Jenner, you talked about farmers feeling that we need to move on. We've had these discussions, and I can tell you I've probably talked in this Chamber a number of times about TB, probably more than I've talked about anything else here. And we do need to have some movement. It's pleasing to hear that Plaid Cymru will be supporting this motion today from what I'm led to believe, and that is a positive step that we've got a majority now that wants to get on and do something about this. Our farming families have waited far too long, and the time for action is now.

Paul Davies, I'd like to thank you for all the work that you've done on this for 20 years, and I also recognise the impact this has had on your family. I know you've been a champion of this. I know your colleague who was here, Sam Kurtz, raised a project in Pembrokeshire around this and the work that they've done, but also the work that the previous Economy, Trade and Rural Affairs Committee did on this. There was another piece of evidence that I'd like to highlight to Vikki Howells. That was a cross-party report that came back that said we do need to take action in the wildlife. But I need to be clear: this isn't, as people talked about, a blanket cull of wildlife. This is a science-led approach, because anybody who knows anything about this subject will tell you that if you have non-infected badgers, the best thing to do with them is leave them well alone. Some people who've had badgers on their farms for a number of years have never had instances of TB. This is a targeted approach where you can go in and remove infected wildlife. I know other Members talked about a vaccine, but the problem we have with a vaccine is that when you have the testing done, they cannot actually distinguish which animals have been vaccinated and which animals have not. So, the vaccine is not quite there yet, but thanks, Paul, for all that you've done on this.

Stephen Senior, I agree with everything you said about farmers shaping our environment and how they need to be supported, but also the bureaucratic elements that come with TB—the paperwork that comes with it, with case vets and all the people who come around you all time; it's an absolute nuisance and it puts a lot of stress on our farmers.

Thank you, Anna Nicholl, for your powerful contribution, highlighting the Ffermio documentary. I can remember in the previous Senedd when that was highlighted. I don't think anybody across this Chamber could not be moved by what was said on there and the cow that was culled on there that had a calf inside her as well. A lot of people were moved by that. I actually thought the previous Government would move on that. They moved a little bit on policy on it, but it didn't have a huge step change, which we all hoped it would.

Paul Rock, I respect your right to an opinion about infection rates, but I'd like to say what I said earlier, that, actually, the herd rate has gone down by 40 per cent here in Wales, so there's going to be less infections.

We do need action now and I think we need to have a clear steer in this Chamber for the Minister that, if the technical advisory group comes out and says we need to have a targeted intervention in wildlife, the Minister's got a clear steer that the majority of this Chamber want to move that way and not have more posturing and debates to stall the issue. We need to move on.

And, finally, to the Cabinet Secretary—. I think I'm doing all right for time. And, finally, to the Cabinet Minister, I should say, not the Cabinet Secretary—thank you for your response. It's actually very refreshing to hear a Minister sat in that chair actually saying that we need to get on and sort this issue and not defending a failed policy for the last 20-odd years. Because I do agree with you on biosecurity, that this isn't just a one-size-fits-all, and no outbreak is the same. So, we need to make sure we're addressing the biosecurity. Working with vets—I think that's very important—to understand your individual circumstances and put that right, and, hopefully, the Welsh Government, when looking at grants—. They did an awful lot of work, actually, about raising feeders so that people aren't feeding on the floor, making sure that stalls are covered, to make sure we can get this disease under control.

But I would just like to say to the Minister, one thing that probably hasn't been mentioned is about case vets—something that you probably have had raised, and me—making sure there is that consistency with case vets when they are going out on farms, because there's nothing more frustrating for people if they have different vets all the time, and that does cause a lot of anxiety in the industry.

I'd like to thank all Members, and I'm testing the Llywydd's patience, because it's gone red and people want to go home, but I will say 'thank you' to all Members who have contributed today. There is a differing opinion, but I think there is a majority in this Chamber now that wants us to move on this issue. So, I'd just like to thank all Members today. Let's get the step change we need, let's support those farmers and let's get this disease, finally, once and for all, under control. I advise all Members to support the motion.

speaker: Nigel Williams AS
text:
No-one in this Chamber should be indifferent to litter, and we've heard that already. No-one wants plastic bottles and cans on our beaches, in our rivers—I spoke about this when I talked in the rivers debate—in our parks or alongside our roads. Wales can be rightly proud of its environmental record, absolutely, but good intentions do not automatically make good policy, and we should be aware of that today. The test of this deposit-return scheme is not whether recycling matters—of course it does—the real question is whether Ministers are proposing a solution to a genuine problem, or whether they are trying to fix something that is already working remarkably well, particularly with regard to glass.

Llywydd, I have increasingly come to the conclusion that, on glass, the proposal risks moving from sensible recycling into, as Laura Anne Jones mentioned, 'recycling madness'. I actually find it quite amusing that some people speak as if recycling is a modern phenomenon. I grew up in a society where reuse and recycling were simply a part of everyday life. My parents and grandparents belonged to the 'make do and mend' generation. They encouraged the same in me. If something broke, you repaired it; if something could be reused, you reused it. Nothing was thrown away unnecessarily and, as a child, a part of that was actually taking bottles back and getting thruppence, which you'd spend on sweets and things like that, and we did it every week. You took the bottles back to the shop for those few pennies. There was no blue bin in the yard at that stage, so you took things back. Nowadays, there is a blue bin in the yard we can throw glass into.

So, I'm not opposed to the principle of deposit-return schemes, because I grew up with one. I understood the logic behind them. Indeed, I believed in deposit-return schemes long before they actually became fashionable. But life has also taught me something else. A deposit-return scheme only makes sense when it improves upon what already exists, and the Government proposal does not improve upon that. That brings us to the fundamental question before us today: what problem are Ministers actually trying to solve here? Indeed, Wales already, as we've heard, recycles around 92 per cent of household glass through existing collection systems. That's an extraordinary achievement, and we're not underperforming in Wales. We are not the laggards of Europe. We are amongst the best performers anywhere in the world, as other speakers here have said.

So, let's be honest about what is being proposed. This is not a debate about moving from failure to success. It is a debate about imposing significant costs and disruption on Welsh businesses and Welsh consumers in pursuit of what may amount to little more than a marginal improvement. That is the point at which sensible recycling, as I've mentioned, risks becoming recycling madness. Now, don't take my word for it. Yesterday, I met with representatives from the food and drinks industry, and this is what they told me: 'Why should we be expected to work harder, comply with more regulation, absorb more costs and take more risks for no profit at all?' These are not multinational corporations, they're Welsh businesses, Welsh breweries, Welsh food and drink producers, people who employ local workers and invest in local communities.

So, what's the potential answer? Welsh consumers could still pay a 20p deposit on containers sold in Wales, despite there being no practical system through which the money could be reclaimed. Llywydd, that would not feel like an environmental policy to many people; it would feel like a tax on Welsh consumers. So, I ask again: what is the problem that Ministers are actually trying to solve here? If reuse is truly the future, then pilot it, test it, prove it, gather the evidence, but do not place additional burdens on Welsh producers before the evidence exists. Environmental policy must be guided by common sense. There's a difference between environmental responsibility and environmental overreach, there's a difference between solving problems and creating new ones, and there's a difference between sensible recycling and recycling madness. So, we should build on the success we've already got, we should improve on what works, but we should not burden Welsh businesses and Welsh consumers with disproportionate costs in pursuit of marginal gains.

When a country already recycles 92 per cent of its household glass, spending millions to chase the final few percentages—1 per cent, actually, so I believe—is not environmental leadership, it is taking a success story, fixing what is not broken and turning sense into nonsense. That's why I can't support the proposal by the Government, and I actually support the motion. Diolch yn fawr.

speaker: Laura Anne Jones AC
text:
Diolch, Deputy Presiding Officer. We do indeed have a lot to be proud of here in Wales, don't we? Credit where credit’s due: in terms of recycling, we are absolutely brilliant and world leaders, and kerbside particularly. And if our system to recycle glass ain't broke, why are we fixing it? Reform are not opposed to a deposit-return scheme, but we do argue whether it's actually necessary to do something different for the sake of it. We support practical measures to reduce litter, to improve recycling and protect our environment. We are in sole support of this motion today, and we are opposed to the Welsh Government's decision to create a system separate from the United Kingdom.

This is where the scheme goes from a sensible idea to bureaucratic eco-madness. We are standing on the edge of yet another economic disaster cooked up right here in the Cardiff Bay bubble. The Plaid Cymru minority Government, backed by the leftovers of left Labour's failed policies, is about to push through a scheme so detached from reality that it would be funny if it wasn't dangerous. Now on paper, it sounds lovely, doesn't it? We're going to help the environment. But let's look at the reality. Under their plan, when you buy a drink, you pay a mandatory deposit, and you only get it back if you drag your empty bottles and cans back to the shop. But here's the kicker, the absolute madness that perfectly sums up this establishment in Cardiff Bay: they have insisted on including glass in the Welsh scheme, completely isolating Wales from England, Scotland and Northern Ireland. Think about what that actually means. England, Scotland and Northern Ireland will operate one broadly aligned system, whilst Wales insists on going its own way. This is classic Plaid-Labour politics, making Wales different simply for the sake of being different. People will be buying drinks in Hereford, Chester, Bristol and bringing them back to Wales, whilst businesses will be expected to understand and administer different rules depending on which side of the border they happen to stand on.

The industry itself has warned that this ideological stubbornness opens up a massive risk of cross-border fraud, with the British Soft Drinks Association warning of a potential £300 million fraud risk because our politicians wanted to look virtuous instead of being practical. It is an open invitation for exploitation. And who pays for this? The hard-working people of Wales, who are already battling a brutal cost-of-living crisis. The British Soft Drinks Association has explicitly warned that forcing glass into the scheme could add up to 50p to the cost of a single bottle of drink—50p on one single bottle. Executives from Tesco, Sainsbury's and Coca-Cola have written to the First Minister, warning that this scheme could cause higher prices and a severe reduction in consumer choice. Major brands are already looking at Wales and saying it's not worth the hassle. They are not going to print separate, expensive Wales-only labels just to satisfy Cardiff Bay. Our supermarkets will have emptier shelves and our Welsh families will have emptier wallets. It is terrible news for our economy.

What about our independent retailers? Our shopkeepers are expected to become waste disposal sites. Wine merchants on the border have already said they are deeply concerned about expanding or investing in Wales because the red tape involved in keeping separate Welsh and English stock is completely unaffordable. Cardiff Bay is punishing the very people who keep the Welsh economy alive. And for what? What is the environmental grand prize here? Wales already has, as I've said, world-class kerbside recycling—credit where it's due. Our communities already recycle over 90 per cent of their glass through normal household collections. The system works. But instead of leaving it alone, this Government wants to dismantle a working system. It wants to force elderly residents, busy parents, those who are disabled to load heavy glass into their cars and drive to a supermarket machine just to get their own money back. This does not reduce carbon emissions. It increases them. Think of all those unnecessary and increased car journeys. It's classic Plaid virtue signalling in its most arrogant and absurd way.

Deputy Presiding Officer, the whole roll-out is a complete and utter mess. With less than 15 months until the October 2027 deadline, the Government has not successfully appointed an administrator even to run this scheme. It rejected the only realistic industry applicant because it was blinded by its own dogma. The rest of the UK is using Exchange for Change, but the Plaid Welsh Government rejected it. [Interruption.]

speaker: Laura Anne Jones AC
text: The Minister just outlined that that is factually incorrect, and I will take that, then. [Interruption.]

speaker: Laura Anne Jones AC
text:
Yes, and you'll explain that. That's great.

If Wales has no compatible scheme in place when the rest of the UK launches, Welsh consumers could be charged a 20p deposit with no easy way to reclaim it unless they cross the border into England. That would turn a refundable deposit into an effective 20p drinks tax on the people of Wales. It is walking straight into the same catastrophic collapse we saw when Scotland tried and failed with this.

Let me clear on Reform's position: we are not against a deposit-return scheme; we are against a separate glass-heavy scheme that creates higher cost, greater bureaucracy and needless divergence from the rest of the United Kingdom. A UK-wide scheme for cans and plastic bottles is one thing, but dragging glass into it, despite warnings, is just silly. We need to unshackle Welsh business from excessive over-regulation. We need to stop treating Welsh consumers like cash cows and ideological experiments. It's time to throw this broken glass policy in the bin where it belongs, align with the rest of the UK, and start focusing on policies that actually grow our economy, lower people's bills and support local business. We will be supporting the Conservative motion today. Diolch.

speaker: Sarah Pochin
section: Waste Management Sites — [Dr Andrew Murrison in the Chair]
text:
It is a pleasure to serve under your chairmanship, Dr Murrison. I congratulate the hon. Member for Blackpool North and Fleetwood (Lorraine Beavers) on securing the debate.

It is so important that I speak on this issue, as in my constituency we have an incinerator operated by a company called Viridor, which has been in operation for the last 12 years. Like the example in Fleetwood, it processes waste from all around the country, very little of which is produced by the actual residents of Runcorn. Local residents have to live with the problems that hon. Members have talked about this afternoon, including dreadful smells at times and rubbish strewn around the approaching roads from the heavy goods vehicles that deliver the waste. There is noise 24 hours a day—the HGVs have an operational licence for 24 hours a day, and there is the mechanical noise from the plant itself. Every day, 275 HGVs are allowed to go in and out of the plant. I have stood there, endlessly watching one after another. The noise and smell are horrific, with 3,000 tonnes of waste processed in the plant every day. The air pollution at times is a disgrace. As we have heard, people cannot hang out their washing. There are even layers of dust on cars. There is a physical and mental effect on health. Local residents cannot sleep or open their windows. Light pollution from the headlights of HGVs coming down the road is constant through the night, which is worse in winter, of course.

As a consequence, local house prices are severely devalued. Why should residents have to move, when some have lived there all their lives? Now, even if they wanted to move, they cannot sell their homes because of the incinerator and they feel trapped. On that note, I ask the Minister to consider offering financial support to those families who are unable to move because they cannot sell their homes due to the proximity of incinerators such as the one in Runcorn.

To return to the operator, in December 2023, Viridor paid out £1 million across 180 local households to keep them quiet. They signed a non-disclosure agreement so they could never talk to the press about the conditions they live in. That £4,500 per household is a lot of money for some of my residents, and would have been especially welcome at Christmas. It was meant to keep them quiet and it is a disgrace.

I would like to echo the points made about the Environment Agency. It should be timely in its response; it is no good residents ringing and the Environment Agency coming out a week later, when the smog or smell has gone. There are now also issues with vermin such as rats and flies, and concerns about diseases spread by birds flying in and out of operating doors left open. Those doors are meant to shut between each delivery but are left open for birds to fly in and out, potentially spreading disease.

The burden of proof is always on the residents to clock and document all this. Why should it be that way? I again ask the Minister to shift the burden of proof from the residents and give the Environment Agency the power to shut down the operation until the complaint or issue is sorted. It is often not just one major incident, such as a fire—it is a continual build-up, wearing down residents until they are desperate. They feel forgotten and unheard.

Deprived towns such as Runcorn have been used as a dumping ground for the nation’s rubbish. The least the Government can do is listen to residents, let their voices be heard and compensate them for what is happening to their day-to-day lives.
