text: Thank you. Business Manager, can I ask for a statement from the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning on how local government's funding supports the third sector and charitable organisations? The Welsh Local Government Association estimates budget pressures of £560 million for 2026-27, but this year local government's settlement only increases councils' core funding by £292 million. When budgets are tight, grants and contracts with local charities and voluntary groups are often among the first to be cut. Yet these organisations provide early support to vulnerable people, and can help ease the demand on statutory services. So, can we have a statement on how the Government is working with councils to protect funding for the third sector, and whether assessments have been made of the impact of funding pressures on voluntary organisations? And can I say that I've got to declare an interest because I've got family working in both sectors?

speaker: Benjamin Hodge Mckenna AS
debate: 4. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care: Review of the Escalation and Intervention Framework
text: Thank you, Cabinet Minister, for giving us advance sight of the statement.

speaker: Benjamin Hodge Mckenna AS
debate: 4. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care: Review of the Escalation and Intervention Framework
text:
I'm glad that we are talking about the escalation framework today, because it's clear to me that the current framework is, frankly, ineffective. Health boards across Wales are sitting in level 4 for certain parts of their domains, or indeed, in the case of Betsi Cadwaladr, level 5, and meanwhile waiting lists continue to go up across the country and patients are not seeing the improvements that they deserve.

There are things in the statement today and within the review, however, that I do agree with. I fundamentally agree with the outcomes for patients being put at the centre of this review, and alongside the outcomes for patients, the addition of the workforce as one of the key pillars within this framework, as I think one thing that is mentioned less than it should be is that the performance of the NHS is not just letting down the patients who depend on it, but it's also letting down those front-line staff who often have to bear the brunt of the frustrations of people interacting with the system.

I also agree that proactivity in intervention should be the objective. We should be ensuring that these health boards are held to a higher quality of standard before the issues arise, and not be seeking to administer remedial action after the issues have already arisen.

One thing that is also mentioned in your statement that I do agree with is the importance of leadership and governance in determining the success of organisational capacity, alongside strengthening accountability for leadership within our health organisations. We at Reform were clear that those who operate our health boards should be held accountable for the performance within them, and we would have considered, if necessary, amending the National Health Service (Wales) Act 2006 to ensure that ministerial authority can be held over these health boards, and if necessary, link pay to performance when it comes to some of these health board bosses who are earning large salaries but failing to deliver for our people.

It's obviously up to Ministers to make the important decisions, and that's something that's outlined in this new framework, but when I was reading through it earlier, there were a couple of occasions where it seemed to me that lines were blurred between Welsh Government taking meetings and providing information versus Ministers. So, I'd like to ask for clarity in terms of where the line drawn is with this new framework. Where will civil servants or other members working for the Government be taking meetings with health boards, and when will meetings be taken by you or your Deputy Ministers?

I'd also like to ask how the lessons learned from intervening with these health boards are being learned and how they will be applied across other health boards in Wales, so that we don't have to keep coming back and deal with the same interventions time and time again.

Another thing that's mentioned in the new framework today is escalation boards. So, once these health boards are put into level 3 or above, escalation board meetings can be held. But there was detail lacking, from what I could read, in terms of how frequent these escalation board meetings will be, what will be discussed within them, and who will be doing the discussing and the decision making within those meetings.

Criteria were also given in terms of de-escalation within the framework, but in terms of the criteria that I read, these were illustrative criteria. So, I'd like to ask: how will the final criteria be determined? I assume they'll be on a case-by-case basis. And who will be determining the criteria both for escalation and de-escalation through the new framework?

Finally, it's mentioned that, in level 5, there will be consideration given to changes of governance within health boards and, at level 4, that there will be leadership and organisational assessments that will be conducted with regard to the leadership of these health boards. So, I would like to ask: how will these assessments be conducted? Who will be reviewed, and on what criteria will they be reviewed by? If, as is the case for many of our health boards across the country, a health board has been sat in level 4 or, indeed, level 5 for an extended period of time, at what point will the Government intervene and pursue organisational changes within the health boards, to ensure that those who are failing to deliver for our patients in Wales are held to account? Diolch yn fawr.

speaker: Louise Emery AS
debate: 4. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care: Review of the Escalation and Intervention Framework
text:
I thank you, Minister, for your statement, and, genuinely, I hope this does work, for all of my constituents in Clwyd, but also for myself and my family. Certainly, with Betsi Cadwaladr health board, you never quite know when you're going there what's going to happen, and we've had some horror stories over the last 12 months, particularly.

But I just wanted to focus on this idea of health boards setting their own criteria and the assessments being made by stakeholders. I'm just a bit concerned about that, because, obviously, there's senior management in place right now, and chief executives in place right now, who are overseeing health boards that really aren't doing a good enough job. And you're sort of asking them to mark their own homework. I'd hope they would be very nervous about this framework coming in and they'd need to pull their socks up. Because this is about leadership and culture. So, that's down to human beings inside organisations just not doing a good enough job, and trying to change that culture has to be carrot and stick. So, I'm slightly concerned about them setting their own criteria, so a little bit more about that, please.

And then, in terms of making the public aware of what we're doing, it's a pretty dry document, isn't it? And it's trying to make sure that the public understand that all of us want to make sure the NHS is a much better-run organisation. How are we going to get that across to the public about these changes? And, particularly, I was interested that the accountability review may be held in public for health boards. So, tell us a little bit more about that, and about setting your own criteria. Diolch.

speaker: Francesca O'Brien AS
debate: 5. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning: The Revision of the National Development Framework and National Conversation
text:
Thank you to the Minister for her response this afternoon. Minister, Wales is not short of plans, it is short of homes, though, and this statement offers the people of Wales potentially four more years of plans. So, this really is just a plan for a plan.

The Minister has told us that this revision will cut costs, bureaucracy and duplication, and I certainly welcome that, Minister, but I've read your party's manifesto, and it points in a completely opposite direction. Plaid promised Welsh language impact assessments in the planning system. They've promised community ownership stakes in larger energy companies, a new Welsh water regulator and a review of second homes and holiday lets, not to mention a new climate and nature action plan. Some of these, though, Minister, are not mentioned in this statement. But every one of those is another piece of red tape, another stakeholder, more paperwork for local sites to wade through, and another reason for planners to say 'no'.

So, firstly, can the Minister tell this Chamber which of these new layers is she prepared to drop in the name of efficiency, which she wants? Because the numbers demand it. When 'Future Wales' was adopted, the Government said that Wales needed 7,400 homes a year. In 2024-25, we built under 5,000, and last year we built just over 5,000, still well below the levels pre-pandemic. Her own experts now say we need 8,700 a year. We in Reform said plainly during the election that Wales needs at least 10,000 additional homes just to catch up. So, I ask the Minister: will this framework finally contain a delivery figure for all tenures that this Senedd can hold her and the Government to account on? And we need to include all tenures because, as I mentioned before, Minister, 83 per cent of Welsh homes are owner-occupied or are private rented accommodation, yet this Government acts like the private sector is irrelevant. Almost every housing headline this Government produces is about social housing, about speeding up development for social housing or anything that ticks the box for net zero.

This country already has one of the largest housing stocks in Europe for social housing. So, in the framework, will the Minister rule out any two-tier systems for private and social, making sure that any cuts to red tape also apply to private developments, to help the majority who are private renters and mortgage holders, because, Minister, private developers deliver almost half of so-called affordable housing? Of course, the only way to have generally affordable housing is by making sure that market supply actually meets demand. The young couple saving up for a home, or a family renting privately, deserve a Government that is on their side too. Where is the ambition for people to want to own their own home?

Then there is drainage. Since 2019, any development in Wales of more than one home has needed a separate sustainable drainage system approval before a spade goes into the ground. England has never switched that regime on; drainage is handled through planning and expected on schemes of 10 houses or more. So, a small, local builder building two houses faces a second approval, a second fee and a second delay that his competitor over the border doesn't have.

So, as you launch a national conversation—perhaps Plaid are out of ideas—let me contribute to it with these ideas that Reform have already published. Put clear statutory time limits on planning decisions and put financial penalties on planning departments that fail to meet them. Limit repeat consultations, relax the rules so that farming families can build homes on their own land and, finally, commit that the new framework carries a burden test, which is what I've asked for previously.

None of this needs a conversation. Our planning system doesn't need another long review. We, on these benches, will back measures that get homes built faster. But if this revision simply adds Plaid's new layers on top of Labour's old ones, this whole process will cause more harm than good.

speaker: Tom Montgomery AS
debate: 5. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning: The Revision of the National Development Framework and National Conversation
text: Can I thank the Minister for bringing this statement forward? But, Members, this revision will include at least seven different reports, 10 different assessments, and is not expected to be completed until the winter of 2029, a matter of months before the next Senedd election and, possibly, a change of Government, who may then choose to start this process all over again. This timeline is symbolic of the planning system in Wales—broken, costly and painfully slow. For example, planning rules require councils to decide on applications within 91 days, but the average wait for a council in my constituency is 223 days. Minister, I often hear from businesses across Wales who point to costly and long waits linked to the planning process as a significant barrier to investment in Wales. Would it not be better to get a grip on the planning crisis at Welsh planning authorities before starting years of work on changing the national framework? We need action now, not a three-year wait. Thank you.

speaker: John Clark AS
debate: 5. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Local Government, Housing and Planning: The Revision of the National Development Framework and National Conversation
text:
Thank you, Deputy Llywydd. Minister, a conversation that closes in November and a framework that arrives in 2029 is not a plan for homes, jobs or high streets now. The current framework already tells north Wales where it sits—national growth in Wrexham and Deeside, while Bangor Conwy Môn is offered only managed coastal growth. If this revision merely re-badges that map, businesses along the A55 will see no change.

Will the Minister confirm three things: first, that the engagement in the north-west will be as serious as in Cardiff; second, that empty and broken high streets will not be treated as lower priority issues; and, thirdly, that this revision will treat Bangor, Caernarfon, Llandudno and Holyhead as more than a supporting act to Wrexham and Deeside and that we won't have to wait until 2029 for a confirmation of that? Conversations do matter, but towns across the north-west cannot wait for the next plan.

speaker: Catherine Cullen  AS
debate: 7. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Social Care, Mental Health and Women's Health: Improving Family-centred Neonatal Care in Wales: Progress Towards the Bliss Baby Charter
text:
I need to declare an interest: I have a close relative who's a hospital consultant.

I welcome the opportunity to respond to the Deputy Minister's statement today, and I acknowledge that the Minister, from previous speeches in the Chamber, values the sanctity of life and how important this is. And I want to begin by recognising the extraordinary work being carried out every day by neonatal doctors, nurses and support staff across Wales.

When a baby is born premature or seriously ill, parents find themselves in a world they never expected to enter. Instead of taking the precious baby home, they spend days, weeks, months beside an incubator. For those families, neonatal care is not simply another NHS service, it just becomes their entire world. This is why the principles behind the Bliss baby charter are so important. Family-centred care means recognising that parents are not visitors to their own babies, they are parents, and, wherever clinically possible, they should be supported to participate in baby's care and contact.

But we must make sure that today's statement represents measurable change for families rather than simply being another commitment. The Welsh Government announced funding for Bliss so that neonatal units across Wales could work towards bronze Bliss baby charter accreditation. So, my first set of questions: can you tell us exactly how many neonatal units in Wales have now achieved bronze accreditation? How many have yet to achieve it, and by what date does she expect every neonatal unit in Wales to have reached that standard? Moreover, why is it the case that out of the 14 accredited units throughout the UK, not one of top standard is located in Wales? These accredited centres elsewhere are rated gold and even platinum in some cases. For a Government that talks about ambition, where is the ambition for these little ones? Can the Minister pledge that at least one neonatal unit in Wales will become gold or above, and an accredited centre, within the term? Because families should not receive one standard of family-centred care in one part of Wales and a different standard elsewhere.

And there is another issue I believe we need to urgently address, and that is keeping families together. Bliss has highlighted the difficulties parents can face in staying overnight to be close to their sick or premature babies. Imagine giving birth, leaving the hospital without your baby, and having to travel back and fore, sometimes hundreds of miles every day, simply to be with them. And for families living significant distances from specialised neonatal care, that means travel costs, parking costs, food costs, loss of earnings and early maternity leave at precisely the moment when their sole concern should be their child. You mentioned family-centred neonatal care, but it can't simply mean telling parents they are partners in their baby's care. We have to make it practically possible for them to be there. You say in the statement you are listening and responding. So, my next question is: what specific action will the Welsh Government take to increase overnight accommodation for parents on neonatal units? And will the Deputy Minister commit to a clear national minimum standard so that, wherever possible, a parent is not forced to leave their sick and newborn child because there is nowhere for them to stay?

Finally, we need to talk about what parents experience emotionally. A neonatal admission is frightening and overwhelming. Parents need clear information. They need staff to listen to them and they need to understand what's happening to their baby and know how to participate in their care. And where they raise concerns, they need confidence that those concerns will be heard. Practices such as placing mothers on wards with mothers who've had their babies and not clearing corridors for bereaved parents have not changed since the 1960s. The Government’s recent introduction of Call for Concern into maternity and neonatal services is therefore welcome, but a system is only effective if families know it exists, staff understand it and parents genuinely feel able to use it.

And psychological support cannot be an optional extra. You said in the statement that care should be compassionate. Supporting the baby means supporting the family around that baby. So, does the Welsh Government have sufficient neonatal and psychological workforce capacity to deliver these family-centred standards consistently, and what support is being provided to units where staffing pressures are preventing progress? And will the Deputy Minister guarantee that every neonatal family in Wales has access to proper psychological support, no matter where they live, and explain how the Government will measure whether families themselves believe that the Bliss charter is actually improving the experience of neonatal care? Diolch.

speaker: Cristiana Emsley AS
debate: 7. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Social Care, Mental Health and Women's Health: Improving Family-centred Neonatal Care in Wales: Progress Towards the Bliss Baby Charter
text:
Deputy Minister, for most women, giving birth is supposed to be the moment when they finally hold and care for the baby they have carried for months. But, when a baby is born premature or is seriously unwell, that moment can instead mean an incubator, alarms, wires and the mother suddenly feeling that everyone else knows how to care for her baby better than she does. A mother should never feel like a visitor at her own baby's bedside.

So, I welcome the progress being made through the Bliss baby charter, because family-centred care must mean mothers and families being listened to, informed and genuinely involved in their baby's care, but Bliss themselves tell us that there are main areas of neonatal care and family support desperately needing attention. So, Deputy Minister, beyond accreditation and targets, how will you measure what really matters—whether mothers across neonatal units in Wales actually feel supported, involved and able to be a mother to their new baby?

speaker: Claire Archibald AS
debate: 7. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Social Care, Mental Health and Women's Health: Improving Family-centred Neonatal Care in Wales: Progress Towards the Bliss Baby Charter
text:
Thank you, Deputy Minister. I welcome the progress being made to the Bliss baby charter today, but I particularly want to highlight the challenges faced by families in rural Wales. You have said in your statement today that individual services should focus on the changes that make the greatest difference locally. Long before the current charter programme, the neonatal team at Glangwili Hospital recognised the challenges of rurality and lack of transport, and the financial pressures facing families travelling backwards and forwards for appointments. They responded by changing the way they worked, bringing specialist appointments together to make things easier for families. Where families couldn't get to the hospital because of rurality, transport or financial pressures, the neonatal team would go out and see them at home.

You mentioned earlier what happens after they leave, which I think is just as important. They bridge the gap between hospital and home—such things as the dietician, occupational therapy, physio, speech and language. All of these are really important afterwards. They actually went on to win the Bliss project of the year award, which I think is really good for such a rural hospital. Minister, almost £1,000 was invested in this national programme in 2025. As the programme is still in its early stages, how will you make sure that good practice, like that at Glangwili, is identified, shared and implemented across Wales, rather than simply focusing on whether units meet the charter standard? Diolch.

speaker: Claire Archibald AS
debate: 9. Short Debate: The importance of local services—Protecting the future of Withybush hospital
text:
And this brings me to something I feel very strongly about, which is social care. Because the pressures faced in Withybush do not stop at the door. We have the best doctors and nurses in the world, but if somebody is medically ready to leave that hospital and support isn't available in the community that person cannot simply go home. And while that person waits, a hospital bed remains occupied, another patient is waiting in A&E and an ambulance may be waiting outside, and the pressure moves backwards like a vicious circle. Health and social care cannot continue to operate as though they are separate worlds. We need health boards, councils, GPs, community nursing, care homes, domiciliary care and the third sector working around that patient as one joined-up system.

And we must include unpaid carers in that conversation, because, far too often, when we say that somebody can be cared for at home, there is a family member behind that sentence—a husband, a wife, a son, a daughter; someone who may suddenly find themselves providing hours of care every day. We cannot solve pressures on hospital beds by simply transferring that pressure onto families. If somebody is going home, care must be waiting for them, the family must know what is happening and unpaid carers must be properly supported. That isn't separate from protecting Withybush Hospital; it's part of protecting Withybush Hospital. Because the answer to pressure on hospital beds cannot simply be fewer hospital beds. We need to prevent unnecessary admissions to make sure they're ready to leave and can do safely.

I also want Withybush to have a stronger future in cancer care and palliative care. For someone living in Pembrokeshire, travelling for cancer treatment isn't necessarily an appointment of an hour or two. So, let's look at what we can deliver locally safely: diagnostics, follow-up care, cancer treatment where appropriate, GP premises, community facilities and, working properly with organisations such as Macmillan and our wider third sector, bring healthcare to people wherever we safely can instead of continually expecting sick people to travel long distances.

And that brings me to transport. You cannot have an honest conversation about centralising healthcare in rural Wales without talking about how people are actually going to get there. You cannot design healthcare for Pembrokeshire as though Pembrokeshire has the transport network of Cardiff. It doesn't. I am seeking discussions with Transport for Wales about improving connections involving Withybush and Carmarthenshire. But transport cannot be an afterthought. If you move healthcare, you must first show us how the patient is going to reach it.

And there is another issue that I believe we need to talk about more openly, and that is accountability. We often hear that these are decisions for the health board and, of course, health boards have a responsibility for planning and running local services, but responsibility cannot simply stop at the door of a health board. Health boards are accountable to the Welsh Ministers; Welsh Government oversees their performance and has powers to intervene when things go wrong. So, when communities are frightened about the future of their hospitals, I don't believe an elected Government can simply point towards a health board and say it is their decision. Health boards must be accountable for the decisions they make, but, ultimately, political accountability must sit with those of us who are elected.

As a member of the Health and Social Care Committee—. I'm really sorry, I've missed a page. But if patients cannot access the care they need, if services continue to deteriorate or if communities lose confidence in their local NHS, somebody democratically accountable has to answer for it. For me, ultimately, the buck stops here, in the Welsh Government.

And that brings me to money and workforce. We cannot keep putting more money into the same structures if patient outcomes and access do not improve. Administration is important. Hospitals cannot function without good administrative staff. But administration supports healthcare; front-line staff deliver it. So, when finances are under enormous pressure, we have to be brave enough to look at the structure itself. Are there unnecessary layers of management? Are roles being duplicated? Could services work differently? Could management structures be simplified? And could those savings be redirected towards the nurses, doctors, healthcare support workers, therapists, carers and other front-line professionals patients actually need? That isn't an attack on NHS managers; it's about making sure that as much of every pound as possible reaches patient care. And these concerns are not mine alone. Thousands of people have signed a Senedd petition raising concerns about healthcare provision at Withybush. The Petitions Committee has now agreed that those concerns deserve further scrutiny, including further engagement with the Health and Social Care Committee. A petition on its own will not decide the future of Withybush, but, when thousands of people take the time to put their names to one, we should pay attention. And I am paying attention. I have listened to the residents, I have spoken to the staff, I have visited Withybush, I have spoken directly with the health board, and, as a member of the Health and Social Care Committee, I will continue to scrutinise the decisions being made, because I don't want the story of Withybush to be one of managed decline.

I want us to protect what works, change what doesn't, specialise where clinical evidence generally shows we need to specialise, but localise wherever we safely can, keep emergency and urgent care strong, build on same-day emergency care and frailty, bring rehabilitation closer to home, strengthen cancer and palliative care, join healthcare and social care together, support our unpaid carers, and make transport part of healthcare planning, not an afterthought. And to the doctors, nurses, healthcare support workers, therapists, porters, cleaners, administrative staff, ambulance crews, and to everyone else working at Withybush Hospital, this debate is not an attack on you. It is quite the opposite. You are the people holding these services together. I used to be one of them, and you deserve to know that the hospital you work in has a future.

So, my message today is simple: Withybush cannot simply become a hospital where more and more patients are assessed and then sent somewhere else. The people of Pembrokeshire deserve safe, specialist care, but they also deserve local care. They deserve honesty. They deserve replacements to be ready before existing services disappear. Above all, they deserve something they have been asking for for far too long: a clear, credible, secure future for the hospital. Diolch, Lywydd.

speaker: Claire Archibald AS
debate: 9. Short Debate: The importance of local services—Protecting the future of Withybush hospital
text:
Diolch, Lywydd. Firstly, I'd like to thank my colleagues, Paul Marr, Cristiana Emsley, Anna Nicholl and Paul Davies for contributing their time today—one minute each, I believe. So, thank you very much.

I want to begin today by directly speaking to the people of Pembrokeshire who are genuinely worried about the future of Withybush Hospital. Because they are worried. They have watched services change, they have watched services move, and now they are asking one very simple question: what will be left at Withybush when we need it most? This question deserves an answer, because, when someone is seriously ill, when someone has a stroke, or when someone needs emergency surgery, minutes matter and, in rural Wales, distance matters too.

So, I want to be absolutely clear today: Withybush cannot simply become a place where patients are assessed before being sent somewhere else. It must retain meaningful emergency and urgent healthcare for people of Pembrokeshire. But I also want to be clear about something else. I do not believe that centralising all our services is the answer. Since becoming a Member of this Senedd, I have visited the health board on numerous occasions, I have spoken to doctors, nurses, consultants and other front-line staff, and those conversations have allowed me to see both sides of this argument.

If we cannot safely staff a specialist service, keeping a sign above a door saying that that service exists does not necessarily mean patients are receiving the best care. I understand that. But I also understand the parent frightened about how far away emergency care for their child might be, I understand the husband wondering how he will visit his wife if she is transferred miles away, and I understand the elderly person who doesn't drive and wonders how on earth they are supposed to get to an appointment.

Both sides of this debate matter, but what isn't acceptable is leaving patients, staff and entire communities in the dark about what their healthcare will look like in the future. Take stroke services, for instance. I want to make my position clear today—I am talking about Withybush. I am not calling in this debate for stroke rehabilitation provision at Bronglais to be removed. Bronglais serves another large rural population and its importance must be recognised individually. My concern today is what happens to patients in Pembrokeshire. The current preferred model will ultimately make Withybush a treat-and-transfer site for stroke, with a 24-hour specialist acute stroke unit at Glangwili Hospital. I understand the clinical argument for bringing specialist expertise together, but I also expect one very important commitment to be honoured. Withybush must not become a treat-and-transfer before that 24-hour specialist stroke unit provision at Glangwili is actually commissioned. Don't remove the existing service and then promise a replacement later: build it, staff it, make sure it works, then make the change. Because patients cannot be left in a gap between one service disappearing and another becoming operational. And even where specialist acute stroke treatment is concentrated, I want us to look seriously at what rehabilitation can be provided closer to home. Because rehabilitation can take weeks, sometimes months, and families matter during recovery. And we should bring people back closer to their communities as soon as it is clinically safe to do so.

The same concerns exist around emergency general surgery. Hywel Dda has decided that, under its future model, patients at Withybush requiring an emergency operation would be transferred to Glangwili. The health board itself has acknowledged that transfers could increase the likelihood of delays in treatment. So, I want to know how quickly will that patient be transferred? Will an ambulance be available? What happens when ambulances are already under enormous pressure? What happens at 2 o'clock in the morning? Emergency care has to work on the worst day, not just the best.

And then there are our children. Families in Pembrokeshire have already experienced the loss of 24-hour in-patient paediatric services at Withybush Hospital. For a parent with a seriously ill child, particularly late at night, Carmarthen can feel a very long way from home. But there is also something positive happening here. Hywel Dda have recently announced a £750,000 investment in a new, dedicated children's facility at Withybush, including a rapid-access clinic. I welcome that, because it demonstrates the very point I'm making today: just because the most specialist elements of care are being provided elsewhere does not mean everything has to follow. We can still build strong local services, and there are already examples at Withybush showing us what can be achieved. I visited the acute frailty unit, and I was enormously impressed by what I saw. Instead of automatically admitting frail and elderly patients into hospital, they can be assessed, treated and, where appropriate, supported back into their own homes or community services. That prevents unnecessary admissions, it helps protect hospital beds and, most importantly, it can provide better care for that patient. The same applies to same-day emergency care. GP and other healthcare professionals can refer patients into this service, where they can be assessed and treated without automatically going through A&E and being admitted. That is the sort of healthcare we should be expanding on.

speaker: Paul Marr AS
debate: 9. Short Debate: The importance of local services—Protecting the future of Withybush hospital
text:
Diolch, Lywydd. I thank Claire for bringing forward this important debate today, and thank you to all Members that have remained to hear it.

For older people living across Ceredigion Penfro, access to healthcare must not become a postcode lottery. At the last census, more than a quarter of Pembrokeshire residents were aged 65 or over. For someone who no longer drives, the distance can mean an expensive taxi fare, dependence on relatives, or maybe not even getting there at all. In an emergency, distance matters. Hywel Dda's 2023 travel survey recorded 38 minutes from Withybush to Glangwili, even with lights and sirens. Specialist care matters; so does reaching it safely. I support Claire's call to protect Withybush. Safe transfers, affordable transport and care closer to home must be built into any changes from the outset. Living in west Wales should never mean being left further from care, with our constituents financially victimised because of where they live. Diolch yn fawr.

speaker: Cristiana Emsley AS
debate: 9. Short Debate: The importance of local services—Protecting the future of Withybush hospital
text:
Thank you, Claire, for bringing forward this important debate. I know how close Withybush is to Claire's heart, but this is an issue that should unite every corner of this Chamber, because access to healthcare should never depend on where in Wales you live.

For people living in rural Wales, distance is not just an inconvenience. When you are frightened, in pain, in labour or facing a medical emergency, distance can become a clinical reality. A hospital like Withybush is therefore more than bricks and mortar; it is reassurance. It's the knowledge that, when something goes wrong, skilled professionals and essential care are within reach. And we must remember the staff too: the doctors, the nurses, the paramedics, the support teams, who understand these communities and have built their lives around serving them. People living in rural Wales should not have to accept poorer access to healthcare simply because of their postcode. We hear repeatedly about bringing care closer to home. Well, protecting viable local hospital services is precisely what 'closer to home' should mean. Withybush matters because rural communities matter, and access to timely, safe healthcare must never become the privilege of geography.

text: I hope you're more than considering it because it's absolutely completely unworkable, and you know that as well as I do. speaker: Laura Anne Jones AC
debate: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
section: Questions Without Notice from Party Spokespeople
text:
Diolch, Deputy Presiding Officer. Firstly, Minister, I want to say 'diolch' to you too for your recent announcements, finally injecting some common sense into Labour's ridiculously rigid nitrate vulnerable zones rules. It's of course welcome and long overdue, as are advance payments for the basic payment scheme and the sustainable farming scheme after such a difficult summer.

Lawfully, we are all, of course, aware that you have to bring down BPS payments, but it is in your power, Minister, as to how much. As I am, you must be aware that the majority of the 51 per cent remaining on the BPS are those small family farms that you claim to want to protect. Pushing ahead with this cut, with SFS remaining wholly unsuitable, inflexible and unworkable, is playing literally Russian roulette with their livelihoods. Minister, you need to make the SFS workable, and fast, and you need to put protections in place to help those that remain on the BPS. So, would you consider dropping the BPS by just 1 per cent, as opposed to the further 20 per cent, unless of course you do want to be the Minister responsible for the genuine end of family farms across Wales?

speaker: Laura Anne Jones AC
debate: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
section: Questions Without Notice from Party Spokespeople
text:
Well, you're putting family farms in Wales at risk, Minister, by saying that. I hope that you do recognise that, currently, on the SFS, people cannot get on it whether they want to or not.

I'd like to bring back to what Sarah Edwards, one of my colleagues, has just asked you in the Chamber. I, too, am aware of the extremely worrying circumstance that Green GEN Cymru surveyors appear to be arriving unannounced on farms to survey land, with huge machinery, and, not only that, they are not even adhering to their own biosecurity measures, with no checks in place to ensure that they are. This is genuinely concerning. This is not about whether you agree with windfarms or not, Minister. Most of these farms have had bovine TB or are at high risk of it. This is not a theoretical concern either; the High Court has already found Green GEN lacking in terms of their biosecurity measures. Without the right measures in place here, there is a real risk of disease like TB being spread farm to farm, and I'm not even mentioning the other environmental concerns that the people of the Towy valley have. Don't you agree with me, Minister, that we cannot have a situation where rural communities in west Wales have to spend hundreds of thousands of pounds to ask a court to help them to merely protect their own farms? Farmers need protection in place. They need support on this, Minister. Green GEN Cymru and contracted surveyors need to adhere to the rules to protect our farms. Will you work with the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy to ensure this happens, please, and perhaps even visit the Towy valley to meet with the communities there that are so concerned? Diolch.

speaker: Steven Rodaway AS

This links back to the Member's question, but I want to go a bit more local. The Welsh Water treatment works in Gowerton serves around 58,000 constituents across Gŵyr Abertawe. text: Diolch, Minister. Farming can be a lonely occupation. Long hours, financial pressures and geographical isolation can place enormous strain on farmers—and their families, of course. speaker: Gareth Beer AS
