speaker: Laura Anne Jones AC
text:
Diolch, Ddirprwy Lywydd. A wonderful old school friend of mine and a constituent, Matthew Cox, was diagnosed in 2025 with motor neurone disease, a cruel terminal illness that progressively takes away the ability to move, speak, swallow and breathe. Faced with that devastating diagnosis, Matt has chosen to turn that negative into a positive and devote his energy to helping others with MND now and in the future. Matt's warmth and generosity has always been extraordinary; now, so has his determination.

He has chosen to complete a number of marathons to help reach his goal of £100,000—which you can follow on his Instagram, @matthewjamescox—driven by his want to give money to the charities that have supported him after his diagnosis, that have helped him when he's felt so lost. This included the MND Connect helpline, which was literally, I believe, a lifeline for him and many others facing this cruel disease. He completed the London, Leeds, Welsh and, recently, the Great North Run marathons, where he doubled the distance he walked every time, which is an incredible accomplishment.

My plea to this Government, and to this whole Senedd, is to help ensure that support is there for every family facing this devastating disease. Matt, you're giving others hope, and I'm proud to call you my friend.

speaker: Andrew Griffin AS
debate: 5. Member Debate under Standing Order 11.21(iv): Contaminated land
text:
Can I begin by thanking Niamh, with Elwyn's support, for bringing this important issue to the Chamber today? Some of what I'm going to say may repeat some things that Niamh and Elwyn have said, but that's because they are important and need to be said more than once.

Wales has a proud industrial history. It has brought jobs and prosperity to communities across the country and made an enormous contribution to the development of modern Britain. But that history has also left us with problems, which, many decades later, we are still having to deal with. Old mines, quarries, chemical works and industrial sites simply did not operate to the environmental standards that we would expect today. And for some of the people I represent, that isn't just history. Close to the north-eastern border of my constituency, as mentioned by Elwyn, near Rhos, Cefn Mawr, Acrefair and Ruabon, is the former Monsanto chemical waste tip. This is not rumour or local folklore. Parliamentary records confirm that Monsanto chemicals were deposited there in 1964 and 1965—prior to my being born, just.

More than 60 years later, people are still asking questions about that site and the neighbouring acid tar lagoon. Wrexham council has investigated the sites extensively. Its position is that contaminants are present, but the sites do not meet the legal definition of contaminated land. It does, however, continue to inspect and monitor them. But I can understand why people living nearby remain concerned. If you live close to somewhere like this, you want straightforward answers. What is in the ground? Is it getting out? Is there any risk to my family or my home, and if there is a problem, who is going to do something about it? These seem perfectly reasonable questions to me, and 60 years is an awfully long time to be asking them.

There have been calls for people living near contaminated sites to be offered blood tests for PCBs. Public Health Wales has considered that, and its advice is that blood testing is not recommended. It cannot reliably tell somebody how or where they were exposed, or what the consequences for their health might be. We should listen to that advice. There's little point in offering people a test that may leave them with more questions rather than fewer.

But that makes investigating the land itself all the more important. We need to establish what is actually there, whether contaminants are escaping and whether they present a genuine risk. This is where councils need help. They have responsibilities for contaminated land, but investigating sites like these is complicated and expensive. I welcome the fact that capital funding has now been agreed, but Wrexham County Borough Council is already making the point that additional funding will be needed if councils are going to investigate potentially contaminated sites properly. I think we should listen to them. There is little use giving local authorities responsibility for dealing with these sites if we don't also give them the means to do the job.

Then, of course, comes, as Niamh has mentioned, the difficult question of who pays if something needs putting right. Where the original polluter can be identified and liability established, every reasonable effort should be made to recover the costs from them. But when something happened 50, 60 or even 100 years ago, that isn't always possible. Companies disappear, businesses change hands and records are lost. We cannot simply shrug our shoulders. The fact that pollution is old doesn't make it any less real. And it isn't reasonable to leave one council and its council tax payers facing an enormous bill simply because the original polluter can no longer be pursued. There is a balance to be struck here.

I don't want to frighten people unnecessarily. Public Health Wales makes clear that PCBs can come from a number of sources and that finding elevated levels in a particular place does not necessarily establish where someone has been exposed. What I do want is for people to have confidence that somebody is actually finding out. If a site is safe, tell them, give them reassurance. If there's a problem, tell them and then do something about it.

The people living near the former Monsanto tip have lived with questions about that site for long enough. There will be other communities across Wales in very much the same position. They deserve answers, they deserve a system capable of establishing the facts, and where action is needed, they deserve to know that the money and the determination are there to see it through. As their representatives, the least we can do is to make sure their questions are heard and keep asking them until they get a proper answer. Thank you.

speaker: Nigel Williams AS
debate: 5. Member Debate under Standing Order 11.21(iv): Contaminated land
text:
My thanks to Niamh for brining this motion forward. I speak in strong support of this motion, but, more importantly, to inject some practical, commonsense and local reality into a debate that goes straight to the heart of public health in Wales, and local accountability right across Wales too. I'd also like to thank Ken Skates for what he said about our area. As Ken knows, we live in one of the most heavily industrialised areas in north Wales, and it's got a huge historical legacy. I'll tell you about that in a moment.

What's buried under our soil doesn't simply disappear. Historic industrial pollution poses severe, as we've mentioned already, long-term risks to human health, animal welfare and our waterways, and the families living along those waterways too. My constituency, and that of Ken Skates and other people here within this Senedd, of Fflint Wrecsam goes right along the Dee estuary, and the industrial legacy is not an abstract concept there. And actually, dare I say it, it's not some inane lines in some academic briefing either. It's something we walk along and we see every day.

Let me tell you, I worked, years ago, as a beach guard, in a former life, as it were, a long time ago. I walked along the Dee estuary, along what's called the marsh there, from Flint castle all the way towards the steelworks. There was lots of industry along there. But one particular area used to be the site of Glanzstoff chemical works. Some people know about this. When I was a beach guard, I can remember walking there, and there were colours within the soil—there were pinks, oranges, awful alkalinity—which are there still to this day. So, if there's one thing I'd like to mention today, it's that that is a place they could look at, because you only have to take one dig with a shovel, and suddenly you've got bright colours. It looks fantastic, although it's covered in grass now, but underneath, it's a huge, awful legacy to the health of the people of the area. And worse still, it leaches straight into the river there, so that's awful.

The other thing I'd like to mention is if you cycle along the cycleway there—and Ken will probably tell you that, as well—at one stage there are pipes coming out of the ground where the old tip used to be. That's a real worry to those people in the area. So, I'd like to note this here today: make sure that people take that on board. And those are just two areas, to be honest. There's Courtaulds works that was there, there's the steelworks that was there. Lots of stuff has been dumped along that area. And places like this exist all over Wales.

A failure of national oversight is exactly what has been highlighted recently in the press and before the Welsh Affairs Committee, following investigations, as we've mentioned here today, by the BBC's Buried series. Analysis shows that, across Wales, there are tens of thousands of potentially contaminated sites and hundreds of areas that are classed as high risk. Yet the vast majority remain untested—as people have said—unmapped, and unmanaged. Hopefully, I've managed to map a couple of those places today. We can't continue with a postcode lottery where local councils and hard-pressed taxpayers are left holding the financial baby for historic industrial liabilities. Crucially, whilst we address the past, we must also stop creating tomorrow's contaminated land today. That's really important. That's why practical modern waste management and infrastructure is vital.

A couple of weeks ago, some of us visited the Enfinium Parc Adfer energy from waste facility on Deeside industrial park. Several people, I think, have been there, actually. There was a bit of historic apprehension to that facility because it was a bit concerning that it was regarded as an incinerator—'What would go into the skies?' We had no idea, really. But, having been there, the stewardship is absolutely fantastic, and stops, if you like, waste now being dumped into the environment, as we've seen in the past. I'd like to praise that company from here now. That's absolutely brilliant. That's what I would call practical environmentalism in action: dealing with unavoidable waste cleanly and domestically rather than burying liabilities or shipping waste overseas, which we've seen a lot of in recent times.

Turning directly to the motion before us, I fully endorse the core principles as set out: acknowledging the severe risks to human and animal health, recognising that liabilities fall unfairly on local communities, admitting the glaring absence of a clear national picture, addressing community uncertainty, and enforcing the vital polluter-pays principle so that the commercial polluters are made to pay wherever possible. But obviously, historically, that's not possible either.

I also acknowledge the work already undertaken by our local authorities and Natural Resources Wales under very difficult circumstances at times. Waste seems to be everywhere at times. Crucially, I support the calls to Government. Firstly, the Welsh Government must work with the UK Government to ensure polluters pay and introduce a dedicated ring-fenced funding mechanism to remediate historic sites where costs cannot be recovered from defunct operators.

Secondly, and most importantly, we must establish a comprehensive national framework for the testing and assessment of potentially contaminated land, prioritising those sites that pose the greatest risk, such as the areas I've just mentioned now, especially when they're leaching into our waterways, and provide real, tangible support to our local authorities so that they can finally fulfil their statutory responsibilities. We cannot leave local councils, our communities, and our taxpayers, more importantly, facing the costs and health hazards of pollution they did not cause—

speaker: Nigel Williams AS
debate: 5. Member Debate under Standing Order 11.21(iv): Contaminated land
text: Okay. Sorry. We need a clear national picture, systematic testing, dedicated funding and urgent action where the danger is greatest. Diolch yn fawr. Thank you very much.

speaker: Art Wright AS
debate: 5. Member Debate under Standing Order 11.21(iv): Contaminated land
text:
Good afternoon, all. My only contribution is to state that also in Casnewydd Islwyn, we have three of these sites. Monsanto itself, very famously, is the site within Newport that was creating much of this, but we also have Glebelands and the Severn river estuary. The Severn river estuary was, essentially, used as a point to just pump out tonnes and tonnes of toxic waste, which would have found its way all the way down the Bristol channel and out into the ocean—shameful, at best. But Glebelands, Glebelands is a site that's very close to where I live; I have a lot of friends that live around that site too. Lots of them played there as children, and now, as my colleague in front stated earlier, they are coming through with very rare forms of cancer.

It's really good that we've got consensus across the house, especially how much support is there. But one area I haven't heard yet that I think is quite critical for us to think of as well, is that, when we do start to look at where there are areas of blame and we can actually hold these people to account, these poor people that have suffered need compensation too. Diolch.

speaker: Jason O'Connell AS
debate: 6. Reform UK Debate: Default 20 mph speed limit
text:
Diolch, Lywydd. I move this motion, submitted in the name of my colleague Llŷr Powell.

Three years ago, Labour imposed the default 20 mph limit across Wales. They told motorists that it was necessary. They told communities it would make them safer and then, after fierce public backlash, they promised to listen. So, let's examine what listening actually meant. In Monmouthshire, residents identified 143 roads that they believed should return to 30 mph. Four were reassessed. How many changed? None. In Denbighshire, more than 300 submissions were received covering 202 roads. How many changed? None. Cardiff reviewed 192 roads, following 933 requests, and only four routes have returned to 30 mph. This is what Government calls progress in their amendment today. An empty reset, once again ignoring cries from the Welsh public, tinkering around the edges, as is becoming common with this Government, afraid to tackle the big issues head on.

This isn't just about frustration for motorists. This policy comes at a real cost for our economy. One billion extra minutes of travel time wasted every year; £38.3 million wasted to implement this policy; and up to £8.9 billion in an act of economic self-harm. That's the price of Plaid and Labour's 20 mph policy. But there's an even bigger issue: road safety.

The inescapable fact is that Welsh road deaths are rising. In 2025, 91 people were killed on Welsh roads. Each one of those is a tragedy. Plaid's argument today will say that, by opposing default limits, Reform want more deaths on our roads; that we want children to die. The transport Minister said the same in this Chamber last week on the record. Think about that for a second. Plaid would have you believe that the mothers and fathers on this side of the Chamber are pushing for the deaths of children, just so that they can claim a warped sense of superiority in a policy debate. That's a contemptible position to take. We should all expect better of each other in this place and I have absolutely no time for it.

So, let me be absolutely clear: we want our roads to be as safe as possible. Plaid blindly pursues 20 mph limits as a fix-all solution to road safety. But 20 mph limits will not stop a drink driver. They won't stop an uninsured driver. And they certainly won't redesign a dangerous junction or fix a collision black spot. Take the Raglan A40 bypass, named Wales's most dangerous junction. Despite years of collisions and a young man sadly losing his life just last year, the only outcome of that tragedy is that the speed limit has been dropped, leaving residents still waiting for real junction safety improvements.

After months in power, has Plaid sped up action on this? No, they haven't. And this is the type of single-minded approach that Reform is fighting against: the idea that lowering speed limits will fix everything, while Welsh families are grieving the loss of loved ones. Ninety-one people have lost their lives and Plaid has been focused instead on breaking up the United Kingdom, plotting with Sinn Féin and making us weaker as a result. They've been big on independence, but silent on road safety.

We all know where this Government's priorities lie, and it's not in improving road safety for our communities. We need a practical, forward-looking road safety strategy that tackles the real dangers on our roads, targeting dangerous junctions, improving road design, investing in safer crossings and road infrastructure, and above all, a strategy that listens and acts upon the local residents' concerns. Because the people who live on these roads know the dangers much better than anyone sitting in this Chamber today. We need a Government that listens and delivers real improvements, not one that hides behind slogans. I'm calling on this Senedd to back our motion today, end the war on motorists, scrap the 20 mph default limits, and let's get our country motoring again. Diolch.

speaker: Helen Jenner AS
debate: 6. Reform UK Debate: Default 20 mph speed limit
text: I welcome the opportunity to take part in this debate, and I thank my fellow Members for their contributions today. Our position on the 20 mph limit is clear. We stood on a pledge to scrap the default policy and to return to speed limits that are based on evidence. That remains our position. We make no apology for standing up for common sense and saving public money.

speaker: Helen Jenner AS
debate: 6. Reform UK Debate: Default 20 mph speed limit
text:
I want to concentrate my contribution on what the 20 mph default policy has actually meant for communities and councils across my constituency of Bangor Conwy Môn. When the default policy—the default policy—was first introduced, local authorities were required to make substantial changes across their road networks before many of those same roads were then reconsidered and, in some cases, changed back again. On Ynys Môn, nearly 700 road signs were replaced ahead of the introduction of the default limit. The council then had to revisit a number of roads, consider 25 proposals to restore 30 mph limits and ultimately approve 22 of them. Is it any wonder our electors get so frustrated when public money is wasted in this way?

Conwy Borough County Council has been through the same process. It received 702 representations relating to 149 streets or sections of road, before further roads were subsequently returned to 30 mph. Gwynedd also identified a significant number of locations where 30 mph was considered the more appropriate limit.

This tells us something very simple. The road network of north Wales cannot sensibly be governed by a one-size-fits-all assumption. Bangor Conwy Môn contains a city, large towns, villages, rural communities, schools, hospitals, residential estates and major connecting roads. A road through central Bangor is not necessarily performing the same function as a road through rural Ynys Môn or Dyffryn Conwy.

Yet the policy started from the assumption that 20 mph should be the norm and then forced councils to work backwards from there. It was nothing less than lazy politics. In 2024-25, the Welsh Government allocated £107,500 to Ynys Môn, £110,000 to Conwy and £20,000 to Gwynedd specifically for implementation of the 20 mph policy. Further funding followed in 2025-26, including £421,000 for Môn, £120,000 for Conwy and £54,000 for Gwynedd. Across those three authorities, that is £832,568 over two financial years. That does not capture all of the officer time involved in reviewing roads, consulting residents, preparing traffic regulation orders, dealing with objections, changing signage and then, in some cases, going back to roads that had only recently been altered. People are entitled to ask whether that was a good use of public money.

I want to be equally clear about what Reform is proposing, because there should be no attempt to misrepresent our position. We are not saying that every road should revert back to 30 mph. There are roads outside schools, hospitals and through residential communities where 20 mph will quite properly be the safest and most appropriate limit. What we reject is the default. The starting point should be the road itself, its location, its character, its collision history, the number of pedestrians using it, whether there is a school or hospital nearby, whether it is a residential street or an important route connecting rural communities. That is what an evidence-led system should look like, a commonsense system.

For many people across Bangor Conwy Môn, particularly in rural communities, the car is not a luxury, it is how people get to work, take their children to school, attend hospital appointments and access shops and essential services. Transport policy has to recognise that reality as well as the importance of road safety. The experience of the last three years has shown that councils are already having to make these judgments road by road. Reform believes they should have been allowed to make those judgments in the first place. Scrap the default, keep 20 mph where the evidence supports it, set limits according to the road and the community it serves. That is a far more sensible approach for Bangor Conwy Môn, for rural Wales and, we believe, for Wales as a whole. Diolch yn fawr.

speaker: David Mills AS
debate: 6. Reform UK Debate: Default 20 mph speed limit
text:
It's a pleasure to be able to speak in this debate today, tabled in the name of my friend Llŷr Powell, on scrapping one of the most hated pieces of legislation to come out of this Chamber in a decade. A policy cooked up by Labour and Plaid Cymru, not in response to public demand, not with solid evidential basis, but because it was a fashionable left-wing policy that was gathering steam elsewhere, and they didn't want to lose out on the trend. The same can be said about the tourism tax, and now plans for rent control—all disastrous policies stolen from other failing far-left governments.

Nobody in this Chamber wants to see people killed or seriously injured on Welsh roads, and I think anybody who says that is disgraceful. The question is whether making 20 mph the default across thousands of miles of roads is the right way to achieve the objective of decreasing road traffic collisions. Three years after the policy came into force, we now have more evidence to examine. As Jason said, 91 people were killed on Welsh roads in 2025, 9 per cent higher than 2024. More significantly, Department for Transport figures from last year show the highest number of deaths on Welsh roads since 2019.

I'm aware that the increase in deaths was not necessarily on 20 mph roads, but the aim of an overall reduction in road traffic deaths has not been achieved. There is also a great deal of confusion. I regularly get stuck behind people going at 20 mph on roads with 30 mph or 40 mph limits. The confusion, I think, contributes to accidents. I literally had somebody last weekend on a 60 mph road going 20 mph. I overtook him, he put his hand on his horn and beeped me. I pulled up and I said, 'Are you okay?' And he said, 'No. Do you know this is 20 mph?' And I said, 'Mate, it's not.' And then we made friends and he was from outside the area. You can argue the details, but it's undeniable that this policy has failed in its overall objective and it has come at enormous cost to the Welsh economy.

We also need an updated economic appraisal. We haven't had one since 2022, perhaps because the Welsh Government wouldn't like the results. But if they are confident in the policy, then let's see the data. Presiding Officer, this should never have been about ideology; it should have been about what actually works. If we want safer roads, let's target dangerous roads, improve road design and crack down on dangerous driving rather than imposing a blanket limit—[Interruption.]—across the entire country. I apologise—default. Let's end the anti-motorist agenda that punishes all road users. I urge all to vote with our motion to scrap this crazy failed scheme.

speaker: Carmelo Colasanto AS
debate: 6. Reform UK Debate: Default 20 mph speed limit
text:
Diolch, Lywydd. I'm going to cover a lot of ground that's already been covered, but there are two separate questions in this debate, and too often they're deliberately rolled into one. The first is whether 20 mph is right in some places. Well, of course it is; we're not going to argue with you over that. Outside schools, around hospitals, on clearly defined residential streets where the evidence justifies it, nobody on these benches disputes that lower speeds make collisions less severe. The second question is very different: should 20 mph be the default for restricted roads—I'm not going to use that term—across Wales, with communities left to argue their way back to 30 mph?

This is where Reform takes a different and pragmatic view. The focus should be on realising the data isn't conclusive—and it hasn't even been properly evaluated yet—and actually focus on that, rather than taking the credit for an initiative that was really poorly executed. Trying to take the credit for a small dip is like me taking credit for Italy winning the world cup in 1982 because I switched my tv on once. It's absolutely preposterous. It's delusional. For me, I'd like to give my own perspective on why we've seen this dip, and it has nothing to do with the B word. We're all getting e-mails, all of us, from constituents regarding speeding on specific roads, in parks at night. I have it in my ward with regard to the A484, which is a racetrack. I have it in North Dock in Llanelli, I have it in Llangennech in my ward. The most common factors, speaking to people and police officers for this behaviour and the change of behaviour, are as follows. Vehicles now have more safety measures than they ever did before—ever. There are fewer pedestrians around at night because they just don't go out because of the state of our roads. And these guys are speeding and driving at night. They do that because the police are spending less time patrolling in the evenings because of limited resources. So, there's another angle as to why you see that slight dip, and I think we're not looking at that.

There is a perception within people that lawlessness is acceptable, and the offenders that we should be focusing on take advantage of that. I'll give you an example of that perception. On 5 March 2026, I witnessed a car overtake me in Felinfoel in a 20 mph zone at approximately 60 mph. The car was going so fast that he actually had to swerve into oncoming traffic and narrowly missed a pedestrian by 1.5 ft to 2.5 ft. I phoned the police on 999 and was told to stay on the line whilst I followed the car in traffic. The registration number was given. Fifteen minutes later, I was told they couldn't do anything because he'd crossed into another force area. That was 5 March. To date, as of this morning, that person has not been visited and spoken to. This is a guy who almost killed someone. So, I would suggest that, actually, we're looking in the wrong place.

Now, Reform believes in far, far stronger enforcement of measures. Target the problem. Don't put a default in there. It's absolutely preposterous. So, back to the default. So, what currently decides whether you need your road to be a 20 mph zone? It isn't a school, hospital or a children's crossing. It's a lamppost because that's how we work our default out, by the space between the lights. So, if the street lights are close enough, it's 20 mph, and it's up to your community to prove otherwise, which is a nonsense.

Now, as I said, collisions on 20 mph and 30 mph roads are dipping slightly and every one of us should welcome that. But they were already falling for around 10 years. This isn't an overnight thing. The post-policy period is short and the Government's evaluation isn't even finished. So, I would say: publish the evaluation in full. Show us which roads actually produced a benefit, because if the gains have actually come from streets where 20 mph was always the default, then that's wrong, isn't it? That's an argument for targeting, not a national default.

Then there is consent: 469,571 people signed a petition to say they didn't want this—didn't want it. And we're accused of always talking Wales down, where it looks like they told you—500,000 people who didn't want it—and you talked them down. So, let's get our facts straight there. Transport for Wales's own monitoring sites in summer 2025 said that barely half of the vehicles are doing 24 mph or less. A default that half the drivers aren't keeping to has a credibility problem in itself. And when communities did push back, what happens? In Carmarthenshire, the council received 1,604 submissions from the general public. One hundred and fifty stretches of road were reviewed, and only 11 of those actually made it back to 30 mph.

Then there's the cost. The Government's own appraisal level predicted a net benefit. It estimated the cost of slower journeys at £6.35 billion over 30 years. And after counting every road safety, active travel and environmental benefit, its central estimate was still minus £4.5 billion.

Now to the Government. Plaid Cymru did not merely inherit this policy, you promised it and co-opted it. You promised it in your 2021 manifesto. You voted for it in 2022. Then, this May, you asked for a mandate to govern without a word about the default in your manifesto. At Reform, our manifesto is clear. Restore 30 mph as the default, keep 20 mph where it's generally needed outside schools and hospitals and on clearly defined residential streets, with a positive evidence-based case for each one. And invest in fixing dangerous junctions and collision black spots, instead of treating a change of signs as a road safety strategy and a cash cow that you can milk.

speaker: Llŷr Powell AS
debate: 6. Reform UK Debate: Default 20 mph speed limit
text:
Diolch, Lywydd. Well, those local authorities next year will be tested on that, if that's what the response was, because we'll be looking forward to taking this issue back out onto the doorstep and letting the people of Wales decide whether this was a good or bad policy.

This question here today was about, for us, honouring what was a manifesto commitment. We on these benches think it would be wrong to tell the public one thing and then stand up in this Chamber and say the complete opposite. A betrayal in trust of the electorate is an absolute disgrace, and we won't tolerate that. We are going to follow every manifesto commitment we did that put us in here. That's why we are discussing this.

The thing you failed to mention in your response there, Minister, was the people of Wales in this. You went through your figures, you spoke about those, but what about all those people who signed a petition to this place saying that it was wrong to do the roll-out, and 20 mph doesn't work for them? We've heard the figure is 469,571—15 per cent of the people of Wales decided to take their time to sign a Senedd petition to try to send a clear signal to this place, and the problem was there were deaf ears in this place that didn't want to listen. Well, guess what? The people of Wales then sent these people here to these benches, so you will have to listen. That's what we are. [Interruption.] We're going in. It's coming.

Now, an opinion poll by the BBC in March showed that 54 per cent of the people of Wales still oppose this policy, and I heard on the Labour benches quite a strange supporting of their policy there. Quite strange that, because all I've heard Ken Skates speak about in the last couple of weeks was how true devolution needs to come, that local authorities should be making decisions, but what you were supporting in this Chamber today was a top-down approach that didn't work. It shows that Labour want to talk the talk, but they won't walk the walk. They can't be trusted again—

speaker: Llŷr Powell AS
debate: 6. Reform UK Debate: Default 20 mph speed limit
text:
What? Oh, Minister, you've got more to say again now, have you? Is this the democracy of Plaid Cymru? Heckle from the front benches after having minutes of your own time. Trust me, I've got a lot to come to, Minister.

This decision today is important to how the electorate look at us. We've heard from Members, good Members, like Gwyn there. I always enjoy his contributions. I can't say I agree with everything Gwyn says. But you were right—the public have told you as well that they are frustrated with this policy.

When you came here today, Minister, I didn't expect you to agree with us, but I thought your tone could have been slightly different. Rather than insulting people that don't agree with this, how about listening to them? Because that there—

speaker: Carmelo Colasanto AS
debate: 6. Reform UK Debate: Default 20 mph speed limit
text:
Thank you. And have evidence-led limits that improve safety without strangling town centres and turning a daily commute into a daily irritation.

So, I ask the Deputy Minister for three things: publish the updated economic appraisal, give this Chamber firm dates for the evaluation, and commit to the Chamber today that if that comes back and it doesn't justify a national default, it goes. That's it—it goes.

speaker: Helen Jenner AS
debate: 6. Reform UK Debate: Default 20 mph speed limit
text: He's not scared of them.

speaker: Llŷr Powell AS
debate: 6. Reform UK Debate: Default 20 mph speed limit
text: Absolutely. I want to hear this one.

speaker: Llŷr Powell AS
debate: 6. Reform UK Debate: Default 20 mph speed limit
text:
Diolch, Lywydd. As I was saying, we heard also from the benches opposite about how some councils hadn't reversed the decision. Maybe, because of the state that Labour left councils in, with a lack of funds, they simply can't afford it. Some people don't want to put the burden on the taxpayer to undo your mistakes. That's the problem.

What we are talking about today are people's lives. Now, you say you're thinking of the children, but how about we think of, actually, the people out there? Minister, you say it adds a bit of time and it's not much impact. We can say that on these benches, but, for people out there, time is money when they're on the roads—actual people needing to get from one job to the next to pay their bills, to put food on the table. There is a real cost to this.

So, I think the remarks today—. Let's think of the bigger picture. I agree, road safety is an important issue, but there's a wider impact here. Even the last Welsh Government's assessment said that this policy could cost up to £4.5 billion in 30 years. That's a huge impact to the Welsh economy—jobs going, livelihoods. How about we think of them when we're here—people we represent? We in here, this Chamber, are servants to the people, not masters, where we get to ignore them. We don't get to turn our back when we don't like what the electorate are saying. It's important to listen, and that's why we are having what should be an important debate.

Now, you mentioned road safety to me earlier, Minister. We've addressed road safety. We've said that there are lots of things we could be doing and focusing our time on, where that money could have gone, from dangerous junctions to potholes galore. There is a lot out there that we could be spending time on, but, no, we have to be sitting here talking about this today, because a failed policy was rolled out.

And the fact that politicians don't accept it—. And I agree with you, Janet, in your intervention. There's a reason the Labour benches are so empty here today. Deaf ears should not be what the electorate get. And I do want to pay credit to you, Carmelo, for your contribution today; Jason, Helen, Janet, for yours, and Gwyn, I do always enjoy it, like I said, but I don't know what the mobile phone—. I don't know how I could possibly get into that; I think that's a debate for another time at the end. Spending more time outdoors, I do agree with you, but—. I always appreciate a Max Boyce quote as well in a contribution.

I urge Members today to vote on what they think their constituents would want. It's easy for some people to say, 'Oh, it doesn't have much of an impact; our lives aren't impacted by it.' My inbox and my colleagues' inboxes, and I'm sure yours, are of people who are impacted by a policy that does have bad consequences. As we have said, we are not in here today saying that we want 30 mph or higher outside schools or hospitals, what we are saying is that roads that were safe before should be back to 30 mph, and to roll that out to councils in the way that it is, so that they have to work backwards, not work forwards—. I'm afraid, Ken, you don't understand your own policies now in the sense of—

speaker: Llŷr Powell AS
debate: 6. Reform UK Debate: Default 20 mph speed limit
text: You didn't answer what I was addressing, your top-down approach, Ken. Let's get back to your true devolution. But, in terms of schools, I went through education under Labour Governments consecutively here. There wasn't 30 mph outside my school when I was younger. [Interruption.] That was your deal. There wasn't when you brought this bad legislation through, drove it through, ignored the wishes of the people of Wales, ignored them with their concerns, and then you as a Minister tried to unravel the chaos of what your party created. It's time to put your hands up and own it.

speaker: Llŷr Powell AS
debate: 6. Reform UK Debate: Default 20 mph speed limit
text:
Apologies, I did name him, so he came to respond, probably. I'm sure he wasn't looking to break any rules.

In closing, I urge Members today to support our motion in getting Wales moving again. Diolch yn fawr.

speaker: Llŷr Powell AS
debate: 6. Reform UK Debate: Default 20 mph speed limit
text: Oh, I—

speaker: Steven Rodaway AS
debate: 7. Welsh Conservatives Debate: The defence sector
text: This is the last sentence. Our ambition should be Welsh apprentices qualifying, Welsh factories securing orders and Welsh families building their futures here. This is the opportunity before us, this Government should be getting on and delivering it. Thank you.

speaker: Steven Rodaway AS
debate: 7. Welsh Conservatives Debate: The defence sector
text:
As a veteran myself, I have to say I am thankful to our defence industry, which allows us to operate in dangerous environments efficiently, effectively and safely. I have to say I'm somewhat baffled by some of the arguments I've heard on Plaid's side of the Chamber. It's bizarre. So, I want to support a motion that allows Wales to build more, make more and win more of the skilled work that helps keep this country safe. I want a young person leaving school to see a future in Welsh engineering. I want graduates to have the opportunity to remain in Wales, and I want Welsh businesses competing for defence contracts to believe they have a Government that is firmly behind them. There is nothing shameful about earning a living helping Britain to defend itself. Our engineers, our manufacturers and our apprentices deserve respect. Being proud of Wales should mean being ambitious for the people who work here.

Defence is reserved to the United Kingdom Government. The Senedd does not direct our armed forces or control the MOD's procurement programmes. But Welsh Ministers have a responsibility for education, training and business support. Those powers matter. Use them properly and we can help Welsh firms compete. Use them badly and we risk putting obstacles in their way. Reform's Welsh manifesto already commits to expanding high-quality technical education and apprenticeships and working with employers to match training to the needs of the Welsh economy. This is a commitment I want applied to the opportunities in defence. Bring defence employers and higher education closer together. Give school leavers a route into skilled work, graduates an opportunity to build their careers here, and experienced workers the chance to retrain.

On 20 February, the UK Government and Wales Office announced their intention to work collaboratively to establish a defence technical excellence college in Wales by September 2027. What's the location? Is it in Swansea? Please say it is. But wherever it is based, we need a clear delivery plan. What funding has been agreed? Is September 2027 still achievable? How will the college work with defence employers? When can students find out what they can study and how to apply? For somebody considering a career in defence, those are details that matter. They should be able to see a route from training into employment here in Wales.

The same practical approach is needed for smaller businesses. A Welsh firm with the skills to produce to a military specification should have a fair opportunity to win the work. There should be support to help it prepare a bid, help it to meet the security requirements, and help to put it in contact with the MOD and major defence contractors awarding work. Give them a clear pathway, then show us whether that support is helping Welsh businesses win contracts and take on staff. Reform would introduce a Welsh industrial strategy built around secure, affordable energy, as our manifesto commits. I want defence manufacturers and their suppliers included in that ambition, with opportunities to invest, expand and employ more people.

That brings me to the Government's proposed ethical framework. On 22 September the Minister said that, wherever legally and practically possible, the new Welsh Government investment support decisions for defence activity should not be finalised until the framework is published and its implementation considered. Existing contractual commitments remain unaffected. Discussions can continue. Decisions needed sooner can go to the First Minister. I have to agree with Darren Millar, as, I have to say, asking businesses to wait while the rules are being developed is the wrong signal to industry. Before committing to expansion and recruitment, employers need to understand the conditions attached to that support. Minister, a company deciding where to invest needs an answer. An order book cannot be organised around your consultation timetable. Set clear standards and, in doing so, explain what this approach will achieve and how you will prevent avoidable delays. Plaid talks about standing up for Wales. Here's the opportunity to demonstrate it. Give Welsh employers clarity and Welsh workers a fair chance of securing the next investment. A Reform Government would be fearless in its support for the Welsh defence industry.

We should equally be focused about the weapons and civilian harms. Some weapons are restricted in their use. Others are prohibited because of their effects. With weapon systems, how they are deployed and used matters enormously. The UK's export licensing criteria already address the risk of equipment being used to commit or facilitate serious violations of international humanitarian law. Welsh Ministers need to explain what their framework will add and why that benefit justifies any further bureaucracy, administration and expense. Delays could encourage businesses to invest elsewhere.

I can't say this framework hasn't already cost Welsh jobs. I can demand that Ministers assess the risk to investment and employment. Welsh workers deserve to know that their livelihoods are being properly considered. I want Wales to play a confident part in a strong United Kingdom, with skilled people making equipment we can rely on and businesses capable of competing for work. I want this motion to lead to apprenticeships someone can apply for, a contract a Welsh business can bid for and a stronger Welsh defence industry. Deliver the training, help firms win contracts and give investors clear answers—

speaker: Jason O'Connell AS
debate: 7. Welsh Conservatives Debate: The defence sector
text:
Reform heartily supports today's motion that's before us today. Wales has a proud defence tradition, and our aerospace and defence sector directly employs 16,000 people. The UK defence investment plan commits £298 billion over the next four years, with almost 60,000 industry jobs created. The investment is coming, the jobs are coming, the contracts are coming, and thank God we are part of our United Kingdom, so we can access these opportunities. The question for this Government is simple: how many of these opportunities are coming to Wales? Because Wales must not simply watch this investment happen elsewhere. We have to fight for our share of it.

I know personally what this industry can offer. I started my career with a three-year apprenticeship at the Ministry of Defence at St Athan. It was one of the best decisions I ever made. I earned while I learnt, I gained skills, experience, and it became the foundation of a 30-year career in aerospace and defence. I later joined General Dynamics, where I had technical teams that led the installation of complex communication systems in military platforms. And that's the power of what a good apprenticeship can do. It doesn't simply give somebody their first job, it can give them a career. It's a foundation for success, it can transform their prospects, and when we get it right, it can transform whole communities as well.

That's why Wales needs an ambitious defence industrial strategy. We have the workforce, we have world-class companies, we have universities, engineers, manufacturers, and the supply chains. What we need is a Government determined to bring those strengths together and compete relentlessly for investment. And that means stronger relationships with the MOD and industry, closer ties with decision makers in Westminster, not ideological division or the pursuit of independence. More apprenticeships, more technical skills, and fighting for every factory, every contract and every skilled job that Wales can secure.

Look at Merthyr Tydfil: General Dynamics has already demonstrated what high-quality defence manufacturing can bring to the heart of the Valleys. We're thrilled that Marshall Land Systems has seen the potential that Merthyr holds and is establishing its new facility there, employing hundreds, and that's exactly the sort of investment Wales should be pursuing. We should make sure that Welsh SMEs and supply chains benefit from this investment too. But this is where the Government needs to answer a very serious question. At the precise moment Britain is embarking upon one of the biggest periods of defence investment in generations, this Government is developing an additional bureaucratic Welsh ethical framework for defence investment—more unnecessary red tape.

Now, we are told, of course, that this will not create more barriers to defence investment, but this claim doesn't pass the commonsense sniff test. And here's the contradiction: this Government says Wales needs defence investment, they say they want the jobs. Yet instead of focusing on how Wales can attract that investment, Plaid wants to put an ethical defence framework at the centre of its approach to this crucial industry. We all want responsible investment, but Plaid's framework is an ideological purity test, putting political conditions ahead of jobs, growth and the economic opportunities Wales desperately needs.

And while this Government is busy putting barriers on defence investment, Russia's foreign Minister, Sergey Lavrov, is openly questioning the future of the United Kingdom, seeking to divide, weaken, disrupt, just as Plaid are trying to do for our union. Now let that sink in: a country that poses a direct threat to our national security sees the break-up of the United Kingdom as an opportunity. And yet Plaid is determined to pursue the very ambitions that Russia sees as being in its interests.

Now, this motion today should be a wake-up call for Plaid Cymru. Wales should be leading the way in strengthening Britain's defence, not undermining the very country that protects us. Plaid needs to stop putting ideology before our national interests and start putting Welsh workers first. Back this motion today, back our national defence, and let's get these defence jobs into Wales and back our communities. Diolch.

text: 1. What assessment has the First Minister made of the provision of public services in rural Wales? OQ64619

text: Thank you, First Minister. During the election campaign, I heard the same concern right across the Gwynedd Maldwyn constituency that rural mid Wales is too often overlooked. We're seeing schools close, continuing problems on the Cambrian line, in-patient beds closed at Tywyn, and potentially fewer community hospital beds provided in Powys. text: 2. Will the First Minister outline how the Welsh Government’s international offices deliver value for money for Welsh taxpayers? OQ64621

speaker: David Mills AS
text: International relations are not the remit of the Welsh Government. Coming from the world of farming and business before entering the Senedd, when I came here I was shocked at the waste—it really shocked me. And nothing symbolises that waste more than the 20 mini embassies that we've got. speaker: Helen Jenner AS
section: Questions Without Notice from the Party Leaders
text:

speaker: Helen Jenner AS
section: Questions Without Notice from the Party Leaders
text:
First Minister, it's clear to anybody with an ounce of common sense that the reason anybody can say anything negative about the post-Brexit era is because the people who were in charge of seeing it through didn't make the most of the opportunities they were given. And I would like to quote. [Interruption.] I would like to quote. He talks about our relationship with Europe—the greatest Briton that ever lived, Winston Churchill, once said:

'We are with Europe but not of it. We are linked, not combined. We are interested and associated, not absorbed.'

First Minister, at your conference you spoke about a new deal for Wales. Well, the public aren't daft. What we're actually getting is a raw deal. You're giving Wales a raw deal by failing to grow our economy. Unemployment is up, and not a week goes by without a negative story of businesses in Wales shutting up shop and cutting jobs. And the education sector is in such a dire state that teaching unions are threatening industrial action against this Government. What have you done to turn the dire situation around? Nothing. The prelude, not the actual question. First Minister, it's quite clear that, once again, your party is on the wrong side of history in failing to stand up for our vulnerable Jewish community.

Another example of Plaid being on the wrong side of history is Brexit. Wales voted decisively to leave the European Union, with almost twice as many people in Wales voting for Brexit than for Plaid Cymru in May. speaker: Cristiana Emsley AS
text: Prif Weinidog, last week your Deputy First Minister told me that childcare must be flexible for families and deliverable for providers. Yet, when I asked what this expanded offer will actually cost, she told me that the figures will only become clear in the forthcoming draft budget. But flexibility has a price tag. speaker: Cai Parry-Jones AS
text: 6. What are the Welsh Government's plans for addressing poverty in this Senedd term? OQ64674

speaker: Cai Parry-Jones AS
text: It's fascinating that your answer did not explicitly state whether you're talking about absolute poverty or relative poverty, and they are very different metrics. Absolute poverty focuses on the welfare of the poorest people in our society, something I want to see all Governments focus on. The other, relative poverty, is in reality a type of inequality, focused on the gap in wealth between people, and that can be a very dangerous metric. As Margaret Thatcher said, those who focus on inequality above absolute poverty would rather the poor were poorer so long as the rich were even less rich, reducing the gap. First Minister, do you accept there is an important difference in the two measures of poverty? To avoid confusion in future, will you and your Government, when referencing poverty, state clearly whether you're talking about absolute poverty or the socialist obsession that is inequality?

text:

debate: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution
section: Questions Without Notice from Party Spokespeople
text: Okay. Thank you for that one. Cabinet Minister, I would also like to know why does the Welsh Government keep creating more bureaucracy instead of reducing it. text:
Thank you, Deputy Presiding Officer. speaker: Louise Emery AS
debate: 4. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Transport: Strategic Priorities for the Menai Strait Crossings and M4 around Newport
text:
Oh dear, oh dear, oh dear, Minister. We were expecting a lot more on this side of the Chamber. But, anyway, we'll start north and then we'll travel south, if that's okay.

So, I'll start with the positives. Nice to see we're doing some baby steps with the current bridges that cross the Menai strait. Wind deflectors—let's get on with that as soon as we can, improve those; we've got a winter ahead of us. And varying the speed limit—we like varying the speed limit in this Chamber, don't we—I'll give you a positive on that one. But, in terms of the actual third bridge, it sounds like you're just thinking about a third bridge, which simply is not good enough. So, you're going to recommence development work and look at design development, environmental assessment, business case preparation. To me, it doesn't sound like you're completely committed to a third crossing, because I thought we'd done all this work before. I thought this was called the purple route and that that work had been done. And obviously what's disappointing to see, and this is why I question your commitment, is there's nothing in here about funding a third bridge. It's going to be an expensive project and is going to need cross-party support, and there's nothing in here about that. So, I want to ask you, and you can answer once I've finished, clearly: are you actually committed to building the third bridge across the Menai strait, 'yes' or 'no'?

Right, then, let's head down south. Now you need more thinking time—18 months of more thinking time—about solutions. And again, I thought we'd been here and gone through all of that with the M4 relief road and the black route. And in between the thinking time—which you clearly need, fair enough—for the next five years, you're going to do some improvements, which, personally, I think is just a sticking-plaster approach that ties in directly to Plaid Cymru's anti-motorist stance.

Let's talk about closing junctions. I do love the statistic about one in 10 cars not making it onto the M4. Of course they can't make it onto the M4, because they can't get onto the M4 because you've closed the junction. Closing junctions doesn't solve congestion and it's going to move that onto Newport's local roads. Newport City Council recently—July 2026—voted unanimously against any measure that diverts traffic onto Newport's already congested streets. I don't think they will be so delighted with your statement today. As we in Reform have said, stopping cars getting onto the motorway isn't a solution that Newport will thank you for. And in your own assessment, the cost of this is £14 million, and reducing traffic by a whopping 3 per cent.

Let's go over to the Heads of the Valleys plan. So, let me just get this right: ferries transport comes off the boats in Pembroke and then goes across east to Dover and on to Europe, and what you want to do is encourage, persuade, divert that freight traffic to go up over the Heads of the Valleys and back down again, and the cost of doing that is £49 million, which is some pretty swanky cafes and some nice rest facilities, and you think that will reduce the traffic on the M4 by 1 per cent. It's just not going to happen.

And then, finally, we get on to rail. Now, let's be clear: Reform supports more rail capacity, but rail should add choice, not be used to justify restricting road access. As Laura Anne Jones pointed out, the M4 users have no realistic alternative. We need to remind ourselves that, unlike us, there are a lot of people who aren't members of the lanyard class who go to work each day with a small briefcase. How are delivery drivers and tradespeople going to get on the train? 'Excuse me, ma'am, can you just move to one side while I put my 12 pots of paint and my toolbox there?' It's not going to happen.

Basically, Minister, I'm asking you to drop your ideology. What you've done here is pretend to be committed to fixing the road issues, but actually you're thinking about a bridge, you've got 18 months more of thinking about the M4, and you've got a five-year scheme, which, essentially, is going to cost millions of pounds and reduce traffic congestion by 4 per cent. So, here is the solution. On your last page of your statement, you say, 'We are developing a long-term roads-based and engineering solution.' Well, I'll tell you, we've got one: it's the M4 relief road, the black route. Reform UK have costed this at £2.8 billion. Yes, that's a lot of money, but I will guarantee here that, if there is a Reform Welsh Government, we will be lobbying and working with a Reform UK Westminster Government—which is coming, ladies and gentlemen—and we will build the M4 relief road. So, Minister, I want to confirm: are you committed to the bridge, completely and utterly committed? And please stop thinking and just get on with it. Diolch yn fawr.

speaker: Art Wright AS

Deputy Minister, much of what I'm going to say some people have already asked, so I'll try to skirt around the edges. These words aren't mine, but those of my residents within Newport. speaker: Claire Archibald AS
debate: 5. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Social Care, Mental Health and Women’s Health: Stronger Safeguarding for a Safer Wales
text:
Thank you, Deputy Minister. I welcome the statement and the recognition that safeguarding is one of the most important responsibilities of any Government. Every single one of us in this Chamber has been given the honour of representing the people of Wales, and with that honour there comes a strong responsibility to protect our most vulnerable and to challenge the system that fails them. However awkward the questions, however uncomfortable the answers, we must have the courage to act. Safeguarding is essential. Children, patients and adults at risk must be protected. People must feel confident about reporting concerns, knowing they will be heard and taken seriously.

I welcome the Minister's emphasis on strengthening safeguarding across Wales and on creating a system that is proactive rather than reactive, one that learns lessons and acts before harm escalates. But we must never judge safeguarding by what it achieves. A policy is only effective if it works in practice. Additional procedures must address and identify problems and deliver a clear benefit. We must distinguish between preventing abuse and investigating allegations against those entrusted with people's care. Both require accountability.

Children can face exploitation in their homes, their communities and online. They may not recognise the abuse. They may even defend the person harming them. Protection cannot depend on a child finding the words to explain what is happening. Warning signs must never be dismissed because an individual is respected, an organisation fears embarrassment or someone is uncomfortable asking difficult questions. That principle applies everywhere, including hospitals and care settings.

Proper scrutiny also demands fair treatment. Doctors, nurses, social care workers, teachers and foster carers carry enormous responsibilities. We want people to enter these roles, stay in them and feel supported to provide good care. An allegation must be taken seriously. It must never be treated as a verdict. Immediate protective action may be necessary while facts are established. The action must reflect the risk, being regularly reviewed and accompanied by a fair and timely investigation. Where a process becomes unnecessarily prolonged or poorly co-ordinated, the consequences of this can reach into someone's livelihood, family life, confidence and mental health. For a foster family, an investigation affects their home. For a nurse or a doctor, it can leave their professional future uncertain. Children, patients and those reporting harm also need answers. Avoidable delay serves nobody. When an investigation continues for months, who is responsible for its progress, who reviews the restrictions, who challenges the unnecessary delay? The statement speaks of stronger leadership and accountability. Those principles must apply not only when concerns are raised, but throughout the safeguarding process itself. Several bodies may have legitimate responsibilities, but there must be clear co-ordination with avoidable duplication identified and removed. Those affected need clear communication, appropriate support and a fair opportunity to respond, subject to necessary safeguards for the investigation. Decisions must draw on relevant clinical and care expertise. Front-line experience must inform the process alongside safeguarding expertise, and decisions must be open to proper challenge.

You announced today a national oversight arrangement, a national social care intelligence hub and a national safeguarding risk register. These may help improve consistency and identify emerging risks, but they must also demonstrate how they will improve outcomes on the ground for vulnerable people and support timely, effective decision-making in front-line services.

We must also examine the effect on recruitment and retention. If foster families withdraw because of how allegations are handled, the Government must establish why. It must examine what any loss of placements means for that child needing a stable, suitable home. The same scrutiny must apply to concerns about nurses, doctors, social care workers leaving their roles. You must explain how existing arrangements of these proposed reforms will protect vulnerable people, how unnecessary duplication is prevented and who takes responsibility if investigations drift. Before introducing further requirements, identify the gap they address and demonstrate how they will improve safety.

I call for a review of existing arrangements, their effectiveness, proportionality, delays and support for everyone affected. That review must listen to children, families, patients, front-line workers and safeguarding professionals, and publish clear findings and actions. Accountability cannot stop with a nurse on a ward or the foster carer in their home. It must extend to those managing investigations and setting those policies. Our constituents deserve protection. Those caring for them deserve fair treatment. The Government must deliver both. Diolch.

speaker: Catherine Cullen  AS
debate: 5. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Social Care, Mental Health and Women’s Health: Stronger Safeguarding for a Safer Wales
text:
Diolch, Deputy Llywydd. To declare an interest, I've got a close family member working in the NHS.

Deputy Minister, nobody disputes the importance of safeguarding. No-one disputes that children need to be safe from neglect, harm or abuse, and in that way, the statement's right. But we have to be realistic about what is happening on the ground in Wales. Across Wales, we have more than 7,000 looked-after children, around 4,800 living in foster placement, yet Wales needs 550 new foster carers every year. And at a time when the numbers of foster carers are declining, demands continue to rise. In Wales, more than 20 per cent of foster parents who left cited safeguarding allegations as the reason.

We also hear of too many cases of individuals in fostering, education, care and other professions spending months or years under safeguarding investigations. They can't move on with their lives, despite no wrongdoing ever being proven. Doctors face triple jeopardy: investigated by the police, the General Medical Council and the trust all at the same time as trying to work, if they're not off with stress. Nearly one in three who experience fitness-to-practice investigations experience suicidal thoughts, and sometimes investigations go on for years.

Does the Minister accept that safeguarding systems must protect the vulnerable, but must also be proportionate, timely and fair to those who are accused? As you say in the statement, we owe it to them to get this right.

speaker: Cai Parry-Jones AS
text:
Before I get into the meat of this debate, I have to ask: what really is the point of tabling this motion today and taking up an hour of Welsh taxpayers' time? The motion was co-tabled by the Plaid Cymru Government and its little helpers, in a spectacular reversal of roles, Welsh Labour. So, unless there is some kind of revolt going to happen on the back benches, we already know what the outcome will be. And yet here we are, spending a full hour of our lives on it, when we could be doing something useful for our constituents.

This Chamber has already come under fire recently for how it spends its time. I saw a post on X, viewed more than 300,000 times, showing last week's Plenary and the row over the word 'blanket'. The caption of the post read:

'Oh my god. This isn't a sketch. This is real. It happened at the Welsh Senedd. Madness'.

We as a Parliament have to be very careful that we are spending our time here wisely, that we are addressing the challenges that the Welsh public is facing, that we walk in their shoes, that we get it. I'm afraid I do not think that the public would put fiscal reform anywhere near the top of their agenda.

Now to the contents of the motion itself. In it, the Welsh Government is asking the Senedd to call on the Welsh Government to work with the UK Government. You already do that, don't you? Working with the UK Government is a fundamental part of a devolved Government's responsibilities. Welsh Labour did it for 27 years when they were in power and your own Government has been doing it ever since. You do not need the Senedd to hold your hand while you speak to Andy Burnham.

My other issue on this motion is the utter vagueness of the wording. Part (a) states:

'enhance the Welsh Government’s fiscal flexibilities'.

Which ones and to what extent? You say that that includes

'removal of all restrictions on the Wales Reserve'.

But, of course, you're asking for much more than that. So, why not be honest and write exactly what it is you are calling for?

Reform's position is clear and unequivocal: prioritise doing better with the existing powers. Deliver better results with the money you have. The Welsh Government and civil service need to prove that they can deliver first-class public services efficiently. Reform welcomes your clear commitment to more transparency, as outlined by the Cabinet Minister for Government effectiveness, but so far, year after year, all we see is more economic decline and an NHS in Wales that is sinking financially.

On part (b),

'review the operation of the Barnett Formula to strengthen fairness and transparency',

I understand that your argument at first is about transparency and reporting, but this is politics. The wording is so general and so open to interpretation that if this motion is agreed, we may well hear a Plaid Government, down the line, suggest that the Senedd backed fundamental change to the Barnett formula and demand more funding on the back of it.

Specifics matter. Precise wording matters. If the Welsh Government knows which fiscal powers it wants, it should name them, cost them and explain the safeguards. If it cannot do that, then this motion is not a plan for reform, it is a request for political cover for the lack of ideas on the left.

I hope the theme of this speech was clear: please, for the sake of the people of Wales, say in clear words what exactly you're asking for, and please remember that our time belongs to the people of Wales and they expect us to use it wisely. Diolch, Lywydd.

speaker: Paul Marr AS
text:
Well, here we go again: Labour and Plaid Cymru lecturing this Senedd on fiscal reform, which, to many of my constituents, will be somewhat like Bonnie and Clyde asking to look after the bank over lunch time. Whilst you admire the confidence, I wouldn't give them the keys. Plaid Cymru and Labour may sit on different sides of this Chamber, but when it comes to the fundamental approach of taxing and spending, we have seen remarkably little appetite for genuine fiscal reform.

Indeed, this current 2026-27 budget was secured through an agreement between Labour and Plaid Cymru, and when Plaid extended to Government, it chose to honour the spending commitments in that budget. So, this debate should not simply be about who spends the money. It should be about something much more fundamental: how Government raises it, how it spends it, whether taxpayers receive value for it, and whether Government itself is prepared to reform, because fiscal reform cannot simply mean changing the name above the door whilst maintaining the same approach underneath it. That is why fiscal reform is ultimately about a choice: a choice between a Government that believes the answer to almost every problem is more spending and more bureaucracy, where Reform UK believes taxpayers have a right to demand value and accountability and results, because Government has no money of its own. [Interruption.] No, thank you.

Every pound spent in this place ultimately comes from taxpayers or borrowing that taxpayers will eventually have to service, and Reform UK starts from a very simple principle: it is taxpayers' money before it is Government's money. That is where I believe the fundamental difference between Reform and Plaid Cymru lies. Plaid Cymru came into Government promising change. Then came its first financial test, the supplementary budget. And what happened? It failed. On 14 July, Plaid Cymru's first supplementary budget was rejected by this Senedd by 49 to 44 votes. Now, Plaid will undoubtedly blame opposition parties, but Government is about more than announcing how much money you want to spend. Government is about leadership. It is all about building confidence in your priorities, demonstrating value for money, and convincing Parliament your financial plans deserve its support. That is precisely why fiscal reform matters, and Plaid cannot pretend that they have nothing to do with the financial settlement that they inherited. Only months earlier, Plaid Cymru negotiated a budget agreement with the previous Labour Government and then abstained to allow the budget to pass. They did not endorse every line of it, but they helped provide the parliamentary route for that financial settlement to take effect.

So, Reform's message on fiscal reform is different. Fiscal reform cannot simply mean spending more, taxing more, creating another scheme. This isn't reform; it's more bureaucracy. Genuine fiscal reforms mean asking the harder questions. What can Government stop doing? What can Government do better? Where is taxpayers' money going and being wasted? And what bureaucracy can be removed? That is what fiscal reform should be about: prioritising expenditure, eliminating waste and ensuring that Government lives within the resources available to it. It commits us to cutting 1p from every £1 across all rates of Welsh income tax by the end of this Senedd term, funded through reductions in expenditure elsewhere without cuts to front-line services, putting more of people's own money back in their pockets. We will review the quango state, merging or abolishing bodies whose functions are duplicated or unnecessary. And we will introduce a tax lock. Reform will not introduce a new Welsh-controlled tax or levy that has not been set out in our manifesto and approved by voters.

That is fiscal reform—lower taxation where it can be afforded, disciplined spending, less waste, and protecting the front-line services upon which people depend, because economic growth does not come from Government's endless moving of taxpayers' money around Cardiff Bay. Prosperity comes from people building businesses, entrepreneurs taking risks, companies investing, and people earning and spending their own money. And Government should create the conditions that allow them to do it. That is the Reform alternative—lower taxes, less waste, less bureaucracy, better infrastructure, stronger front-line services, and a Government that understands that economic growth ultimately pays for public services upon which we all depend.

So, when Plaid Cymru return to this Chamber with further spending plans, Reform should ask a very different question: not simply, 'How much are you spending, and where can savings be redirected towards front-line services in—?' Sorry, bear with me. Apologies. So, this includes politically fashionable projects that Governments are often reluctant to challenge, because fiscal reform requires us to confront spending driven more by ideology than outcomes. The test should not be whether a policy makes a Minister feel virtuous. The test should be: does it work, does it improve people's lives, and is it worth what taxpayers are being charged for it? If the answer is 'no', then Reform should have absolutely no hesitation in challenging that expenditure. There should be no sacred cows here when it comes to taxpayers' money.

speaker: Paul Marr AS
text: Yes, certainly. Our Welsh manifesto sets out a cost-neutral programme, cutting waste and funding additional expenditure, rather than assuming that every new priority requires additional funding or borrowing. We set out our fiscal approach clearly. If we want to spend more—

speaker: Paul Marr AS
text: Yes, certainly. I'll do that now. That is what fiscal reform in Wales needs, not another Government asking taxpayers to dig into their pockets, but a Government prepared to look into its own pockets first. That is the difference—

speaker: Stephen Senior AS
debate: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care
text: 2. How is the Welsh Government monitoring late cancellations by the Welsh Ambulance Services NHS Trust of non-emergency patient transport in Monmouthshire and Torfaen? OQ64614

speaker: Stephen Senior AS
debate: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care
text:
Cabinet Minister, the Welsh ambulance service quite rightly complains that patients cancel non-emergency transport at the last minute, with it reported that 20,000 had been cancelled until July, and around 60,000 last year. However, it seems that no such monitoring happens when the service itself cancels transport. Indeed, a recent consultation on the proposed changes to the service contained this statement:

'Demand for transport continues to increase, and journeys regularly have to be cancelled because demand exceeded available capacity.'

In other words, bookings are taken for seats that might not even exist. That's a failure of organisation and a real failure of the NHS. Very recently, a care home in my constituency was instructed that a resident would be collected earlier than planned, otherwise the transport would be cancelled. The home managed to comply, but it was stressful, and the patient arrived two hours early for her appointment and was out of the care home for over five hours. This is wholly unacceptable. Cabinet Minister, cancelled transport means wasted NHS appointment time and undue stress on patients and carers. Will you instruct your officials to establish the extent of the problem, the causes and the solutions?

speaker: Benjamin Hodge Mckenna AS

I'm glad to hear the commitment from you that you will be eradicating two-year waits in May. I hope I'm not going to be stood here holding you to account on that next year.

speaker: Benjamin Hodge Mckenna AS

Well, I don't understand why that means your party couldn't support the statement of opinion.

One area that we do agree on is the need for and use of surgical hubs in Wales. speaker: Benjamin Hodge Mckenna AS
debate: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care

speaker: Art Wright AS
debate: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care
text:
Cabinet Minister, one in two of us, or someone we know, has experienced pregnancy or baby loss. During Baby Loss Awareness Week, from 9 October to 15 October, we remember babies' lives, including those lost before 24 weeks. From April 2027, these parents will be entitled to two weeks of unpaid leave, yet some families still face choosing between time to grieve and paying the bills. speaker: Steve Bayliss AS
debate: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care
text:
I'd like to declare an interest, as my partner works within the NHS.

Cabinet Minister, in Afan Ogwr Rhondda, around 27,000 people are living with cardiovascular disease, and it causes more than one in four deaths—around 630 people every year. More than 36,000 people are living with diagnosed high blood pressure, one of the biggest risk factors for heart attacks and strokes. speaker: Catherine Cullen  AS
debate: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Health and Care
section: Decarbonising the Health and Care Sector
text:
Thank you for that answer. More than 540,000 patients are on NHS waiting lists in Wales. Behind those figures are people in pain, families living with uncertainty, and patients waiting desperately for the treatment that they need. The public sector decarbonisation programme is a staggering £38.7 million, plus £40 million targeted at the NHS. Based on average Welsh salaries, that money could employ nurses, doctors, surgeons and not forgetting those students coming out of university who still cannot get jobs. I'm not suggesting that we ignore the environment, but when our hospitals are struggling, waiting lists are growing and front-line staff are under immense pressure, we must ask whether taxpayers' money is being spent on the right priorities.

Will the Government review its climate-related NHS spending and redirect funding, wherever possible, towards clearing waiting lists and recruiting more front-line staff that our health service desperately needs?
