speaker: Cristiana Emsley AS
debate: 5. Welsh Labour Debate: Palliative and end-of-life care
text:
There are some areas of public policy where we can talk comfortably about budgets, targets, frameworks and commissioning arrangements. But end-of-life care is ultimately about something much more fundamental. It's about how we treat another human being when they're at their most vulnerable and how we allow families to spend those final irreplaceable moments together.

For me, this is deeply personal, because I did not get to say goodbye to my father. And anyone who has experienced that will understand that there are some moments in life that simply cannot be recreated later. There is no second opportunity for a final conversation, no second opportunity to hold somebody's hand, no second opportunity to say what you wanted to say. That is why the quality of care in those final days and hours matters not only to the person who is dying, it matters profoundly to those who are left behind. Good palliative care provides dignity to the dying, but it also gives families something extraordinarily important: time, support and the opportunity for closure. We cannot change death, but we can change the experience of dying, and that is why the situation facing hospices across Wales should concern every one of us in this Chamber.

Hospices in Wales support around 20,000 adults and children affected by terminal illness every year. Yet around 70 per cent of the cost of hospice care is funded through charitable donations, and Hospice UK has told us that an estimated 10,000 people in Wales already have unmet palliative care needs—already. Yet demand is projected to increase by a further 21 per cent by 2050, whilst hospices simultaneously face rising staffing, national insurance and operational costs. So, this is not a crisis somewhere over the horizon. There is unmet need today, and we are asking the same services to prepare for substantially greater demand tomorrow.

We are already seeing the consequences. Nearly 30 per cent of Welsh voluntary hospices surveyed are reducing in-patient beds or wider services because of financial and workforce pressures. And this is not an abstract national statistic for those of us in north Wales. At St David's Hospice in Holyhead, a four-bed in-patient unit has been temporarily closed. Four beds might sound insignificant on a Government spreadsheet, but a hospice bed is not simply a number. It may be the place where somebody spends their final night, where a husband says goodbye to his wife, where a daughter holds her father's hand, where a family has one final conversation with somebody they love. So, when we talk about losing four beds, four hospice beds, we are potentially talking about four families losing something they can never get back. And there is another important point here. Allowing hospice provision to deteriorate does not make the need disappear. Community services, hospice services, can support people closer to home, prevent unnecessary hospital admissions and relieve pressure on an NHS already under enormous strain. Fail to fund care properly in one part of the system and the human and financial cost simply appears somewhere else.

The Welsh Government provided £3 million for hospices in 2025-26, and committed to developing a sustainable funding solution. But Hospice UK and Hospices Cymru estimate that £30 million in additional funding is required during the remainder of this Senedd term. So, my question to Government is straightforward: where is the sustainable settlement? Hospices cannot recruit and retain specialist staff on warm words, they cannot keep in-patient beds open with another announcement, and families facing the most difficult days of their lives should not also have to wonder whether the care they desperately need will actually be here.

We spend a great deal of time in this Chamber arguing about priorities. Surely, there can be few greater tests of ours than how we care for people at the end of their lives. For the person dying, it's about dignity. For the family, it's about compassion, the time, the chance to say goodbye. And for those left behind, those final moments can become memories carried for the rest of their lives.

For those reasons, Llywydd, I will be supporting the motion before us today and I urge Members of the Chamber to do the same. I know what it means not to have that goodbye, and that is why I want other families to have the opportunity that I did not, because there are many things that Government can postpone, but a final goodbye is not one of them.

speaker: James Evans AS
debate: 5. Welsh Labour Debate: Palliative and end-of-life care
text:
I want to start by thanking the Labour group for bringing this motion forward today, and this important debate. Because this is an issue that should unite every single one of us in this Chamber, regardless of our political differences. Like Sam Rowlands, I want to thank Mark Isherwood, who's no longer in this Chamber, for all the work he did in this space. He was a leader in this area for us. We do miss him, but we look forward to seeing what Sam can do in his stead.

Over the years, I've had the privilege of visiting a number of charities and organisations across Wales that provide care and support for people facing some of the most difficult moments of their lives. I've visited St David's, like Natasha Asghar mentioned. But one particular visit that has stayed with me was a visit to a children's palliative care centre, Tŷ Hafan, close to Cardiff. Seeing the compassion, dedication and extraordinary care provided to children with life-limiting conditions, and support offered not just to the children, but the parents and the families, is something that really does put life in perspective. I want to thank all those people who work in Tŷ Hafan for the amazing work that they do.

But palliative care isn't simply about helping someone at the end of their life, it's about helping people live as well as they possibly can for as long as they possibly can. It's about dignity, comfort, compassion and giving families the opportunity to make precious memories together. I want to pay tribute to every nurse, doctor, healthcare assistant, volunteer and charity worker who makes that possible across our country.

But, Llywydd, behind that incredible work lies a deeply worrying financial reality. Across Wales, hospices support more than 20,000 adults and children every year, yet around two thirds of their income still relies on charitable fundraising. Just last month, Hospice UK and Hospices Cymru warned that an additional £30 million is needed over the remainder of this Senedd term just to protect these essential services. Those are deeply concerning figures for everybody. They're not simply financial pressures on a balance sheet; they have real consequences for patients and families who depend on these services. I welcomed the additional funding that the Welsh Government has provided, including that £4.3 million package announced earlier this year and the work being undertaken to improve how hospices are commissioned, but we must recognise that short-term financial support cannot overtake that long-term security that the service and sector has asked for. We cannot expect our hospices to continue to provide reassurance to families in those most difficult circumstances.

I think there also sits a wider issue of fairness. The Welsh Government itself has acknowledged that around one in four people in Wales currently lack access to hospice care or equivalent specialist palliative care support, and that simply cannot be acceptable. Whether someone lives in Cardiff, the Valleys, rural Powys or north Wales, they should be able to access the same dignity and compassion and that quality of care. We must remember that good palliative care is also about supporting families, providing respite, helping people remain in their own homes and reducing unnecessary pressure on our hospitals. People at the end of their life do not want to end up in accident and emergency departments sat on hard chairs waiting to be seen. That's just not where they want to go.

But I'd just like to say to the new Cabinet Minister: you made a lot of promises to this sector when you were the shadow Minister for this. In January 2024, you led a debate in this Senedd, calling for long-term funding. On 16 July that year, you also said you were unhappy about the delays to the sector. In September, you talked about inefficient progress, and in January and March of this year, you said that funding levels were unsustainable. So, in responding to this debate, Cabinet Minister, I hope that officials haven't got in your ear and changed your mind, because I think some of those assurances that you have given to the sector over the years are going to be held to account. I would like to see that you've listened and are going to act now you're in Government to deliver for this key sector, and deliver for those families and people across Wales who are relying on you to stand up to your promises. Thank you.

speaker: Benjamin Hodge Mckenna AS
debate: 5. Welsh Labour Debate: Palliative and end-of-life care
text:
The fundamental concept of our healthcare system in Wales is that it provides care free at the point of use from cradle to grave, and, unfortunately, it's the latter part of that statement that is at risk at the moment. It is the duty of our health services to ensure that people facing terminal illness and their families receive dignified and compassionate care at the end of life. Approximately 20,000 children and adults depend on our hospice services each year, and therefore they must be protected. But words alone won't protect them. Almost 30 per cent of Welsh voluntary hospices that were surveyed said that they had to reduce in-patient beds or services due to financial or workforce pressure already.

Several hospices across Wales have already closed, either permanently or temporarily, such as a four-bed unit in St David's Hospice in Holyhead. More than 70 per cent of hospices with in-patient units expect that cost pressures will make further beds unavailable. A significant majority of hospice care providers in Wales still depend on charitable donations. Now, in 2025-26, the Welsh Government provided £3 million and committed to finding a sustainable funding solution, but Hospice UK estimate that that is just 10 per cent of the £30 million that will be required over this Senedd term just to safeguard existing services.

As Ken Skates mentioned, Marie Curie have already suggested that the current system is failing people, that nearly a third of people in Wales have unmet palliative care needs. And what's worse is that the demand is expected to rise by more than 25 per cent over the next 25 years. That's a significant increase in demand for a system that is already having to scale back its services due to cost pressures. And while I'm glad that Labour did bring forward this debate today, the fact is that they had years in power in which they could have dealt with the issues that are currently facing hospice care in Wales. And now that Plaid Cymru are in charge, they must explain how they're going to support the sector, as patients cannot be cared for by an announcement or framework.

Essential end-of-life care must be protected, and the current model is clearly unsustainable. Community hospice and palliative care services help people to reduce avoidable hospital admissions and they relieve pressure from elsewhere in our healthcare system. In Reform, we will support measures that place our hospices on a sustainable footing, strengthen community and out-of-hours capacity, and develop the workforce that is necessary to meet growing demands. Hence, we will be supporting this motion today. Diolch yn fawr.

speaker: Cai Parry-Jones AS
debate: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
text:
For too many people across Wales, opening the annual council tax bill is something they absolutely dread. Families are struggling with the cost of living. They're working hard to pay their mortgages whilst grappling with energy bills and weekly shopping, yet they're also being asked to find more and more money every year to pay their council tax. In my constituency of Caerdydd Ffynnon Taf, a standard band D bill in Cardiff has risen from around £1,637 in 2022-23 to over £2,000 this year—an increase of almost 23 per cent. And it's not just my constituency. Let us look at the figures elsewhere. In 2025-26, Wrexham and Flintshire increased council tax by 9.5 per cent, Pembrokeshire by 9.35 per cent and Ceredigion by 9.3 per cent. In Conwy, residents have faced successive increases of 9.67 per cent, 8.95 per cent and a further 6.5 per cent this year. And on Ynys Môn, the council's band D charge has risen more than 31 per cent since 2022. On average, that's over £425 more each year added to their council tax bill. Staggering. Yet, the Plaid Cymru-led council on Ynys Môn reported a budget underspend, totalling over £8 million across the last three financial years, and holds £19 million in general reserves. Surely, it is reasonable to ask whether residents were charged more than was necessary.

It isn't just about the money they haven't spent. It's also about the stupid decisions they've committed to spend on. A few weeks ago, the Isle of Anglesey County Council passed a motion to spend £1.1 million swapping household black bins for smaller ones. Only one councillor voted against that proposal, and I am proud to say that that was a sole Reform Cymru councillor—[Interruption.] There'll be more than one soon. A lonely voice of common sense in a crowded room of nonsense. Let me be clear, of course councils face genuine pressures, from social care to schools, roads and waste collection—these all need funding. We understand that and we want to see them fairly funded, but that does not mean that ever-higher council tax bills should be accepted as the norm. Wales has 22 principal local authorities, so let me ask a straightforward question: do we really need 22 separate back offices when councils could work together to save money? Do we need duplicated payroll systems, separate IT contracts and independent procurement arrangements when sharing services could deliver better value? Could councils combine their purchasing power to secure better prices, reduce duplication and free up money for front-line services, such as social care? This is not an attack on local government employees. They are common-sense questions about the political leadership of Welsh councils.

Greater efficiency is one reason Reform wants to introduce a democratic lock on annual council tax increases above 4.99 per cent. We see this policy working as an active deterrent against wasteful and unnecessary spending. If Welsh councils want to raise tax above this threshold, they must make a convincing case through a local referendum. It is up to local people to decide whether their money is being spent efficiently. Consider a household paying £2,000 a year in council tax. A 4.99 per cent increase would add £100 to its bill and an 8 per cent increase would add £160. During a cost-of-living crisis, every pound matters. In England, councils are generally required to seek approval through a local referendum if they want to increase council tax beyond the relevant threshold. So, why shouldn't Welsh taxpayers have the same democratic safeguard? Our objective isn't to force councils to make indiscriminate cuts or undermine essential services, it is to challenge unnecessary duplication, improve procurement, review administrative overheads and encourage councils to work together, wherever that delivers savings.

We would also expect greater transparency so that residents can see how their money is spent, what savings have been achieved and why any proposed council tax increase above the threshold is necessary. The people of Wales work hard for their money. They deserve responsible spending, effective services and a fair deal from local government. The answer to every budget pressure cannot simply be another inflation-busting increase in council tax. Plaid Cymru talk about a new deal for Wales, but what the people of Wales really need is a fair deal from all layers of Government within Wales. It's time for the Welsh Government to set the bar.

But I know what will happen. Like every other major issue in Wales, Plaid will say it's somebody else's job to fix, someone else's responsibility. 'Council tax is a local matter for councils.' We've heard it before. This is where Reform is different. We will stand up for Wales and fight the corner of local people. We will make sure their voices are heard loud and clear. We will set the standard, and in this case, that means giving taxpayers the final say on high council tax increases. If Members here today want to help people with the cost of living, put your money where your mouth is and back this democratic lock. Their money, their decision.

speaker: Cai Parry-Jones AS
debate: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
text: Thank you, Llywydd. It's a pleasure to open this debate on behalf of Reform UK Cymru as the shadow finance Minister.

speaker: Cai Parry-Jones AS
debate: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
text: Reform calls for more democratic powers to be put in the hands of local taxpayers. Where Welsh councils propose council tax increases above 4.99 per cent, residents will have the right to approve or reject them through a local referendum. This policy would finally put Welsh taxpayers on an equal footing to their English counterparts. If council leaders want to implement inflation-busting council tax rises year on year, it is only right that they justify it directly to the people who pay—the people who they supposedly work for.

speaker: Cai Parry-Jones AS
debate: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
text: Support the motion. Thank you.

speaker: Andrew Griffin AS
debate: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
text:
I'm pleased to support the motion tabled by my colleague Llŷr Powell, but I want to approach it from a slightly different angle, because I've been a town councillor myself, and know something about setting budgets and council tax precepts.

I know it's not always easy; the constituency I represent covers parts of four council areas—Gwynedd, Wrexham, Powys and Denbighshire—and each faces its own challenges. But there's one thing they all have in common: every year, people receive their council tax bill and almost without fail it's gone up again. For someone on a good income, another £100 or £150 might not seem particularly significant, but, for a pensioner or someone living on a fixed income, that's money they've got to find from somewhere, and the trouble is that these increases don't happen in isolation; they build up year after year. A 5 per cent increase this year is added to all the increases that have gone before it, and next year's increase is calculated on top of that. That's why I think we need to look at what people are paying today compared with five or 10 years ago, rather than just looking at the latest percentage, because household incomes certainly haven't kept pace.

Now, having been a town councillor, there's something else I think that's worth explaining. When your council tax bill arrives, you might reasonably assume all that money is going to your county council, but it isn't. Part of it goes towards policing, and, depending on where you live, there's also a contribution to your town or community council. Fire and rescue services are funded through council budgets too. In fact, the police element alone accounts for roughly £1 in every £6 on the average council tax bill in Wales, and that's not an amount your county council decides. I mention this because I think people deserve to know exactly who is responsible for the different parts of their bill, and, if we're going to introduce a referendum threshold, we need to be clear about which increase it applies to.

Now, I don't want anyone to think I'm suggesting councils have an easy job; they don't. Social care costs are rising, schools are under pressure, and councils are being asked to deliver services with increasingly stretched budgets. But that brings me to something else that matters. Is the way we fund local government in Wales actually fit for purpose? Because delivering services in large rural counties like Powys, Gwynedd and Denbighshire is very different from delivering them in a city. You've got smaller communities spread over much greater distances. School transport costs more, providing services costs more, and, in many cases, there simply aren't the economies of scale that larger urban areas can achieve. So, we need a funding system that recognises those differences, not a one-size-fits-all approach that assumes every council faces the same circumstances.

The Welsh Government has a responsibility to get that right, because, if we're going to hold councils accountable for the money they ask residents to pay, we must also hold the Welsh Government accountable for the funding decisions that affect them. None of this changes the position of the person who has to pay the bill—they don't get to choose whether their income goes up enough to cover another council tax increase, they just have to find the money, and that's why I support giving them a greater say when particularly large increases are proposed. It doesn't mean councils can never put council tax up by more than 4.99 per cent; it means that, if they believe they need to, they should be prepared to explain why and put that decision to the people who are going to pay for it. I don't think that is unreasonable, because, ultimately, this isn't about figures on a spreadsheet or arguments between politicians, it's about what people have left in their pockets at the end of the month, and I think those people deserve a say. So, I'll be supporting this motion and urge other Members to do the same. Diolch, Lywydd.

speaker: David Hughes AS
debate: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
text: Do you think that the taxpayer, local tax payers, should pay for everything, Mike? How high do you think the council tax should go up every year, because, under Labour, it's going up and up and up?

speaker: Tom Montgomery AS
debate: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
text: Before I start—. Mike, I've got to take the bait. You talk of ignorance; we are standing up for taxpayers. Ignorance is your party sitting on its hands for 27 years and doing nothing but cripple our local government. So, let's start—[Interruption.] Yes, of course.

speaker: Tom Montgomery AS
debate: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
text:
Twenty-seven years of failure. We're putting taxpayers first, Mike, that's what we're doing. And this is an incredibly effective tool. We've already seen it work in England. [Interruption.] Not a single local authority dares go to the electorate this year in England because they recognise that people are under enough financial pressure. Unsurprisingly, these rules have already made careful financial management in local authorities the preferred option, compared to simply asking residents to pay evermore taxes. Inflation-busting tax rises are no longer the default option in England. Currently, these protections offered to English taxpayers are not afforded to Welsh taxpayers.

Our residents in Wales are paying more than average. Over the last decade, residents in Denbighshire have seen their council tax rise by 61.9 per cent; in Flintshire, 75 per cent; Wrexham, 76 per cent; and in Conwy, 84 per cent, in a decade. The inflation rate over the same period was 34 per cent. Despite those excessive increases, this financial year, all of those local authorities increased council tax by above inflation again. And this pattern is set to continue because our local authorities are fighting with their hands tied behind their backs.

As my colleague Cai Parry-Jones has highlighted, we need council mergers. Welsh Labour was wrong to reject the offer made by Conwy and Denbighshire to merge; stopping a proposal that could have seen savings of over £1 million on middle and front-line services, over £2 million on back-office functions and the creation of a single management team that could have saved thousands.

Then we come to the funding formula. We are told that data is fundamental in driving budget allocations through the revenue support grant. But, again, local authorities are being failed in Wales. The formula uses data, Members, that is older than me. It comes from the 1991 census. Unsurprisingly, the WLGA have explained that calls from local authorities have grown for a thorough independent external review to be undertaken. I agree, and we need to see the Government get on and do this, and bring forward the proposals for the formula change urgently.

But why make this change now? There needs to be a wake-up call in this Chamber, Members, about the level of debt that local authorities are carrying. Conwy council has around £230 million of debt; Flintshire, £360 million; and Wrexham over £0.5 billion in debt. This situation is only going to get worse. From my time as a county councillor, I know that when these loans are taken, they are assumed—[Interruption.] I'll take a second intervention.

speaker: Tom Montgomery AS
debate: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
text: Thank you, Alun. If you let me get through, I'll explain why we need the cap now, before the burden of debt cripples taxpayers.

speaker: Tom Montgomery AS
debate: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
text:
The situation is getting worse. Councils borrow the debt on repayment terms expected to be 10, 15 or 20 years or more, but the repayment periods are only, often, five years. So, this means that when the loans mature, new deals need to be made and, with current interest rates, they're often much higher than originally forecast, meaning financing often falls to local authorities to find the extra money to continue to finance these debts. These debts are a ticking financial time bomb.

The solution is not more excessive council tax rises, which is the option that many local authorities will turn to, not more reliance on borrowing, not the decline in offers for mergers. It is not continuing a funding formula system based on data that is older than me. The solution is fundamental reform of local government in Wales. That must start with greater protection for our taxpayers. Council tax referenda will do just that. They will raise awareness of the serious state of our local government finance, they will challenge the cabinet and officers to work in a more effective way, and give voters the final say on the financial direction of their local area. Members, I urge you to support this motion.

speaker: Nigel Williams AS
debate: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
text: Yes.

speaker: Iain McIntosh AS
debate: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
text: Would you take an intervention?

speaker: Nigel Williams AS
debate: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
text:
I'll take no—. In terms of this—. Where it comes from Plaid, who've operated around Labour in this, we're in this mess, where we are, because of what's happened over the years, because of people there and people here. So I'll take none of that.

Reserves are not a magic pot of money that can simply solve every problem. Some reserves—[Interruption.] No. Some reserves are earmarked, some are legally committed and some can only be used for specific purposes. [Interruption.] I did.

There's one thing I would like to mention, by the way, and it just came to me when Sarah Cooper-Lesadd was speaking, and I just wanted to finish on that, actually. On 2 October 2014, under the provisions of the Local Government Act 1972, a referendum was held in the town of Flint on the question to reinstate in-patient beds. The referendum drew 3,500 residents to vote, with 99 per cent saying 'yes'. So, referendums do work in towns, completely.

I've missed some of the speech out, because I realise I'm actually going on now. This is local democracy in action, and I urge Members to support the motion. Thanks very much.

speaker: Francesca O'Brien AS
debate: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
text:
Diolch, Lywydd. I thank everyone who has participated this afternoon for all the contributions, and for the humorous interjections, shall I say. It certainly kept us entertained this afternoon. Our motion rests on a simple principle: if a council wants to raise council tax by more than 4.99 per cent, it should ask the people who pay for it. England has had that rule for years, Wales currently has no limits.

If I can turn to Cai, who is sitting behind me, who opened the debate and highlighted the council tax bill that every year each and every one of us and those that we represent in our constituencies absolutely dread, because, like I say, there is no limit. We do not know what's going to hit that doorstep. He also highlighted that in his own constituency, they have seen rises of over 23 per cent, which is absolutely scandalous. We talk about the cost of living. How are families going to be affording that increase?

He has also highlighted some of the misspending, shall I say—£1.1 million on changing the size of black bins. If that's a government's priority, I seriously question it. Janet, I'm glad you highlighted that it was the one Reform councillor. Thank goodness for that one Reform councillor who objected to that stupid notion.

We also had Andrew, who shared his experience of being on a town council and highlighted the vital services that the fire service does in our communities. I'm sure the Cabinet Minister would agree that the fire service have had their hands full this year with the wildfires and they do a sterling job. I met with them recently and they are under huge financial pressures. I know in our own constituency in Gower and Swansea, they're actually taking on more financial burden from the Welsh ambulance service with the co-responder unit in Reynoldston. So, again, they've taken on more pressures, more statutory duties without the resources. I think it's important to mention the fire service and also the police service, which also contribute to the council tax bill. I don't think many of the public realise that is included.

Tom, I know you were another councillor as well in north Wales. The borrowing amounts are eye-watering that councils are having to do. Again, it goes back to those statutory duties. We are putting those councils' backs against the wall. I know, speaking of when I was a Swansea councillor, we were lucky we had a fantastic responsible finance officer who borrowed at the right time. But I am equally aware that not all councils, not all 22, borrowed at the same rates that we did in Swansea.

Nigel, I think you hit the nail on the head about transparency for the public. Referendums do work. I think we need to be held accountable. If we are elected to serve our public, we are civil servants. We are there to serve. We should be held accountable and have the transparency at every opportunity—[Interruption.] Well, we are. We're there to serve the public, so whether you like it or not, we're not here to pat each other on the back and be in an echo chamber. We're there serving the people.

To the speakers across the floor, Sarah, I ask the Member, you stood on the Reform manifesto back in May. Did you mislead the public then, or are you misleading them now on your new stance on council tax reform? And what a referendum actually does do—I know you argued against it and you don't think it works. Again, going back to Nigel's point, they can work, actually. I'm a believer in democracy. It's giving the people a democratic right; our country is based on a democratic right. Also, with councils, if they've got a limited amount of budget, they need to sharpen that pencil and make priorities work as well. So, it gives people that power.

Mike, I always love your interventions. I know we represent the same constituency, but I am glad you mentioned procurement, because when I was last on Swansea Council, procurement was a little bit odd, because we actually imported, in one constituency, in Merthyr, 99 per cent of our chicken from China and Thailand. That's a great example of how procurement doesn't work, so I disagree with you on procurement there.

Carrie, I know you also mentioned—. I need to go over my notes. Mike and Carrie both mentioned Reform councils. Actually, they do work. I know you don't like to admit it, but in County Durham, Reform's first budget raised council tax by less than 2 per cent, with no rise at all in core charges. So, across the nine councils where Reform hold a majority, the average increase was under 4 per cent, against nearly 5 per cent in parts of Wales and parts of England. Our councils also face the same pressures of social services. But we in Reform have the willingness to go through the budget line line by line.

Janet, you were doing so well. And yes, I'm so glad you recognise we are a twinkle in Nigel's eye. Absolutely. [Laughter.] It's shining bright from over there. It is, absolutely. But you highlighted some really good points, Janet—the fact that there's a lot of money coming into Wales, but with statutory duties, that money is not always going down to local councils, and that is a worry that many of the councils are facing for next year. In my shadow Minister post, I've met with a lot of councils over the course since May, and they're all worried about the budget. You've got the growing cost of social services, which is spiralling out of control, the additional learning needs—they are all worried how they're going to make it work. So, that is something I'm a little bit worried about, because that's been the topic of debate the last couple of days of the supplementary budget—not enough is going to ALN—but that's a different debate for another day. But let me go on to—[Interruption.] Well, it's £60 million out of, what, £233 million that was coming from Westminster? So, yes, and I'm sure the headteachers are pleased with that.

I will end the debate. We need to bring back trust in local government, Llywydd, and councils should be able to communicate with the public and justify the reasons for the increases in council tax. That should be the social contract between the public and politicians. Our motion says if a council wants to raise more, they should make the case and win the local vote. Plaid Cymru told voters its budget deal would prevent unaffordable rises. If they really believe that, then surely they've got nothing to fear from letting residents decide. Put your money where your mouth is. People across Wales are not asking for miracles. They want their council taxes spent with care, and before it goes up sharply next year, we should be asking: do we need a referendum? This motion gives them that right, and I urge Members across the floor to support it. Diolch, Lywydd.

speaker: Iain McIntosh AS
debate: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
text: Thank you. You've moved on to what I wanted to challenge you about, really. Would you acknowledge and agree with me that if local authorities had been funded properly over the last 27 years and continued to be funded properly, they wouldn't need to put council tax up by more than 4.99 per cent?

speaker: Nigel Williams AS
debate: 6. Reform UK Debate: Local referendums on council tax rises
text:
Well, we all get that brown envelope, don't we, through the post, or sometimes it's an email nowadays? Council tax is not voluntary, is it? It arrives every year and households have got to find the money to pay for it. When a council wants to raise the bill by more than 4.99 per cent, Reform UK believes that the people paying for it should have the final say. This motion does not ban a higher increase, it simply says: make the case, publish the consequences and ask permission.

The Welsh average band D council tax rose by 7.7 per cent in 2024-25, and by a further 7.2 per cent in 2025-26. Over the last five years, council tax rises across Wales have accelerated significantly, with the Welsh average increasing 7.2 per cent in 2025-26. And nowhere is that seen more than in north-east Wales where I live. In Flintshire, the council tax increase for 2025-26 was 9.5 per cent, and in Wrexham, residents faced an increase of approximately 8.9 per cent. These rises came on top of substantial increases in previous years. Where does it stop? Yet both councils continue to face severe financial challenges in themselves.

From a Flintshire and Wrexham perspective, the situation has become increasingly difficult to manage. Both authorities are forecasting budget deficits in excess of £25 million, as pointed out by Cai. Adult social care, there are issues, demand for services, additional learning needs provision, homelessness services and expensive out-of-county placements continue to grow faster than the funding available to support them.

Councils have had to make difficult decisions for well over a decade now—I'm aware of that. Flintshire and Wrexham have delivered millions of pounds of expenditure reductions since about 2010, but there comes a point where efficiencies are exhausted and residents are simply asked to pay more to cover a growing funding gap.

Before Flintshire approved its recent budget, residents were consulted. Many expressed concern about the rising council tax increases to bridge budget shortfalls during the continuing cost-of-living crisis. Despite these concerns, local people had no binding vote on the outcome—no binding vote, and that's important. When you speak to residents across Flintshire and Wrexham, you hear a common message: council tax keeps rising, but many people believe services are being reduced.

I've seen it myself. Your bins—they don't get emptied every week now. There are all sorts of places where we're seeing things cut. Potholes in the road, local road infrastructure—there are loads of issues. Whether every criticism is justified or not, the perception is clear: people are paying more and feeling they are receiving less in return. That's why local democracy comes into its own. Of course, supporters of the status quo argue that local elections are sufficiently accountable. I disagree with that. A local election provides a general mandate. A referendum provides a specific mandate for an exceptional tax increase.

And, of course, we must be honest about council finances. Reserves are not a magic pot of money that can simply solve every problem. Some reserves are earmarked, yes. Some are legally committed. And some can only be used for specific purposes. Flintshire, for example, reports significant levels of usable reserves, but much of that money is allocated for identified risks and future commitments. However, transparency is absolutely essential. If councils—

speaker: David Mills AS
debate: 8. Short Debate: Green across the aisle: Making environmental stewardship a common cause
text:
Environmental stewardship should not belong to one political party, one ideology, or one side of the Chamber. It should be a common cause. For small c conservatives, environmental conservation is central to our political philosophy. Yes, too often the tradition is overlooked because the debate about the environment has become almost entirely dominated by carbon reduction, which, whilst important, should not dominate Government action over other concerns. Many to the right, myself included, object to the direction of current environmental policy, but we should not allow that disagreement to be mistaken for indifference towards the environment itself. I believe climate change is a serious, potentially existential challenge that must be addressed, and we cannot simply ignore the evidence to pretend that a changing climate presents no risks, but we must distinguish between the challenge we face and the policies Governments choose to pursue in response to it.

I have profound concerns about the approach to net zero. The UK can impose ever more ambitious targets on itself and introduce costly regulations, but climate change is a global problem driven by global emissions. The effectiveness of our response must therefore be judged in a global context. My concern is that policies pursued in the name of net zero will make little difference to the global climate trajectory if they are not matched by meaningful international action, while not imposing enormous costs on ordinary people here at home, because those costs are not borne equally. We should not ask people on the lowest incomes to shoulder disproportionate costs for policies whose global impact depends on what the rest of the world does, when the UK's impact is so minuscule.

If the United Kingdom reached net zero by next week, would the climate stop changing? Of course it would not. That does not mean we should abandon efforts to reduce emissions, it means we should pursue them sensibly, in concert with other countries, and in a way that is economically sustainable and commands public support.

We should also be honest about the need to adapt to the changes in climate we face. We need resilient infrastructure, effective flood prevention, healthy soils, restored peatlands, and landscapes better equipped to withstand drought, wildfire and extreme rainfall. We must also consider the standardisation of air conditioning in homes and schools, and fund agricultural science that looks at how crops may have to adapt to a changing climate.

Mitigation and adaptation must go hand in hand, but my concern is that the single-minded focus of carbon targets has distracted us from other pressing environmental problems—problems where we could make tangible difference to people's lives and the natural world around us.

As we have been racing towards ever more ambitious carbon targets, our rivers and our seas have been filling with sewage. Natural Resources Wales reported that Dŵr Cymru was responsible for 155 pollution incidents in 2024. That was the highest number of sewage pollution incidents recorded by the company in a decade. We should be just as determined to stop sewage entering our rivers as we are to meet carbon targets.

Another area where we should be able to find common ground is the protection of our habitats and our beautiful landscapes. Species are disappearing, habitats are under pressure and too many landscapes are failing to reach their ecological potential. Tree planting, habitat restoration, healthier soils and protecting native species can all make a real difference, but this must be done in partnership with farmers and landowners, not through top-down diktats. We should reward long-term stewardship rather than simply measuring compliance with administrative requirements. We also need tougher penalties for environmental crime and better policing. While law-abiding citizens face increasingly costly waste disposal, criminals are dumping toxic waste and despoiling our countryside with apparent impunity.

Michael Sheen's recent documentary Buried has highlighted the illegal dumping of forever chemicals and acid sludge across England and Wales. In March, Natural Resources Wales reported that nearly 50,000 fly-tipping incidents had been recorded in Welsh local authorities in the previous year—an increase of almost 15 per cent. That's about 133 incidents every day. We need effective investigations and meaningful penalties. This is not about punishing well-meaning landowners for missing a clause in a regulation; it's about ensuring that those who wantonly destroy our natural environment face prison.

Presiding Officer, this brings me back to the central argument of this debate: environmental policy should not be judged solely on carbon targets, but by whether our rivers are cleaner, our habitats are recovering, our wildlife is thriving and our countryside is protected for future generations. Achieving this means working with farmers, landowners, conservationists, volunteers, communities and businesses. Good environmental policy need not be prohibitively expensive. Often, the best solutions are practical, locally led and rooted in an understanding of the landscapes. We can disagree about net zero and the pace of decarbonisation, but surely we can agree that sewage should not pollute our rivers, that endangered species should be protected, illegal dumping should be punished and those restoring habitats should be encouraged rather than obstructed. These aren't left-wing or right-wing objectives; they're commonsense objectives.

I'm confident the new Minister for climate change and rural resilience shares my desire to put sound land management and the protection of our natural inheritance at the heart of environmental policy, and I look forward to hearing how he intends to deliver that. Our responsibility as custodians is to ensure the next generation inherits a natural environment richer, healthier and better protected than the one we inherited. That's what environmental stewardship means to me. I look forward to hearing the other contributors to the debate. Thank you.

speaker: David Mills AS
debate: 8. Short Debate: Green across the aisle: Making environmental stewardship a common cause
text: Shall I start?

speaker: David Mills AS
debate: 8. Short Debate: Green across the aisle: Making environmental stewardship a common cause
text:
Thank you, Presiding Officer. I'm pleased to have the opportunity to open the debate today. I will be giving a minute of my time to John Clark, Paul Rock, Anna Nicholl and James Evans. I want to begin by outlining why I am personally invested in this issue. I have been a lifelong environmentalist. I run a farm where I've dedicated a significant amount of my land to habitat restoration and tree planting. Prior to farming, I have a background in conservation and countryside management. I have also run an organic, environmentally conscious farm in France, where I saw first-hand the value of good land management, protecting biodiversity and working with nature rather than against it.

The ease of operating in France has helped me identify where we have gone wrong in Wales. For me, environmental stewardship has never been an abstract political concept; it is something I live and practice every day. It's about the condition of the land you pass on to the next generation, it is about the wildlife that inhabits your fields and hedgerows and it's about the health of our rivers, the quality of our soil, the responsibility we all have to leave our countryside in a better condition than we found it. And it was precisely because of that commitment that I became increasingly frustrated with the bureaucracy I encountered in Wales. Too often, I found a system more interested in penalising conservationists for breaching some trivial rule buried deep in a dense guidance document, rather than encouraging landowners to do the right thing for the environment. The spirit of the guidance should be more important than a strict, legalistic interpretation where conservationists can be fined for petty reasons. People who want to restore habitats, plant trees and improve biodiversity should be treated as partners, not potential rule breakers. That experience helped spur me to stand for elected office, and that brings me to the purpose of today's debate.

speaker: John Clark AS
debate: 8. Short Debate: Green across the aisle: Making environmental stewardship a common cause
text:
We're told that even though Britain only emits 1 per cent of global carbon dioxide emissions, whilst China and India emit 40 per cent, we should pursue net zero as an example. Ironically, our main emissions cuts have come from exporting steel and other heavy industries to those same countries. But they cannot follow our example; they cannot export their emissions to themselves, and the goods we now import are often produced under weaker environmental rules.

Net zero in its current form is ideologically driven, it is damaging our economy and it will not deliver its aims. We need to look after the environment without crippling our industry or sacrificing our energy security. Nuclear power offers that practical path. It's carbon neutral, highly reliable and statistically the safest form of large-scale energy. Yes, the upfront costs and build times are significant, but the long-term benefits outweigh them. It's time to stop delaying. Let's re-industrialise, invest in nuclear and protect both our economic and environmental future. Thank you.

speaker: Andrew Rosindell
text: Since 2020, the Royal Navy has lost more than half of its frigates, its entire landing craft capability and its only icebreaker, and all of its attack submarines are now inoperable. speaker: Danny Kruger
text:
In the seven years that I have been a Member of this House, I do not think that I have been in a more respectful, positive and high-quality debate. There have been some absolutely outstanding contributions from across the House. I am not going to reach that standard, but I am proud to participate in the debate. I particularly acknowledge the contributions made by colleagues from Northern Ireland. Having visited a number of times recently, I can attest that they do politics pretty well there; there is a standard of speech-making that reflects the seriousness of politics there, and we have all benefited from that this evening.

My observation about the Bill and the amendments brought forward by the Government is that they essentially still fail on a core moral principle, which I will come to. The amendments that have been adduced as improving the Bill and addressing the concerns that have been raised do not, I am afraid, offer new protections. Many of them relate to measures that are already in force and could be applied, particularly those on the opportunities for anonymity and remote hearings.

The amendments and the new clauses are mostly simply important moral statements of what should be obvious. In particular, new clause 32 states that there is no equivalence between terrorist action and legal actions. It is extraordinary that it needs to be said that “a relevant person” in an inquest or proceedings

“must have regard to…the fact that force may lawfully be used to prevent unlawful violence”.

And what a thing to need to say that lawful action is not equivalent to terrorism! Why would that have to be stated in law, unless the Bill might be thought to suggest the opposite—that the law as it stands, and the Bill, could imply that equivalence?

At the heart of why the Bill remains inadequate is the essential imbalance in the legal procedures that the legacy of Northern Ireland applies. I pay tribute to a group of veterans I met recently—some special forces and some others—led by Dr Robert Parr, an academic at Oxford who was a Royal Marine and in special forces. He has written a very powerful paper that makes the simple point that the legal system—this is not addressed by the Bill; in fact, the Bill consolidates it—

“privileges the claims of former paramilitaries over those of the men and women who served the Crown”.

Of course, that is not intentional—the intention is to provide equity and parity—but the problem is structural.

The fact is that only a 10th of the deaths that happened during the troubles were caused by the security services, but it is men and women in uniform who must bear almost the whole institutional burden under the law as it stands, and that will not change under this Bill. The IRA and other paramilitary organisations got letters of comfort, early release and pardons. They had their weapons decommissioned without any forensic testing being done. Meanwhile, the British Army kept its records—indeed, it operated under the chain of command. It had accountability built into the work that it did; in fact, it had all the elements that made its decisions as safe as possible, as a military operating under the laws of a democracy. It is those elements that are now used against the Army, and that is the structural imbalance we face. That was apparent right at the beginning, when the Good Friday agreement was being implemented.

A letter has been released recently from John Reid, the Northern Ireland Secretary in 2001. He was writing to Tony Blair, the Prime Minister, and he made it clear that the proposed arrangement, in which an amnesty would be offered to terrorists but not to British veterans, was asymmetric and unjust, but that for reasons of political necessity, that is how it had to be. As Dr Parr has pointed out, the asymmetric exclusion of the security forces was therefore not the product of principled legal reasoning or an honest assessment of comparative culpability; it was the price of republican acquiescence in a political settlement. Just consider the insult that that represents to our soldiers.

I pay tribute to and honour the point that the right hon. Member for Rayleigh and Wickford (Mr Francois) made. Our soldiers beat the IRA to a standstill. They fought it to the negotiating table, and then they had to take the final indignity, which is that they, not the IRA, would face the threat of the law and of prosecution.

speaker: Danny Kruger
text:
That is absolutely right.

There was a question from the hon. Member for Spelthorne (Lincoln Jopp) earlier about who won. The answer is that, in so far as this was a military conflict, we know who won: it was the British Army, particularly with the help of special forces, but it had to suffer that indignity in consequence. It accepted as the price of peace the indignity and injustice of being exposed to the principle of liability and the threat of prosecution, while the IRA was indemnified. That was a bitter enough pill, but the actual practice of repeat prosecutions on the scale that we have seen—not the threat, but the reality—is unacceptable. That is not what was expected or accepted at the time, but back in those days, people reckoned without the European convention on human rights, the consequences of the Human Rights Act 1998, and the lawfare that the convention has brought into reality in our time, in this century. In particular, article 2 of the ECHR applies retrospectively to the investigations, based on the inadequacy of the investigations under standards that did not apply back in those days. That is the essential injustice of the law as it stands and of this Bill; there is a fundamental violation of the principle of legal certainty. Let me quote Dr Parr again. He says that

“the requirement that individuals be able to foresee the legal consequences of their actions at the time of those actions”

is itself

“a foundational element of the rule of law to which the ECHR is ostensibly committed.”

In passing, let me turn to one other indignity and injustice that, I am afraid, has been consolidated by this Bill. No accountability has ever been forthcoming from the Irish state, elements of which were arguably responsible for enabling, colluding with and covering up the actions of terrorists during the troubles, and none is expected in the future, despite the warm words of the Secretary of State. Thanks to this Bill, though, the Irish Government will play a crucial role in our own justice system. That is wrong.

What is happening is that the Government—and I honour them for doing this—are trying to reconcile common sense and decency, and the obvious appeal for justice on behalf of veterans, with the human rights framework that we have. I am afraid to say that that simply cannot be done, so I will end with a few thoughts about the future and the system that we need. We must start by reverting to the Good Friday/Belfast agreement, and to the principles that Tony Blair oversaw back then. He chose peace over justice, and he was right to do so. That was the right principle. Now, in our time, we need to choose truth over individual justice for people who can never realistically hope to attain individual justice. That is the way to heal a community; evidence from transitional justice programmes around the world, particularly in South Africa, demonstrates that that is the way to achieve healing in a community. The hon. Member for North Northumberland (David Smith) put it very well when he talked about the need for positive peace—national peace and reconciliation. Mrs Jones, the lady we have adverted to throughout this debate, is not going to get justice through the law, but if we genuinely open the archives—including the archives in Dublin—and encourage truthfulness, she could get the truth.

Going forward, we need to stop all future prosecutions of the sort that have persecuted our veterans, and we need a Bill that draws a line under the Northern Irish troubles, as well as the Haddon-Cave inquiry. We need a new process for war crimes under English law, and a new legal basis for military conduct without European law. I pay tribute to the right hon. Member for Goole and Pocklington (David Davis) and the private Member’s Bill he has introduced; I think that Bill goes in the right direction, but we can go even further. It particularly emphasises—this is the core point—that the chain of command is ultimately responsible for the actions of soldiers on the ground, and Ministers are ultimately responsible for the use of force, not the poor bloke who had to take a decision in a split-second, at risk of life.

I suggest that something more is needed even than what the right hon. Member for Goole and Pocklington suggests. We need to go further—we need to pull out of the ECHR altogether. There are many reasons for leaving it, and my party makes those points repeatedly. It protects terrorists and stops the deportation of illegal immigrants, but the most important reason is that it enables the prosecution of our soldiers. On those grounds, we must leave it.

speaker: Danny Kruger
text: We are very familiar with that argument. I do not think this is the time to have that debate, but I am confident—and there has been a lot of learned advice to this effect—that it is totally possible to withdraw from the ECHR while maintaining our obligations under the Good Friday agreement.

speaker: Suella Braverman
section: Clause 72 - The Independent Commission on Information Retrieval
text:
We are debating the parts of the Bill relating to the Independent Commission on Information Retrieval, inquests, and relaxations of the restrictions on police investigations. There is only one word to describe the measures in those parts of the Bill, and indeed the totality of the Bill, and I am afraid that is betrayal.

The Government demand much of their soldiers. They ask brave men and women to put their life in danger, and to sacrifice huge amounts. What do they get in return? We ostensibly have a military covenant, but the truth is that it is honoured more in the breach than the observance. The question really is: what do our troops get in return, at a time when the Government propose cutting the defence budget for military equipment by billions of pounds, will not promise to increase defence spending to 3% of GDP by 2030, and are asking men and women to step up and serve as reservists? The truth is that this country treats our enemies better than our heroes. [Interruption.] I am afraid the truth is that our bravest people get treated worse than those who terrorise us. That is what the litigation shows and what the Bill reflects.

The reality is that these measures will build more architecture and more process, and the process becomes punishment. The measures perpetuate the retrospective prosecution—and persecution, if you will—of our brave troops, many decades after their national service. This extension of litigation and lawfare wholly fails to comprehend and appreciate the complexities of battle and military action.

When terrorists are planning to attack us, they have the cards stacked in their favour. They can decide what to do, who to target, when to do it and how to do it. Our military, on the other hand, often have zero notice, and they have to make life-or-death decisions in split seconds to defend themselves and others. Now, many decades after those acts of bravery, lawyers, officials and Government Ministers are applying harsh rules to people who put their life at risk for our security. The decisions they made at the time were lawful; they were following orders and adhering to rules of engagement often set by their superiors, by officials at the Ministry of Defence or by Ministers, none of whom is being held to account decades after the act.

Let us remember: our armed forces are known around the world for upholding the highest standards of engagement in battle. They uphold the rules of the Geneva convention and the law of armed conflict, and they are known for engaging appropriately and proportionately with lethal force. This legislation and, indeed, the minefield of human rights legislation have operated to build a labyrinthine level of complexity when it comes to military action. We are tying our brave soldiers up in knots and, as a result, dragging them through the courts.

Surely the cases of the late Dennis Hutchings and Soldiers F, A and C, some of whom were exonerated after several investigations over several decades only to be re-prosecuted on charges of murder, should provide a salutary warning to the Government that the measures in the Bill are not fit for purpose. They risk reopening historical investigations and avoiding the finality that many of our soldiers and many people involved in the troubles need and deserve.

It is not just me and others on the Opposition Benches who say that. So egregious are the contents of the Bill that the regiment associations, unused to getting involved in politics, have come out and strongly opposed the contents of the Bill. The SAS, the special forces, the Paras and the veterans associations have united and campaigned vociferously against the contents of the Bill, because they know that its impacts will be devastating.

In my part of the world, in Fareham and Waterlooville, and in Gosport, Portsmouth, Aldershot and Hampshire we have thousands of brave veterans and serving personnel. Many of them have spoken to me about their real concerns about the Bill. The truth is that many people from the veterans community—in fact, all of them—come from good, traditional, patriotic families. They are people who believe in standing up for what they believe in, and they believe that this Bill and this Government are betraying those values, targeting them unfairly and persecuting them through legalese, lawyers and lawfare, unfairly and unjustifiably. It is a slap in the face and, frankly, the contents of the Bill move the goal posts and make it an incredibly unfair piece of legislation.

I worked on this subject many years ago before I was an MP, as a barrister. I was involved in working on behalf of the MOD, defending our soldiers against vexatious and malicious claims brought by people in Iraq against our brave soldiers who were engaged in military action out there. Litigation and class actions—resulting in zero convictions, mind you—were initiated by Shiner, and Starmer and, I am afraid, Hermer were involved. That disgraceful trio should hang their heads in shame for the part they played in bringing legal actions, unfairly and unjustifiably, against our brave British troops.

speaker: Suella Braverman
section: Clause 72 - The Independent Commission on Information Retrieval
text:
It is in response to discussions by various colleagues. The point is that the contents of the measures that I have talked about are wholly unacceptable. They do not answer the fundamental question about this Government continuing the prosecutions and allowing inquests, investigations and inquiries to continue many years after the act. The Government cannot guarantee that our brave veterans will not be hauled again in front of the courts after they have been exonerated or allowed to proceed. I am afraid that because the Government cannot provide that guarantee, the Bill and the clauses are not fit for purpose.

As Attorney General, I worked to build some of the measures contained in the legacy Act. It was challenging to make it compliant with the European convention on human rights, particularly article 2, and it was working on that legislation that convinced me that the UK needed to withdraw from the European convention on human rights. The legacy Act was not perfect, but it was progress because it brought finality to a lot of the investigations and prosecutions. The reality is that jurisprudence from the European Court of Human Rights, such as the cases of McCann, McKerr and Finucane, has meant that the interpretation of article 2, on the right to life, has been expanded, extended and, frankly, distorted beyond all recognition, which has given grounds to these endless and repetitive claims 30 years later.

speaker: Suella Braverman
section: Clause 72 - The Independent Commission on Information Retrieval
text: The hon. and learned Member puts it incredibly powerfully. The European Court of Human Rights has wholly distorted the application of article 2. Article 2 protects the right to life. No one here would disagree with that. It is an absolute right, and it was designed to protect individuals from state-sanctioned and arbitrary killing. That was the right intention behind the article’s drafting. But, because of decisions such as the one he refers to and many more, article 2 has now come to mean that people are entitled to an unlimited level of investigation and inquiry, that terrorists are entitled to compensation and that families of the IRA are entitled to be paid out because, as he says, their human rights have become more important than the human rights of law-abiding citizens and the victims of terrorism. It is an absurdity, and that is why my position remains that we must leave the European convention on—[Interruption.]

speaker: Suella Braverman
section: Clause 72 - The Independent Commission on Information Retrieval
text:
This Bill is, I am afraid, a retrograde step. It takes us backwards, not forwards from the legacy Act. It is really tragic, because the Government are asking for many young people to join up and serve their country, but why on earth would a young person take up that offer today? Traditionally, our soldiers have gone into battle to fight for our country. They have shown incredible heroism, courage and bravery, on levels that many of us can never imagine, and they have always felt confident that the Government would have their back and that they would be supported by those whose orders they were taking.

Today, however, many people serving in the armed forces tell me that they seriously question whether the Government would indeed back them. When they take the decision to pull that trigger today, will they have the confidence that the Government will stand up for them, many years down the line? Will their bravery today be twisted against them in years to come? Today, frankly, they cannot be sure that the Government will support them in their acts of courage. I am here speaking on behalf of veterans in my constituency of Fareham and Waterlooville, who tell me—[Interruption.] Opponents may be shaking their heads and chuntering, but I am here representing what has been told to me by those serving on our frontline.

The first duty of a Government is to defend the realm. Surely for that to mean anything, it must mean that the Government will stand by those men and women who put their lives in danger to defend our security. This Bill has failed in that duty, and it should not proceed.

speaker: Adrian Mason AS
section: Co-operation with the Republic of Ireland
text: First Minister, collaboration from the Irish Republic is something that I, like you, strongly support, particularly on trade, Holyhead and the resilience of our links across the Irish Sea. But co-operation between two Governments is one matter; advancing a party political constitutional objective is quite another. Your Government's shared statement, as you just mentioned before, with Ireland, specifically refers to co-operation in areas for which the Welsh Government has devolved responsibility. So, will you give this Chamber a categorical assurance that Welsh Government offices, officials, public money and ministerial visits to Ireland will not be used directly or indirectly to promote Plaid Cymru's campaign for Welsh independence? And can you give that assurance today?

speaker: Steven Rodaway AS
text: First Minister, once an annual health check identifies a need, responsibility should not fall on the individual to fight for treatment. People with learning disabilities need a clear, funded pathway to further tests, specialist assessment and treatment. Welsh Labour's Lynne Neagle cited £550 million over three years from Westminster for ALN. We know not all this money will be allocated to ALN, and much will go to other manifesto commitments and pledges. Last week, your finance Minister didn't, couldn't or wouldn't answer my question on Cynnal, but delivered another Plaid word salad with no answers. Show some transparency on what the rest of the £550 million is being used for. Will it support treatment protocols for people with learning disabilities? If not, please identify the specific NHS budget that funds this pathway. Thank you.

speaker: Catherine Cullen  AS
section: Adopted and Care-experienced Children and Young People
text: 3. What action is the Welsh Government taking to improve the support provided to adopted and care-experienced children and young people? OQ64755

speaker: Catherine Cullen  AS
section: Adopted and Care-experienced Children and Young People
text:
In the August 2026 report, Care Inspectorate Wales found that adoption support remained inconsistent, with waiting lists across almost every regional collaborative. The average number of days taken for children to move from the decision that they should be placed for adoption to actually being in place varied considerably across Wales, with the lowest figure of 248 days waiting in the Western Bay Adoption Service to a high of 450 days waiting in the Adoption Mid and West Wales collaborative. It is apparent that you want to build a united Wales, but in what modern nation is it acceptable for a child to wait an additional 202 days to get the outcome they need in one region compared to the other? This is not timely.

Having experienced the care system myself, both as a child and as an adoptive parent, I know the struggle first-hand. So, my question is simple: what specifically is this Government going to do to close these gaps and ensure equitable support nationwide?

speaker: Helen Jenner AS
section: Questions Without Notice from the Party Leaders
text:
Diolch, Lywydd. I want to firstly pay tribute to the Aberfan tragedy, which took place 60 years ago tomorrow. We'll never forget the lives lost and the community forever scarred by this devastating event. I appreciate the Government is making a statement on this later today, and I welcome the opportunity to pay further tribute then.

Llywydd, we are coming to the end of a very long half term, but whatever fatigue we might be feeling here in this Chamber, quadruple that and you might get somewhere near to how our teachers are feeling. It's not just down to the day-to-day workload; teachers are under immense strain when it comes to managing students' behaviour. More and more teachers are reporting high levels of verbal and physical abuse from students, and many are beginning to feel unsafe at work. First Minister, we've heard a lot about this Government's new literacy and numeracy frameworks, but will your Government now commit to delivering a robust behaviour framework, and will it include zero tolerance on violence, which would protect school staff from the sort of abuse that isn't accepted in other public institutions, because what's currently in place across schools in Wales is clearly not fit for purpose?

speaker: Benjamin Hodge Mckenna AS
text: The NHS in Wales now employs more than 100,000 members of full-time equivalent staff across the organisation. Those staff are the backbone of our NHS, and they do vital work to provide the care that so many people in Wales depend on. But, too often, they are overburdened and under-resourced, and those problems are exacerbated when staffing levels are insufficient. Official statistics show that there are currently more than 5,000 unfilled posts across our NHS, with medical and dental vacancies nearing 9 per cent. Sickness absences are elevated, and many clinicians are reporting that staffing levels are currently inadequate to meet patient demand. What specific action is the Government taking to reduce our dependency on agency and temporary staff, so that we can recruit and retain more home-grown workers and deliver a measurable improvement for our patients in Wales?

speaker: Helen Jenner AS
section: Questions Without Notice from the Party Leaders
text: First Minister, a well-known issue with behaviour in schools is linked to students having access to their mobile phones. At the end of July this year, schools across the border in England were given clarity on mobile phone use. What was initially guidance became law and, from the beginning of this academic year, a statutory mobile phone ban was in place. Yet, here we are in Wales, the first half term down, and teachers from my constituency are contacting me to say that the problems with phones are persisting, and headteachers are holding their hands up, saying there's nothing they can do because they're waiting for guidance from the Welsh Government. So, First Minister, when can teachers in Wales be given the same clarity as in England? When will this Government make a decision on whether or not to ban mobile phones from the classroom?

speaker: Francesca O'Brien AS
text: 7. What action is the Welsh Government taking to support high-street businesses in Gŵyr Abertawe? OQ64730

speaker: Francesca O'Brien AS
text: Thank you, First Minister. Our high streets are being taken over by dodgy vape and barbershops. Last week, in my constituency, two vape shops were shut down due to their suspected involvement in trading illegal goods, including drugs.
