speaker: David Hughes AS
text: 8. What action is the Welsh Government taking to ensure efficiency and waste reduction when delivering public services to achieve better value for money for taxpayers? OQ64796

speaker: David Hughes AS
text: Minister, Welsh taxpayers are continually being asked to pay more, yet many feel they are receiving less in return. Does the Minister agree that rather than continually demanding more from Welsh taxpayers, the Welsh Government should first demonstrate that it can spend the money it receives responsibly? And will the Minister commit to an independent, comprehensive audit of Welsh Government spending, identifying wasteful projects, unnecessary bureaucracy and duplication of services, with a clear commitment to redirect those savings towards front-line NHS services, education and local communities, because surely the priority should be delivering value for taxpayers, not simply spending more money?

speaker: Gareth Thomas AS
text: 11. How is the Welsh Government supporting the mental health of veterans in Wales who face investigation or prosecution relating to their service in Northern Ireland? OQ64774

speaker: Gareth Thomas AS
text: First Minister, soldiers from Wales answered their country's call in Northern Ireland. Some never came home, and this Remembrance Day we will rightly honour their memory. Those deployed as part of Operation Banner witnessed violence, experienced loss and lived under constant threat. For some reason, the scars, both physical and mental, have lasted a lifetime. Today, veterans face investigation or prosecution for events that did or did not take place decades ago. They are asked to account for a split-second decision when memories have faded, records have been lost and fellow soldiers, who could speak to them, have passed away. They've lived with years of uncertainty, questioning and public scrutiny. Those who served this country deserve to know that they will not face this ordeal alone. Yet Veterans' NHS Wales receives only £8 per veteran. Will the Welsh Government review the funding of Veterans' NHS Wales, so that the Welsh veterans receive the support they deserve? And will the First Minister take this opportunity to recognise the service and sacrifice of Welsh veterans who served in Northern Ireland?

speaker: Helen Jenner AS
section: Questions Without Notice from the Party Leaders
text:
You're talking about empowering schools to make the necessary choices around phones, and that leads to this notion of guidance as opposed to bringing something into law. First Minister, the fact is that you are speaking, as you know, to a former teacher, and I can tell you that schools interpret guidance very, very differently. So, what we really need is leadership from this Government on this matter. It is vital that a consistent approach is enforced across all schools in Wales, not only to benefit teachers dealing with poor behaviour associated with phone use, but for the well-being and academic success of our students. I would like to read out a quote from a former year 11 pupil of mine, word for word:

'It's like you're distracted by your phone. You can't get anything done. I know the school says, "Keep your phone in your bag", but I know it's there, and if I hear it buzz, I just have to check it, and I can't focus on anything else. If they banned phones in schools, I know I'd hate it'—

she was very honest—

'but I'd keep thinking about all the things I'd be able to get done if they did.'

This is a 16-year-old GCSE student crying out for a boundary with phones for the good of her education. First Minister, the Government can't control what goes on in people's homes, but it can lead the way when it comes to removing the distraction of phones from schools. We've got the worst Programme for International Student Assessment scores in the UK and a mental health catastrophe on the way. So much of this can be linked to excessive phone use. So, First Minister, I ask will you today commit to an outright ban on mobile phones in schools and, if so, when can we see that happen?

speaker: Catherine Cullen  AS
text: 1. What legal advice has the Counsel General provided to the Welsh Government regarding the legal rights of adopted children to seek specialist support when their needs continue into adulthood? OQ64742

speaker: Catherine Cullen  AS
text: Counsel General, for many adopted young people, turning 18 does not mean their need for support disappears; in fact, it can be the point when they need it the most. Adopted young people can face complex challenges around identity, trauma, attachment and mental health, yet as they transition into adulthood, the support available to them can become fragmented, leaving them struggling to navigate adult services at the time they need it. We wouldn't expect a young person to suddenly overcome the impact of early childhood traumas just because they've reached a certain age. So, will the Counsel General clarify whether existing Welsh legislation provides sufficient protection for adopted young people into adulthood, and whether the Government is considering introducing a statutory duty to ensure continuing specialist support up until the age of 25?

speaker: Adrian Mason AS
section: Questions Without Notice from Party Spokespeople
text: Thank you, Counsel General. I know you wouldn't stand there making excuses—I'm quite fully aware of that. But considering Plaid Cymru's fierce commitment to promoting and preserving the Welsh language, which has rightly received support across the Chamber, of course, it remains unclear why the Welsh language versions of statutory texts are repeatedly attracting reporting points concerning inconsistencies between the English and Welsh texts. So, going forward, Counsel General, what is the Welsh Government doing to ensure that translation of statutory texts into the Welsh language are accurate, clear and contribute positively to the accessibility of Welsh law?

speaker: Iain McIntosh AS
text: It's probably no surprise, but as a Member with Powys in my constituency, I'm going to be asking the same kinds of questions. Counsel General, when a health board proposes cutting hospital beds in rural communities, despite serious concerns from patients, families and local representatives, surely Welsh Ministers should have the power to step in and stop it. That's exactly what we're seeing here with Powys Teaching Health Board at the moment and their proposals affecting hospitals in Ystradgynlais and Llandrindod Wells. These decisions can have devastating consequences for communities that already struggle to access healthcare. If Ministers don't have sufficient powers to intervene, isn't it time they were given them? This Welsh Government cannot keep ducking and diving and telling people that health boards make these decisions independently while expecting the public to hold you to account for the NHS. Surely accountability must come with the power to act.

speaker: Adrian Mason AS
section: Questions Without Notice from Party Spokespeople
text: I thank you again for your honesty, Counsel General. In light of the often elusive nature of inter-governmental communications between the Welsh and UK Governments, can you commit to ensuring that, where it is appropriate, the Legislation Committee is provided with a clear record of discussions, negotiations and agreements reached on draft legislation? Whilst I do recognise, Counsel General, that the Welsh Government may consider these discussions are subject to privilege, there must be some exceptions to facilitate proper scrutiny. So, basically, to ensure that draft legislation can be scrutinised, of course, it is vital that both the Legislation Committee and the wider Senedd understands the context of these negotiations. So, Counsel General, transparency is of paramount importance if we intend to collaboratively create a clear, cohesive body of Welsh law for the remainder of the seventh Senedd. Would you agree?

speaker: Adrian Mason AS
section: Questions Without Notice from Party Spokespeople
text: Diolch, Lywydd. Good afternoon, Counsel General. The two-week time frame required under Standing Order 29.2 is not merely an administrative suggestion. It's in place to ensure that proper scrutiny of the relevant provisions of UK legislation can be conducted by committees. The Welsh Government's repeated failure to adhere to this time frame impedes proper scrutiny. Counsel General, in light of this, can you provide the Senedd with an update on the clear action planned to be taken by the Welsh Government to ensure that committees are able to effectively scrutinise legislation made by your Government in the interest of fair and accountable governance?

speaker: Adrian Mason AS
section: Questions Without Notice from Party Spokespeople
text: Thank you.

speaker: Helen Jenner AS
text: Thank you. The inquiry has confirmed that it will examine matters involving devolved services in Wales. You started to clarify the legal obligations there placed on the Welsh Government to co-operate with the inquiry. Will this include provision of relevant documents and evidence, and will there be any legislative changes necessary following its findings?

speaker: Catherine Cullen  AS
text: 6. What legal advice has the Counsel General provided to the Welsh Government regarding whether removing parents' right to withdraw their children from relationships and sexuality education is consistent with the European Convention on Human Rights? OQ64740

speaker: Catherine Cullen  AS
text:
Relationships and sexuality education, as you say, has been a compulsory element of the Curriculum for Wales since 2022. In its own words, the framework covers relationships, rights, equality and diversity. What parents may not be aware of, however, is that education is compulsory and in force in Wales from the age of three, including in funded nursery education. Moreover, unlike previous sex education arrangements, RSE is mandatory until 16, and parents do not have the general right to withdraw. Now, whatever our views on the ECHR may be, we are as lawmakers in the Senedd totally bound by the European convention on human rights. Article 2 of protocol No. 1 plainly states that

'the State shall respect the right of parents to ensure such education and teaching is in conformity with their own religious and philosophical convictions.'

So, quite simply, do parents in Wales actually still have the right to withdraw their children from RSE when it does not conform to their religious and philosophical convictions?

speaker: Francesca O'Brien AS
text: Thank you, Counsel General. The last Labour Government introduced a £5,000 grant for teacher training, but it was only available to student teachers from ethnic minorities, not on merit, but purely based on their skin colour. The current Plaid Cymru Government has carried on this scheme. Will the Counsel General agree to publish any legal advice given to the Welsh Government that they've received on this policy, and will he commit to ensuring that the Welsh Government makes any advice public, so that the people of Wales can see how their money has been spent on this piece of anti-white discrimination?

speaker: John Clark AS
text: 8. What legal advice has the Counsel General provided to the Welsh Government regarding Welsh Ministers’ powers to call in planning applications for large-scale data-centre developments, including the statutory criteria under the relevant planning legislation and the legal duties that apply when such a request is received? OQ64745

speaker: John Clark AS
text: Given that several call-in requests for data centre schemes, including the one at the former Ferodo site near Caernarfon, are currently under consideration, what does the legal advice say about the statutory criteria under section 77 of the Town and Country Planning Act and the threshold of 'more than local importance', when issues such as grid capacity, energy demand or the absence of a specific national data centre policy are raised?

speaker: Francesca O'Brien AS
text: 7. What legal advice has the Counsel General provided to the Welsh Government on the compatibility of its policymaking with the Equality Act 2010? OQ64736

speaker: Francesca O'Brien AS
text: Thank you, Counsel General. Young white women and children in this country were groomed, raped and trafficked, often by groups of mainly Pakistani men over decades. The worst injustice this country has seen, in my opinion. Wales needs its own inquiry. There are strong suspicions that it happened in Swansea, in my constituency, along with many other places in Wales. Section 29 of the Inquiries Act lets Welsh Ministers hold an inquiry into anything they have functions over. So, my question is simple, Counsel General: does the Welsh Government have the legal power to hold its own inquiry into how devolved services in Wales failed these children and young women—'yes' or 'no'?

speaker: Helen Jenner AS
text: 4. What legal advice has the Counsel General provided to the Welsh Government regarding its legal responsibilities in relation to the independent inquiry into grooming gangs? OQ64725
