section: Establishing a Distinct or Separate Legal Jurisdiction
text: 11. What legal advice has the Counsel General provided to the Welsh Government on the legal implications of establishing a distinct or separate legal jurisdiction for Wales? OQ64744

speaker: Louise Emery AS
text: I'm sure you just made a political statement about the strong broadcasting sector required to be devolved, but, okay, I'll forgive you on that one.

speaker: Louise Emery AS
text: Okay, fair enough. It's obviously currently largely reserved to the UK Parliament, so the question is: how do you assess the implications of such a change with broadcasting to the overall existing constitutional settlement? So, how does that work by taking something out of the constitutional settlement?

speaker: John Clark AS
section: Establishing a Distinct or Separate Legal Jurisdiction
text: What legal advice has the Counsel General provided on the practical implications of moving from the existing distinct body of Welsh law to a fully separate jurisdiction, specifically for the single England and Wales legal profession, cross-border practices, access to justice, and legal certainty for businesses operating on both sides of the border?

speaker: Louise Emery AS
text: Yes, I thought you'd just made quite a political statement, because she asked you whether you agreed it should be devolved, and you said you did.

speaker: Nigel Williams AS
text:
I ask the Welsh Government for a statement on capital investment into north Wales's civic and sporting infrastructure, specifically regarding the urgent need for a 50m Olympic-sized swimming pool. Currently, Wales has just two 50m facilities—one in Cardiff and one in Swansea; and from Holyhead right along the A55 corridor there is not a single one. Our young, talented athletes and their families are forced to make multi-hour round trips across the border into England several times a week just to train on equal terms with their peers. With 80 per cent of Welsh public pools over 20 years old—and I can tell you that for a fact because I worked in one many years ago—and Betsi Cadwaladr under immense strain, a modern aquatics hub would deliver a vital preventative health dividend and teach life-saving skills.

Will the Trefnydd arrange for the Welsh Government, alongside Sport Wales, Swim Wales and local authorities, to commission a formal feasibility study to finally deliver regional equity for north Wales and commit the Welsh Government to putting an end to years of regional underinvestment, get this project on the table and deliver the fair funding and preventative healthcare infrastructure that the people of north Wales deserve? Diolch.

speaker: David Mills AS
text: I'd like to ask for a statement from the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability on the state of dog breeding in Wales and whether the Welsh Government intends to review the current regulatory framework. The RSPCA has raised concerns that dog breeding continues on a considerable scale in Wales and that existing legislation may no longer be fit for purpose. There have also been calls for a review of current laws, a centralised microchipping database, consideration of a national scoring system for breeders and whether a national representative body could provide greater support to responsible breeders. Given the importance of protecting animal welfare, while ensuring that responsible breeders have the support and the clarity they need, can the Welsh Government outline whether it will review the current regulatory framework to ensure it remains effective and fit for purpose and whether it will consider combining and streamlining the regulation into a single piece of legislation?

speaker: Art Wright AS
text: Can I request from the Cabinet Minister for Social Justice and Equality a statement on how the Welsh Government will work to end the need for foodbanks in Wales? Around a quarter of adults, or 260,000 people in Wales, are going without enough food because they cannot afford it. Last year, over 150,000 food parcels were distributed by the Trussell foodbanks alone, with many more needing food from food pantries and other sources. With the expected huge increase in the cost of living coming in January, I am concerned that this will drive more people to need emergency food aid. Failure to tackle hunger and hardship leads to Wales spending an additional £560 million a year on public services. Overall, public finances and the economy in Wales could benefit by £3.6 billion each year if people were protected from hunger and hardship. Diolch.

speaker: Laura Anne Jones AC
text:
Trefnydd, I would like two statements, please. I've just returned from the Welsh Dairy Show in Carmarthenshire this morning. It was a fantastic showcase of what the industry has to offer here in Wales. But it was also a great opportunity to speak to our dairy farmers and hear directly their concerns. And, on the back of that, I would like an oral statement on the dairy industry in Wales, outlining what this Welsh Government will do, and how it's working with Westminster to ensure that our Welsh dairy farmers are getting the support that they need.

Secondly, Trefnydd, NHS England has now finally banned biological males from women's spaces, following the Supreme Court ruling that sex means biological sex. I would like an urgent statement from this Government reassuring this Chamber that NHS Wales will soon follow suit, because women and girls in Wales have waited far too long for these basic protections. Diolch.

speaker: Llŷr Powell AS
text: Could I have a statement from the Trefnydd and the Welsh Government on what efforts are being taken to address rough-sleeping and homelessness in Wales? As we're coming into the winter time, it's becoming very concerning about how many people are sleeping out in horrendous conditions right now, and I'd be grateful if the Government could come forward on what we can do, and, hopefully, we can find consensus around the Chamber to address this, so we don't see more lives lost by rough-sleeping this winter.

speaker: Steven Rodaway AS
text:
Thank you, Llywydd. Trefnydd, at a recent meeting, I heard that delays over Morriston Hospital's access road are holding back proposals for a proposed new emergency department. We understand that much of the planning sits with local government, but where is the ministerial leadership? What has Plaid done to bring the health board, the planning authority, and Natural Resources Wales around one table, agree what remains outstanding for major projects, and set deadlines for resolving them?

Delays have consequences beyond the hospital. Construction work means jobs and spending with local suppliers. Every delay postpones these benefits. The local economy needs investment moving, not paperwork circulating. Plaid promised tangible action from day one. One hundred and sixty-one days later, where is that action for Morriston? Your delivery efforts appear to need resuscitation, just like those of your Labour predecessors, who are now your partners in this cozy budget deal.

Will the Minister schedule a statement setting out the meetings Ministers have convened, the obstacles still outstanding, and a clear timetable for action? The NHS, its patients, and my constituents need action. Thank you.

speaker: Helen Jenner AS
debate: 4. Statement by the First Minister: 60th Anniversary of the Aberfan Disaster
text: Wales produced some of the best coal in the world. For generations, Welsh miners sustained our communities, our industries and our economy. They represented the best of what we might today call 'alarm clock Britain'—people who got up, went to work, and undertook very difficult and dangerous labour to support their families and their country. But as we celebrate their contribution, we must never forget the terrible price that was sometimes paid. We must learn from those disasters. We must remember the communities that suffered. And, above all, we must never forget those who went to work or went to school and who never came home again. Thank you very much.

speaker: Helen Jenner AS
debate: 4. Statement by the First Minister: 60th Anniversary of the Aberfan Disaster
text: I thank the First Minister for his statement marking this solemn occasion. Sixty years ago, on 21 October, staff and pupils at Pantglas went to school on the last day before half term. Tragically, for so many of them, that would be the last day of their lives. What happened in Aberfan was one of the most devastating disasters in the history of Wales and one of the darkest in our coal mining history. One hundred and forty-four people lost their lives in Aberfan, including 116 children and five teachers. Parents and families were left to live with the unimaginable grief for the rest of their lives. And yet, this disaster was avoidable. D.C.W. Jones, an engineer from Merthyr, had warned of the dangers for more than three years, but the National Coal Board failed disastrously to ensure that appropriate safety standards were followed. The horror of Aberfan destroyed not only the village, but also affected communities across Wales, the United Kingdom and, indeed, the entire world.

speaker: Helen Jenner AS
debate: 4. Statement by the First Minister: 60th Anniversary of the Aberfan Disaster
text:
The depth of its impact is reflected in the fact that Her Late Majesty Queen Elizabeth II visited Aberfan on eight occasions, including in the immediate aftermath of the disaster. This week, the King, Queen and Prince of Wales are set to visit, and I thank the royal family for the respect and commitment they have shown in commemorating Aberfan.

It is often during the very worst of times that we see the very best in people. Sixty years ago, Aberfan, an ordinary Welsh mining village, showed extraordinary courage and resilience, as the First Minister has referred to. As a former teacher and as somebody who has always championed the school staff who do so much for our children, often while feeling underpaid and undervalued, I particularly want to pay tribute to Nansi Williams. Nansi was a dinner lady at Pantglas junior school. She was also a woman of extraordinary courage. Her actions that day saved the lives of five children, but in doing so, she made the ultimate sacrifice. Nansi gave her own life protecting those children, who were later found alive, shielded beneath her body. One of those survivors, Paul Harries, has said that had it not been for Nansi Williams, instead of 116 children dying that morning, the number would have been 121.

I also pay tribute to Hettie, the aunt of the Deputy First Minister, whom the First Minister referenced in his remarks. And I want to pay tribute to Denise Morgan, who was just 11 years old at the time and whose nine-year-old sister tragically died in the disaster. Denise had been a pupil at Pantglas and was left deeply traumatised, yet, inspired by her teachers and despite all she'd endured, she went on to become a headteacher herself, dedicating her career to giving new generations of children the very best start in life.

Our children are our future. In their innocence, their curiosity and their sense of fun, we place so many of our hopes and dreams for a better tomorrow. But on that day 60 years ago, so many futures were taken from the village of Aberfan in the most unimaginable way. The tragedies left a lasting reminder of just how cruel life can be. Yet, the Aberfan community also showed us what is possible when people pull together, whatever the odds. Villagers stood side by side with dignity. They supported one another, cared for one another and honoured those they had lost. That sense of togetherness can sometimes feel as though it is disappearing. But, across many parts of Wales, it remains strong. We must cherish that community spirit, hold on to it with both hands and never let it go.

There is also a responsibility on us today to ensure that the lessons of the past translate into action for the future. The UK Government has made a multi-year commitment of £118 million over the 2026-29 period to the Welsh Government for disused coal tip safety. That is welcome, but we must go further. I sincerely hope we can take a cross-party approach, working hand in hand with the UK Government, to secure more support.

The Disused Mine and Quarry Tips (Wales) Act 2025 was an important step, as the First Minister said, establishing a regulatory framework for the management of disused tips and creating the disused tips authority for Wales, which will take responsibility for tip safety from April 2027. I call on the Welsh Government to do everything it can to support that authority in its work, because the risks have not disappeared. One in 10 households in Wales is within 1 km of a coal tip rated as posing a potential risk to public safety, while households close to the highest risk coal tips have reportedly faced home insurance costs up to 40 per cent higher. This cannot be right and must be addressed.

Finally, I want to take this opportunity to remember another terrible chapter in our mining history, the Senghenydd disaster of 14 October 1913, near Caerphilly, the anniversary of which fell just last week. That disaster claimed the lives of 439 miners and one rescuer.

speaker: Jason O'Connell AS
debate: 4. Statement by the First Minister: 60th Anniversary of the Aberfan Disaster
text:
First Minister, 60 years ago, we know that 144 lives were lost in Aberfan, and 116 of those were children. Now, I cannot comprehend what it must be like to send your child off to school and not have them return. For the families, the survivors and the community of Aberfan, the pain of that day will never go away.

Now, as one of the Members representing this community in this Chamber, I know that Aberfan is not simply a tragedy recorded in our history books. It's a community that carries the scars of what happened that day, and will do so for the rest of time. I had the honour yesterday of attending the University of South Wales, where the last remaining survivor, Jeff Edwards, gave a talk—a powerful account of loss, of grief, but also the fight for justice after the event itself, and the events that the community had to go through to get that justice.

First Minister, remembrance must be about more than words. It must also be about responsibility and ensuring that those lessons are never forgotten. So, 60 years on, what assurances can you give the families of Aberfan that the lessons of that terrible day remain at the heart of how we protect our Valleys communities today? And can I have your assurance that the physical coal tip remediation will receive priority, and can you please outline how the remainder of coal tips at risk across Wales are to be made safe? We owe those 144 souls and the families nothing less. Diolch.

speaker: David Hughes AS
debate: 4. Statement by the First Minister: 60th Anniversary of the Aberfan Disaster
text:
Like Lis, I was brought up in Aberfan and had many friends who were there that day. So, today, we pause with heavy hearts to remember the lives lost in Aberfan's disaster. Sixty years on, the pain of that terrible day remains deeply felt by families, friends and the community whose lives were forever changed. We remember the children whose lives were taken far too soon, the adults who lost their lives and all those who witnessed such unimaginable grief. Aberfan was not simply a tragedy in history; it was a community's heartbreak and a reminder of how precious every life is.

Today we honour those who were lost, remember all those who carry on and hold the families and people of Aberfan in our thoughts. May the memories never fade, may the compassion, courage and strength shown in the aftermath continue to inspire us. We will remember them, we will grieve and we will never forget. That's all I ask of this place: that we never forget. Thank you.

speaker: Cai Parry-Jones AS
debate: 5. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Finance: Taxation (Wales) Bill
text:
Thank you, Minister, for introducing this Bill. In your statement you say that the consultation received detailed responses from taxpayers, professional bodies and industry representatives. However you didn't say how many responses the public consultation received. I have the answer—it was nine. And of those nine, up to only four were individual Welsh taxpayers—four—four in a population of 3.2 million. This is hardly the wide-ranging ringing endorsement your statement would have us believe. I got more responses from exposing the Welsh Government's whisky-tasting trip to France.

Moving on to the details of this legislation, I am concerned about the new powers being gifted to the Welsh Revenue Authority. Under current rules, the Welsh Revenue Authority generally needs either the owner's agreement or approval from an independent tribunal before inspecting private premises, however, this Bill would allow the Welsh Revenue Authority to carry out certain landfill tax inspections without either form of approval. We are talking about Welsh officials without independent approval entering privately owned land and premises, potentially without the occupier having prior knowledge of the inspection. Removing an existing layer of independent scrutiny is a big change and one that needs justification. Could you explain what evidence demonstrates that removing prior tribunal approval is necessary? Also, what safeguards will ensure that inspections are justified and proportionate and stay within the limits of their powers, especially when carrying out unannounced inspections on private land when the occupier may not be present?

Beyond the inspections, the Bill would also allow the Welsh Revenue Authority to share more taxpayer information with local authorities and their service providers, withhold certain tax repayments during inquiries, and request information after property transactions. While the Bill includes safeguards and appeal rights, questions remain about how these additional powers will operate in practice. What safeguards will ensure that confidential taxpayer information is only shared where necessary?

The Bill will also allow the Welsh Revenue Authority to withhold certain tax repayments to people while an inquiry is ongoing. If the Welsh Revenue Authority is meant to pay tax back to someone, they have wider powers to withhold that payment, potentially for years, before actually having to pay it out. It would also allow the Welsh Revenue Authority to request information about certain property transactions years after they have taken place. How will taxpayers be protected from lengthy delays to legitimate repayments, and how will the Welsh Revenue Authority ensure that information requests remain proportionate? Diolch, Lywydd.

speaker: John Clark AS
debate: 5. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Finance: Taxation (Wales) Bill
text: Minister, thank you for your statement today. Section 4 would allow the Welsh Revenue Authority to withhold certain tax repayments while an inquiry is ongoing. Your own explanatory memorandum acknowledges that some inquiries can take months, or even years, potentially creating cash flow difficulties for taxpayers. Beyond the existing appeal right, will you commit to clear, published service standards for these inquiries, and to reporting how long repayments are being withheld, so that small businesses and taxpayers are not left facing prolonged uncertainty?

speaker: Iain McIntosh AS
debate: 5. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Finance: Taxation (Wales) Bill
text:
Diolch, Lywydd. Cabinet Minister, your Government's own impact assessment estimates that this Bill will cost an additional £422,000 over 10 years, while claiming only £2.6 million in benefits. But much of those supposed savings are simply staff time being freed up, rather than actual money being saved for taxpayers. And when it comes to additional inspections of businesses, your assessment dismisses the disruption as negligible, without even putting a financial figure on it.

Can you tell us how much of that £2.6 million will actually translate into reduced public spending? What assessment have you made of whether those additional powers and administrative costs are genuinely necessary? Because taxpayers deserve real savings, not just theoretical efficiencies on what appears to be a spreadsheet whilst the cost of government keeps growing.

speaker: James Evans AS
debate: 6. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Social Care, Mental Health and Women’s Health: Update on the National Care Service Programme
text:
Thank you, Deputy Presiding Officer. Can I thank the Minister for her statement this afternoon? As you're very well aware, I have always been against the establishment of a national care service, for reasons I won't go over again because you've heard them 100 times and they are a matter for the record.

You mentioned the people who work in social care, and I absolutely agree with you, they do deserve more than thanks. You've celebrated, along with a lot of politicians in here, that we pay social care staff the real living wage. We need to go further than that. If we want to see more social care staff in the system, they need to be paid more than the real living wage. So, I'd like to know from you, when is this Government going to put a proper pay structure in place to make sure that our social care staff are paid appropriately? One way in which we think you could do that is by integrating social care into the health system, something that I've advocated for for a long time. I'd like to hear: is that something that you and the Cabinet Minister for health are looking closely at?

Your statement also highlighted equitable and high-quality support across the country, and I think it is very important that we do have equitable care across the country, but we all know the challenges of delivering social care in rural areas, and that didn't come through in your speech. Can you explain to me and the rest of the Members in this Chamber what is the Government doing to ensure that we have good-quality social care in rural areas? We know that is an exceptionally difficult place to recruit our social care staff, so I'd like to know what the Government is doing around that.

You did mention in your statement fair funding, but one thing I didn't hear right the way through it was how much funding you're actually going to provide as well, so it would be quite useful to know, as part of the budget discussions that are going on with the Cabinet Minister for Finance, how much money you're allocating to the national care service, as the Cabinet Minister walks in through the door. [Laughter.] We're going to find out how much money you're going to give, Cabinet Minister, to the national care service, and how much you're allocating to this area of policy, because I think that's something that is very interesting to know and not something that you raised in your statement.

You also raised unpaid carers as well, and I think they are actually the unsung heroes of our care system across the country. We all know that they save our NHS, not just millions but billions of pounds, and if we actually had to start paying them for the work that they're doing looking after their loved ones, it would bankrupt the Welsh Government, and I'm pretty sure it would bankrupt the UK Government as well. So, I'm interested to know what extra support you're going to put in place for them, because you did mention, as you went through, community-based services, and I'm sure I'm not the only Member in my area that has actually seen those day-centre services being removed from local government control because they can't afford to run them anymore. So, there is a bit of joined-up thinking that needs to happen here, isn't there? If you talk about strengthening community-based services, that means our local authorities have to be funded properly to provide those services as well, because if they haven't got the money to provide them, it puts more pressure back on the people who are caring for people at home.

You also mentioned prevention, and it is important that we keep people in their homes for as long as possible, because we do know that that does take pressure off the care service. But as someone who was a local government cabinet minister in a previous life, I also know about the disabled facilities grant, which is actually always overspent in local government. And I'm just interested, from your perspective, how much money, working with the Cabinet Minister for local government, you're putting into this area, because if you are talking about prevention, you need to make sure the measures are in place in people's homes to make sure they can stay there for longer and to make sure they can actually get around their own home.

What else did you talk about? You talked about an awful lot today. You raised also the national social care academy. This is something that's actually quite an exciting piece of work—I think there is something that could be developed here—but I'd like to actually know when this academy is going to be developed, because the contract is still on Sell2Wales, and we all know how long things take to move through the sausage machine in Welsh Government, and it's probably going to take an awful long time for this to be developed. So, from yourself, I'd like to know, when do you see that national care academy coming online? Because if there's anything to go by by Government contracting, we're actually not probably going to see it for another three to four years, which I'd actually think would be a big shame, if we're trying to get more people into the profession.

And finally, about Senedd scrutiny, I think it is very important, as this piece of work goes through, that the Senedd is given more opportunity to scrutinise this. I know the Chairman of the health committee is in the Chamber here, and I'm sure this is a piece of work they will be looking into. So, I'd just like to know, will you be committed to providing regular updates to the Senedd on the development of this national care service to make sure all Members across the Chamber have got the opportunity to scrutinise you about the accountability, the funding that's going to go into it, and ultimately the delivery? Because that's the way—. I keep saying to this Government, 'Talk is cheap, but delivery is more', and you said at the start that our social care staff across the country deserve more than warm words, and they need action, and they do need it now. So, if you can answer some of my questions, I'd be very grateful. Diolch.

speaker: Nigel Williams AS
debate: 6. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Social Care, Mental Health and Women’s Health: Update on the National Care Service Programme
text:
I'd like to reiterate my praise for the hard work of carers right across Wales, and unpaid carers as well. We keep hearing ambitious promises about a national care and support service, yet front-line social care in places such as Flintshire and Wrexham remains under severe pressure. Around 1,300 to 1,400 patients across Wales are waiting in hospital despite being medically fit for discharge because the care packages and supported accommodation they need are simply not available. In north Wales, those pressures are felt particularly acutely as Betsi Cadwaladr continues to face significant challenges. While care providers struggle with workforce shortages, rising demand and commissioning pressures cause problems.

Deputy Minister, much of your statement, as stated by Natasha Asghar, focuses on new structures, leadership arrangements, intelligence hubs, academies and national conversations, but for the families waiting for support and patients stuck in hospital beds, those initiatives will mean little unless they deliver real improvements on the ground. So, my question is: given that you say success should be measured not by structures you created, but by whether people can access the right support at the right time, when can older and vulnerable people across Wales expect to see a measurable increase in the front-line care capacity, a reduction in delayed hospital discharges and better access to the care and support they need, rather than more administration, new bodies and further planning?

speaker: James Evans AS
debate: 6. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Social Care, Mental Health and Women’s Health: Update on the National Care Service Programme
text: The devil is in the detail.

speaker: Catherine Cullen  AS
debate: 6. Statement by the Deputy Minister for Social Care, Mental Health and Women’s Health: Update on the National Care Service Programme
text:
Diolch, Deputy Llywydd. I welcome the Deputy Minister's statement today, but it seems that the statement is doubling down again on this Stronger Safeguarding for a Safer Wales. As you know, I have already expressed serious reservations about this, because while it looks fluffy on the outside, it is not so on the inside.

We already know about the damage that overly burdensome safeguarding procedures can cause in the care and health services. At the moment, it is quite reactive. We only need to listen to some of the stories of people who have been under this to understand what it is like. So, we must ensure that social care does not suffer the same fate. Safeguarding must protect people without drowning front-line workers in paperwork and without placing front-line professionals' lives on hold while they are subject to safeguarding inquiries. How can we recruit and hope to retain in the care sector with these strict safeguarding measures in line? It does not go well.

The statement says that success will not be measured by structures created or documents published, but how exactly, then, are you going to measure success? And what measurable targets, timescales and outcomes will be published to demonstrate improvements in care recruitment and retention? Diolch.

speaker: Tom Montgomery AS
debate: 7. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Finance: An Update on Council Tax
text: Minister, in your statement, you say you want to explore new ideas around council funding. We heard several clear ones last week from these benches. One was local government mergers. Here in Wales, we have local authorities serving much fewer residents than our English counterparts. The average number of residents served by a council in Wales is 144,000, with 14 local authorities falling below that average. Compare that to local authorities in England: the average number of residents served by a unitary authority in England is around 250,000 to 300,000 people. Cornwall serves almost 600,000, whilst North Yorkshire serves almost 650,000. This provides us with clear evidence that Welsh council tax payers are funding an enlarged local government sector that is too big and too expensive. So, Minister, would you agree with me that we now must seriously consider mergers as part of the fundamental reforms of local government in Wales? And will you here, now, promise to create a package of financial support for local authority mergers to help make our local government more effective and sustainable for taxpayers?

speaker: Steve Bayliss AS
debate: 7. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Finance: An Update on Council Tax
text: Diolch, Ddirprwy Lywydd. Cabinet Minister, families across Afan Ogwr Rhondda needed certainty, and so I give you credit for finally giving them the answer. But when the previous Government put 2028 into law, the Institute for Fiscal Studies hoped that would prevent further delays. Today, you're proposing 2032, beyond another Senedd election. So, you say protecting households that face higher bills could cost up to £80 million in the first year. The previous Government estimated £11.7 million to implement revaluation over 2026-27 and 2027-28. So, before asking this Senedd to approve another four-year delay, will you publish exactly how much taxpayers' money has already been spent or committed, including with the Valuation Office Agency, and what postponing the programme will cost? Diolch.

speaker: Francesca O'Brien AS
debate: 7. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Finance: An Update on Council Tax
text:
Can I thank the Cabinet Minister for her statement? I do welcome this u-turn. It's not often we do welcome a u-turn, but we do on this occasion. Families have waited with uncertainty for months, Minister, to find out what this Government plans to do with their council tax. In that time, we had the First Minister say revaluation would go ahead, and the Minister for local government said Ministers were still actively looking at it. So, I'm glad to see you've changed your mind.

This is the second time a Welsh Government has pushed this back, and I'm pleased to see the Welsh Government will be removing the 2028 date from the legislation instead of leaving this hanging over Welsh families' heads for any longer. I note that this legislation will come forward next month and we will wait to see the finer details. When people are struggling and we have a UK Government budget looming, families can't afford the risk that they'll be dragged into higher tax bands, because Wales already suffers from higher bills. Council tax in Wales has risen by an average of 5 per cent every year since 1999, against 4 per cent in England, and just 2 per cent in Scotland.

This year, 16 out of 22 councils in Wales put their bills up by more than 5 per cent. And that is why, last week, Reform brought forward their debate on the council tax referendum to the Senedd on exactly this topic. We believe that residents should have the final say in a referendum on any rise above 4.99 per cent. This would have protected households whatever the bands may look like in the future.

The issue is clear for anyone who's looked at the numbers. Last time Wales revalued, more than 20 years ago, a third of homes moved up at least one band, and only 8 per cent moved down. In Cardiff, 64 per cent went up. Some of the poorest communities were the hardest hit and the total rise in council tax that year reached over 9 per cent. In Swansea at the moment, for an average band D property, we are already paying higher council tax than those living in Kensington. In the Government's own research, around a quarter of households would have seen their band go up, and protecting them would have cost up to £80 million in the first year alone, and that is confirmed by your statement there. That tells you the scale of the increase families were facing under the current plans.

How many households would have moved up a band, council by council, and will that be published with the Institute for Fiscal Studies analysis before the Senedd votes on any regulations? Will you also, Minister, commit to protecting the single person discount for those living alone, whatever changes you bring forward? And furthermore, Minister, will you guarantee today that any new policies this Senedd term won't increase bills in Wales relative to England, making the gap even wider?

In your statement, you said you still want to look at adding more bands to higher-value homes. Creating higher new bands on 2003 values is a tax rise by another name. How much would new top bands rise by? Would that money bring bills down for everyone else, or will it simply go into councils' budgets? Because a home valued in 2003 could be anyone's—a friend, a family member, a farmer trying to run their business. It's not their fault the value has increased. House prices have skyrocketed purely because of the housing crisis.

Cabinet Minister, you may point to the council tax reduction scheme, but the people I am worried about are those just above that line. Ordinary working families and pensioners on modest incomes and fixed incomes are paying the full price. What assessment have you done, Minister, on how the Welsh Government policies will affect them specifically?

And finally, people in Wales want a fair council tax bill, as you suggested in your statement, and a democratic say before their bills go up is what the people would want. With revaluation now dead for this term, your Government will be judged on whether it delivers these goals, and I look forward to the Cabinet Minister's answers to these questions.

speaker: Jason O'Connell AS
debate: 8. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy: Update on the National Energy Strategy
text:
Thank you for your statement, Minister. Across Wales, families have faced and continue to face some of the largest energy price increases anywhere in the developed world. Yet the statement today makes it clear that this Government is committed to one thing, and that's more bureaucracy. Minister, your new publicly owned energy company is no doubt in your mind a key tenet of your energy strategy, but it's just not needed. It's a waste of taxpayers' money, and just like the Welsh Development Agency 2.0, it's an exercise in Government by quango, committee, council, advisory body and any other bureaucratic body to avoid actually taking responsibility. Now, when this inevitably goes wrong, there will be a plethora of other agencies to take the burden of blame in your place. So, what are you doing? To transfer functions from public bodies that already exist and calling it progression—why should the public of Wales stand for that?

Yet again, and as usual, we have little detail on cost, nothing on timelines and nothing on actual delivery. Now, I understand that the consultation is still under way, but why shy away from letting the public know exactly how much of their money you intend to waste? And when do you plan to update the Chamber on the details? Now, this isn't the first time I've made these comments, and I would have hoped that these details would be available for us as opposition Members to scrutinise effectively.

Minister, we welcome offshore windfarms. We welcome solar panels on school roofs, warehouses, factories and on car parks. But we do not support renewable projects that ruin the Welsh countryside and the outstanding natural beauty of Wales. We are the custodians of this land, and we must take that responsibility seriously. We, in Reform, we certainly do.

Yesterday, travelling through Merthyr and the Cynon valley, I saw multiple wind turbines on green land and across our mountainside. They are an eyesore to local residents, and I've had many constituents raise that with me. In Newport, Candwr Solar Farm is proposed to be built on 300 acres of prime agricultural land. Plaid claim to support the countryside, to protect our environment, but you can't do that without protecting green spaces from windfarms and excessive pylons. Minister, in your statement, you mentioned working across departments. How will you work with the Minister for rural resilience to make sure that these spaces are protected?

While the statement offers warm words, it will not lower energy bills for Welsh people at a time when a staggering one in four are in fuel poverty. It says nothing about working with the housing Minister, about making homes more insulated in a nation with some of the oldest homes in the UK. It says nothing about the potential that nuclear solutions have to offer. And as I've already stated, it lacks the detail and accountability that leads to meaningful change for the Welsh people.

Now, Minister, in your statement, you mention changing targets on sources of renewable energy to emissions-based targets. But you haven't mentioned how you're working with the UK Government to make energy more affordable for Welsh people. How exactly are you doing that, what conversations are you having with the UK Government, and what actions are you taking towards this? And how can you call this a serious update on the national energy strategy for Wales without mentioning nuclear energy once? What is Plaid's attitude towards the nuclear industry? Diolch.

speaker: Sarah Edwards AS
debate: 8. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy: Update on the National Energy Strategy
text: Can I thank the Minister for today's statement? Plaid Cymru's manifesto policy establishes a clear presumption on undergrounding new electricity transmission cables up to 132 kV. I attended the recent Green GEN Cymru consultation in Llandovery, where all the plans showed miles and miles of pylons. One of my constituents reports that he received three different answers on the cost of undergrounding versus overgrounding from three different Green GEN officials: four times the cost, nine times the cost, and, 'I don't know because we haven't costed it'. If this is a proper business proposition, surely Green GEN should know what the cost is and not pure guesswork. Interestingly, the maps showed only a tiny amount of undergrounding near Llanarthne, where I believe several of Plaid's high-profile politicians reside. Minister, can you explain where you stand on undergrounding, as Green GEN does not appear to be listening?

speaker: Louise Emery AS
debate: 8. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy: Update on the National Energy Strategy
text: Thank you, Minister, for your statement. I want to ask you a question specifically about energy being more affordable from this strategy—and maybe I'm misunderstanding it. I appreciate single home owners can go and purchase solar panels with a grant, possibly, and then they can see their energy bills reduced for that household. I also get about communities that can perhaps put a panel of solar panels on a nearby field and feed into that, and they get their own reduction in energy. But we are part of the national grid, so any energy that we produce, whether it's clean or fossil fuel, goes into a national grid. We're part of an energy market across the UK. We've got household prices fixed by the UK Government. We've got international fuel fossil markets that dictate that. So I'm trying to understand, with the community ownership and the national public energy company, what is the actual mechanism by which this strategy will eventually lower bills for the majority of Welsh people that go onto comparison sites and just choose a provider? The majority of people. How is that mechanism going to work when we have a national grid and the UK Government dictating energy prices? Diolch.

speaker: Cristiana Emsley AS
debate: 9. Legislative Consent Motion: The Cyber Security and Resilience (Network Information Systems) Bill
text:
Diolch, Lywydd. I thank the committee for its work on this legislative consent memorandum. Last week, I spoke in the debate on the consent motion for the Armed Forces Bill. The committee's report on the Cyber Security and Resilience (Network and Information Systems) Bill contains many of the same themes. We received the Cabinet Minister's response to our report last Thursday. While the committee may disagree with the responses to some recommendations, we nonetheless welcome the timely responses and we encourage other Welsh Ministers to follow suit.

The committee agrees with the Welsh Government's assessment about the provisions in the Bill that require the Senedd's consent. However, in our report, we ask whether consent should also be sought for clause 37(7) of the Bill. Changes to the relevant consultation requirement under clause 37 could affect a code issued by the Secretary of State under clause 36, and the Cabinet Minister believes consent is needed for clause 36. But the Cabinet Minister considered that the regulation-making power in clause 37(7) falls short of meeting the consent test in Standing Order 29.1. He told us it is not possible to conclude at this stage that the regulation-making power would be used to make provision that would affect consultation with regulators on codes of practice. He was also unable to conclude that, as a result of the changes made to the consultation requirements, provision would be made that would affect how regulators in Wales exercise their functions.

The Welsh Government's view on whether the Senedd should grant consent to the relevant provisions in a Bill is an important part of the legislative consent process, because it helps the Senedd committees make an informed decision on a consent motion. This memorandum did not include a recommendation on consent. We eventually received the recommendation in a letter on 28 September, in which the Cabinet Minister said that, as a result of engagement with the UK Government, he could now recommend the Senedd does consent to the relevant provisions in the Bill. We acknowledge this letter in our report, but we were not given full details of the inter-governmental discussion, and so we asked for those details. It is disappointing that, in responding to our report, the Cabinet Minister has only gone as far as to say the Welsh Government is satisfied that the Bill provides appropriate safeguards. So, we still don't have the details we requested.

The Bill confers several delegated powers on the Secretary of State to act in devolved areas. Members will be aware that, in July, the Welsh Government published its principles on UK legislation in devolved areas. The fourth principle states that delegated powers in UK legislation, including Henry VIII powers, should be conferred on the Welsh Ministers alone. The principle further states that any departure from this position needs to be justified by exceptional circumstances on a case-by-case basis. The committee could not identify the exceptional circumstances. In the memorandum, the Cabinet Minister himself calls them broad delegated Henry VIII powers. Members may know that the House of Lords Delegated Powers and Regulatory Reform Committee performs a similar role to that of the Legislation Committee. That committee has deemed two powers in the Bill, which are relevant to the Senedd's consent decision, as unacceptable. Again, the Cabinet Minister's responses to the committee's fifth and sixth recommendations are disappointingly sparse on detail. We asked for an explanation for the apparent breach of the Welsh Government's principles in relation to each delegated power in the Bill that may be used in a devolved area. The Cabinet Minister does not consider that the Welsh Government's principles have been breached and the committee has not received the explanations it asked for.

As for the report of the House of Lords committee, we thought it was fair to give the Cabinet Minister an opportunity to reflect on the concerns of that committee, and we invited him to comment. The Cabinet Minister did not comment, stating that the UK parliamentary committee is entitled to its views and it's the responsibility of the UK Government to consider those views. The Cabinet Minister may wish to reflect on his written response to the committee's report in his closing remarks. Diolch.

speaker: Jason O'Connell AS
debate: 9. Legislative Consent Motion: The Cyber Security and Resilience (Network Information Systems) Bill
text: Thank you, Presiding Officer. Now, at a time when threats to our national security are growing, protecting Britain and Wales from cyber attacks has never been more important. We live in a world where a single cyber attack can bring businesses to its knees and cripple essential, life-sustaining services. Having spent over 30 years working across aerospace and in the defence industry, I fully understand the importance of national security. National security isn't something we can afford to get wrong. Now, Reform UK will always put the security of our country and its people first and foremost, and that is why we support this legislative consent motion. Thank you.

speaker: David Mills
text: How is the Welsh Government promoting wind and solar projects on brownfield and industrial sites?

speaker: Andrew Rosindell
text: It is a pleasure to serve under you, Sir John. I have been a Member of Parliament for 25 years, probably longer than anyone else in this debate, and I believe that the House of Lords, for all its faults over the years, provides a balance to an elected Chamber. I am afraid to say that the hon. Member for Stroud (Dr Opher) misses the point of the House of Lords. We do not want another elected Chamber to rival the House of Commons. We need a house of experts—or elders, if you like, Sir John—people with knowledge, expertise and experience who have served this country over many decades in different walks of life.

speaker: Andrew Rosindell
text:
In a moment. We need also those who represent continuity. Sir John, you will know better than most that continuity is the foundation of the success of this nation. To ignore what has gone on in the past and to lose all that continuous wisdom from the ages is pure vandalism. We do not want another elected set of politicians who we know will be, effectively, appointed by party headquarters—the leader’s favourites will be put on some list and put into the House of Lords, even though many of them would prefer to be in the House of Commons—as a second set of politicians.

I want a House of Lords that is depoliticised in many ways, so I am not keen on the fact that Labour, the Conservatives and the Liberal Democrats have put so many people into the Lords who were friends of the leader at the time, or special advisers to Ministers and suchlike. What I want to see is more people who are truly representative of the whole country but can provide knowledge, expertise and experience to make our parliamentary democracy stronger and better.

It cannot be right that a political party that came third at the last general election has zero representation in the House of Lords. There are 80 Lib Dem peers, yet their party received 600,000 fewer votes than Reform UK. The Greens, I believe, have three representatives—

speaker: Andrew Rosindell
text: Two? Okay. Plaid Cymru also has representatives. The Democratic Unionist party has six, but only five MPs. The thing is disproportionate. There should at least be representation of all political parties. Based on the votes at the last election, there certainly need to be a number of Reform UK Members of the House of Lords.

speaker: Andrew Rosindell
text: The hon. Member will know that the way it works in the House of Lords is that it is based on party appointments. The Prime Minister will make nominations; so will the Leader of the Opposition; so will the leader of the Liberal Democrats; so will the leader of the Greens. They will nominate a sprinkling of new peers every so often, usually once a year. Well, where was the invitation for the leader of Reform UK to nominate a number of Reform UK Members of the House of Lords? The hon. Member must surely accept that that is very wrong when we consider that Reform UK was the third largest party in terms of votes at the last election.

speaker: Andrew Rosindell
text:
I will in a moment. I go back to my original argument: we are getting this wrong. We will regret the day that we become just one of two elected Chambers. We will regret that day. It will create a rivalry between two sets of elected politicians, who will both claim to be truly representative of the people who have put them there, instead of having the primacy of the elected House of Commons—ultimately, we are elected by the people of this country and we can make the final decision through the Parliament Acts. At the end of the day, we do not actually have to be obedient to the House of Lords.

What I do know is that, within the House of Lords, there is an opportunity to have people with enormous knowledge and expertise, whether they are former Cabinet Ministers, former ambassadors or high commissioners, heads of industry, heads of trade unions or representatives of the different faith groups. It is good to have people like that. It is right that we still have the established Church of England represented through the bishops; although, these days, they are rather more to the left than I would like, they still represent the established Church of this country.

speaker: Andrew Rosindell
text:
Well, I did not stand on that manifesto. I joined Reform UK after that manifesto. I can tell the hon. Member now that that is not our policy today. We are not going to abolish the House of Lords. We are not going to engage in constitutional vandalism.

Throughout the ages, we have evolved our constitutional and parliamentary democracy in a way that has given us strength and continuity, and has allowed us to change not in some radical direction, whereby minorities and people with vested interests can finish up controlling the institutions of this country, but in a way that is evolution rather than revolution. There is no requirement to abolish the House of Lords. There should not be an elected second Chamber.

New Zealand got rid of its second Chamber, so it has only one elected Chamber. I would prefer that, frankly, to a second load of politicians in the House of Lords who wish that they were MPs, but could not get there, so they were put in place by their friends in party headquarters. We do not want that. If we eventually do abolish the upper House, frankly it would be better just to have one Chamber than to have a second elected Chamber, because there would be rivalry between the two.

Look at it like this: if we choose carefully, change the system and make it more meritocratic in terms of experience, knowledge and the kind of people who we really want in the House of Lords, we will be buying in expertise at low cost. Otherwise, we will be paying consultants and experts that work for companies to do an effective job of scrutinising legislation. What is the point of that when we can give someone a peerage? That could be someone with vast knowledge, perhaps someone who has been an ambassador to another country, headed up an important institution or contributed to the establishment of an amazing charity, and who has vast knowledge from that. It could be someone like Sebastian Coe, the Olympic gold medallist who went on to run the London Olympics in 2012. Those people have value, but they will not stand for election, so we would lose all of them—[Interruption.] Well, they would not stand for election to the Lords.

As I say, we would lose good people. The great and the good would go and we would finish up, as I said earlier, with people who want to be politicians but would have to settle for being second-best. That is not good enough. We should do what we have always done in this country and allow our constitution and our parliamentary democracy to change—yes, change by all means—in a gentle and evolutionary way, so that we do not get rid of a tried and tested system that has lasted for generations and, with all its faults, done this country rather well over the centuries.

speaker: Andrew Rosindell
text: Is the hon. Lady also calling for the disestablishment of the Church of England? Is she asking that the cross be taken off the Crown so that the Christian foundations of this country are no longer part of our constitutional arrangements?

speaker: Andrew Rosindell
text: On that basis, would the hon. Lady abolish Royal Assent for Bills? Does she accept that our constitution is the King in Parliament—the King, the House of Lords and the House of Commons? Is she actually arguing for the abolition of the monarchy?

speaker: Andrew Rosindell
text: On the question of appointments, does the hon. Gentleman agree that it is only right that the third largest party in this country should have some representation in the House of Lords today?

speaker: Sarah Pochin
text: What steps he is taking with the Secretary of State for Defence to support veterans and their families in Northern Ireland.

speaker: Sarah Pochin
text: Why does the Secretary of State think that he and his Government know better than the SAS, the SBS, all other Northern Ireland veterans and the former Defence Minister, the hon. Member for Birmingham Selly Oak (Al Carns), who all warn that this troubles Bill will risk further prosecutions of our brave veterans?

speaker: Lee Anderson
text: Time after time, the previous Energy Secretary stood in this House and told us that drilling in the North sea would not bring down domestic prices. Just today, the Prime Minister has stood at that Dispatch Box and said that prices will come down as a result of drilling in the North sea. Who is right: the former Energy Secretary or the Prime Minister? [Hon. Members: “No, he didn’t.] Yes, he did.

speaker: Danny Kruger
debate: Church Appointments (Repeal of Discriminatory Provision) Bill
text: I support the principle of the Bill and obviously will not oppose it. May I ask the Minister to unpack the point he just made about the role of the Prime Minister in conveying the advice of the Church on appointments? That is exactly how it works at the moment. As the Minister said, the Prime Minister is the principal adviser to the sovereign, and ultimately it is the sovereign who has authority to make episcopal appointments. Does he agree that the Prime Minister has a function to play in the advice given to the sovereign, or does he think this is purely a procedural matter in which the Prime Minister is simply transmitting advice that he receives from the Church hierarchy?

speaker: Danny Kruger
debate: Church Appointments (Repeal of Discriminatory Provision) Bill
text: The hon. Gentleman is making an important speech. Does he agree with me that the value of this Bill is that it could strengthen the Church of England and reconnect it with the political community of which it is properly a part? Does he agree with me that, as I said when I intervened on the Minister, it is not right to leave the appointment of bishops purely to the bureaucrats at Church House and committees there, and that it is a proper subject for politics? We have heard the suggestion that this is a second-order priority, and I recognise that there are more pressing concerns for the country, but this stuff matters—Gladstone thought the most important part of his job as Prime Minister was appointing bishops. My concern about the debate so far is that the Bill has been interpreted as some great step of progressive modernisation that clearly ends with the exclusion of Christianity from political life altogether. Does he agree that what we actually we need to do is strengthen the role of the Church of England in the political community and remind the Prime Minister of this very important part of his or her job?

speaker: Danny Kruger
debate: Church Appointments (Repeal of Discriminatory Provision) Bill
text: I am sorry to jump up again, but I want to challenge the right hon. Gentleman. That was no doubt the case in the 19th century, but if he reads the brilliant book by Mark Vickers called “God In Number 10”, which is a history of 20th century Prime Ministers from Balfour to Blair, he will see that it is an opposite story. The book is a remarkable account of how very different Prime Ministers all took their responsibilities seriously, as the right hon. Gentleman said, right up to John Major. They honoured the fact that different dioceses had different traditions, and they tried to ensure that there was ecumenical balance in the Church of England. I do not think it is beyond a Prime Minister of any party to take their job seriously, think about the right balance of the Church of England and maintain the broad church. What we do not want bureaucrats in the Church of England appointing each other, which is what we have at the moment—that is why they are all left wing. Surely the right hon. Gentleman would acknowledge that we need a genuinely broad church that includes people from different political traditions.

speaker: Jason O'Connell AS
debate: 10. Short Debate: Full-face coverings are against British values
text:
Face coverings have no place in British and Welsh society. Let's take a look at the city of Newport, the city that holds the unenviable title of the worst high street in Britain. Disaffected young people have run through businesses, causing a decimated high street and rundown shopfronts, leading to a loss of inward investment and hope for the future deserted, thanks, in part, to balaclava-covered youths running riot over those that are just trying to make a living—people who've worked hard, paid their taxes, and contributed to their communities. But this is not just about one Welsh city; this is a Wales-wide issue.

Plaid will say this is a pointless debate because it's a non-devolved matter reserved to Westminster. But that doesn't mean UK councils are powerless. Look at what Nottingham has achieved as an example. They introduced a targeted restriction against face coverings, and they've seen a 40 per cent reduction in city-centre anti-social behaviour. Newport City Council has voted to explore similar options, and I, alongside every Reform MS, will be encouraging all Welsh councils to do the same.

Adam Price disappointed me today with his response to spokespersons' questions. Imagine being a victim of crime, of violent theft or some kind of violent robbery, only to listen to Plaid's economy minister today saying balaclava bans are a gimmick, that businesses don't care. But the reality is that Plaid doesn't care. Plaid cares more about promoting foreign cultures than our own. They clearly don't care about keeping Welsh people and businesses safe.

When a Welsh person supports Reform, Plaid often accuses them of questioning their loyalty to Wales. But when foreign people who can't speak any British language enter Wales for a life on the welfare system, they are celebrated as trophies of the benefits of mass migration. They don't care about how a lack of integration by face-clad unknown people impacts Wales, our working-class communities. All they care about is supporting mass migration in all its forms, no matter the cost to our communities. We see this today. They defend balaclavas, all because they want some in our society to be able to hide their faces. Some will lazily say we're being Islamophobic, whatever that means. Some, no doubt, will roll out the old classic and shriek, 'Racists!' These tropes are tired, ineffective, and clearly wildly inaccurate, but I will address them.

Reform supports freedom of religion in all its forms. But where that freedom oppresses women and damages assimilation into Welsh communities, a line must be drawn. In Afghanistan, under Taliban rule, women are under a system of gender apartheid. They can't study above the age of 12, they can't speak loudly in public, and they're forced, by law, to wear the burqa. If they don't, they could be denied healthcare, they could be beaten, or even worse. For these women, raised under an extremist form of Islam, the burqa is a symbol of oppression. This symbol is what Plaid Members are attempting to back today: an extreme ideology that is anti British, anti women and against assimilation, forced on young girls and carried on into adulthood.

In numerous countries, the burqa is already banned. But we cannot allow this form of oppression to become the norm in Wales. Walk through any areas across Wales, and you will see it for yourself. The Muslim Council of Wales has tried to silence this debate today, saying we are hateful and divisive. So, I say again, and let me be very clear: Reform has no issue with the hijab, we have no issue or problem with Islam or Muslims, but we do have an issue with people living in our communities hiding their identities. We say the same thing to protesters that cover their faces, whatever their political persuasion. In modern Britain, we are polite people. We say 'hello' to our neighbours, and we do not hide our faces. That is our culture, that is our way, regardless of race, creed or religion. Reform wants safer streets and strong communities for our families to live, work and thrive. Diolch.

speaker: Steven Rodaway AS
debate: 10. Short Debate: Full-face coverings are against British values
text:
I am proud to be Welsh, proud to be British, and unapologetic in defending our culture. In Britain we show our faces. It builds trust and, more importantly, it keeps us safe. In certain Islamic countries, under Islamic law, girls from puberty must cover their faces, and some countries will arrest females above the age of nine for showing too much hair. Whether balaclava or burqa, face coverings have no place on our streets here in Wales. It is oppressive, and it is a risk to Welsh public safety. We have written to the First Minister urging him to make a much-needed representation to the UK Government.

This summer, the Prime Minister and the First Minister managed to meet together to ban the barbecue. While those on the left want us to ban the barbecue, we in Reform want to ban the burqa, or the balaclava. Face coverings are incompatible with our British way of life. It is an outright betrayal of the dignity and freedom of women.

Beyond this, we must look at banning cousin marriages and address religious attitudes towards women and homosexuals. Women's freedom and their safety here in Wales deserve urgency, which is why we must, at the very first possible opportunity, ban face coverings in public, and I urge every Member across this house to support this motion. Thank you.

speaker: David Mills AS
debate: 10. Short Debate: Full-face coverings are against British values
text:
Gosh, I don't know how to follow some of this. Thank you, Presiding Officer, and thank you, Jason O'Connell, for tabling the debate. We're a nation that prides itself on our tradition of constitutional liberty, which has always included freedom of expression to dress as one chooses, including garments that most people find offensive or objectionable, such as face coverings. This stands in opposition to the tradition on the continent where restrictions are commonplace. However, I think we need to re-examine our position on this, as the wearing of face coverings has become normalised in recent years, and consider banning them.

In Swansea, Neath and many other areas of Wales, there has been a growing problem with anti-social behaviour committed by youths wearing face coverings. No-one should have to tolerate this sort of hooliganism. We should recognise too that face coverings are not normal practice in any religion, and they're only employed by a tiny minority of ultra-conservative adherents. Whilst religious freedom is an important tenet of British values, our laws and cultural norms should not bend to the whims of an ultra-conservative minority. We should recognise too that many countries across Europe, the middle east and central Asia ban the use of face coverings and do not make religious exceptions. So, I agree with Jason that the use of face coverings is a growing issue and we must look to banning them.

speaker: Francesca O'Brien AS
debate: 10. Short Debate: Full-face coverings are against British values
text: Face coverings, including the burqa, are anti British. Not all cultures are equal. We can't continue to import alien cultures into this country and expect integration. These oppressive beliefs are totally at odds with our history and culture. Banning these coverings is simple common sense. European countries like Denmark, Belgium and Austria have already banned them. We should do the same. Muslim countries like Kazakhstan and Tunisia have already banned face veils. France is currently on fire; this country could be next. We can't allow a parallel society to develop in this country, or we could be facing the consequences sooner than we think.

speaker: Joe Martin AS
debate: 10. Short Debate: Full-face coverings are against British values
text:
The burqa and niqab are two of the many ways in which fundamentalist Islam is uniquely incompatible with western civilisation. They represent ideas that are oppressive, misogynistic and anti-British. Mass immigration was sold to the public with the assertion that those arriving would assimilate into British culture. That was a lie—we can't even see the faces of thousands of people who've moved here. If two Muslim women live in the same street and they both wear burqas, how are we meant to tell them apart? I can't believe this needs to be said, but being able to tell people apart is an important part of British culture.

Proponents will argue that they promote modesty and stop women from being sexualised. For thousands of years, the west achieved the same result—not by oppressing women, but by requiring men to employ an ounce of self-control. If the people who've moved here can't do that, they should live in countries where it's accepted that men can't control themselves. I've also seen children wearing face coverings; anyone who struggles not to feel lust when looking at a child should not be free to walk around in our society. There are countries where that might be normal. This is not one of them. Assimilation means losing religious face coverings, and to encourage that, they should be banned.

speaker: Jason O'Connell AS
debate: 10. Short Debate: Full-face coverings are against British values
text:
Diolch, Lywydd. It's good to see the Chamber so full for a short debate. I had no idea I was so popular. I'd like to give a minute's time in this debate to Joe Martin, Sarah Cooper-Lesadd, Francesca O'Brien, Carrie Harper, Steven Rodaway and Kiera Marshall.

Llywydd, our town centres were once the bright and beating heart of our communities, where businesses thrived and families felt safe. But years of economic decline and political failure have let our town centres, sadly, rot. As a result, a new dangerous culture has emerged. From Newport to Rhyl, balaclava-clad young men, often dangerously riding illegal e-bikes, have been fuelling anti-social behaviour and making our streets feel unsafe. For these individuals, face coverings are a way to conceal their identity, to make it harder for authorities to hold them accountable. And while Governments across the UK turn a blind eye to this, Reform says, 'Enough is enough'.

Yet electrical contractors are generally excluded from the Construction Industry Training Board apprenticeship grants available to other construction employers. speaker: Jason O'Connell AS
debate: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy

Thank you, Minister. The biggest word in that statement I picked up on was 'if' we get this right. That's a very big 'if' indeed.

But, moving on, today, Reform UK will lead a debate calling for a ban on face coverings used to conceal identities and intimidate the public. Wales has become a country where criminals can hide their faces while law-abiding citizens are frightened to walk down their own high streets. Across Wales, hard-working businesses are struggling, shopkeepers face intimidation and theft, customers are being driven away, and once-thriving town centres are suffering, leading to damage to our economic outlook. All too often, those responsible are hiding behind balaclavas, riding illegal e-bikes, making it harder for the police to identify them. Minister, we both know that enough is enough. Our high streets belong to families, shoppers and hard-working businesses, not masked thugs. We know this matter is reserved to the police, but councils across Wales are considering using their powers to ban face coverings, including balaclavas. We in Reform will do everything we can to support them. Minister, do you agree that Reform UK's face coverings ban would curb anti-social behaviour and help protect Welsh town centres?

speaker: Jason O'Connell AS
debate: 1. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Enterprise, Connectivity and Energy

Thank you. I thought I was going to get called—excuse me.

As Reform UK's Richard Tice has been calling for for years, the Jackdaw project has now been given the green light, and, as we know on this side of the Chamber, that's nowhere near enough. speaker: Tom Montgomery AS
debate: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
text:
Can I start by declaring an interest? My wife works in an additional learning needs provision within a school in Conwy.

I thank the leader of the Welsh Conservatives for bringing this question forward. Minister, I was speaking to a teacher in Rhyl, and it was explained to me that the school in which that teacher worked can't afford pens or pencils, and staff are currently using their own money to buy learning resources. speaker: Stephen Senior AS

section: Questions Without Notice from Party Spokespeople

Okay, thank you, Minister. I see that later on there's a question regarding teachers leaving the profession. Surveys show that poor pupil behaviour is a factor. However, Plaid's recent programme for government, whilst acknowledging workload concerns, makes no mention of behaviour.

Staff working in schools have a legal right to use reasonable force to control or restrain pupils. Welsh Government guidance explicitly states that no school should have a 'no physical contact' policy. However, there are still occasions when school staff face lengthy investigations and possible suspension for having operated within the law. This can have a devastating impact on both them and pupil behaviour in the school, whenever staff, unsurprisingly, decide that no physical intervention is their best policy.

Minister, will you ask your officials to establish whether schools are advising staff on their legal right to use reasonable force and whether disciplinary processes are being initiated despite staff having operated within the law?

speaker: Steven Rodaway AS

For a small business, taking on an apprentice requires a financial and resource-heavy commitment. Announcing an audit does nothing on its own to meet these costs. Since your Government took office, another group of young people have left school hoping to secure an apprenticeship and employment. Employers need immediate funding. Your manifesto promises better use of existing city and regional growth deal funding to support apprenticeships. speaker: Stephen Senior AS

section: Questions Without Notice from Party Spokespeople
text: Thank you, Deputy Presiding Officer. Cabinet Minister, additional learning needs funding remains a contentious issue, with a debate scheduled next month in response to a petition. ALN funding by the Welsh Government is up 14 per cent on last year, and has more than doubled in eight years. Inflation over that period has been around 35 per cent. The percentage of the education budget assigned to ALN has risen from just below 15 per cent to nearly 19 per cent over the same period. At local authority level, there have been huge variations, with increases over the last decade ranging from 65 per cent to 297 per cent. One authority now spends more than a quarter of its education budget on ALN. These figures suggest that there has been a rapid change within Welsh education. Whatever is happening looks unsustainable in terms of funding. Minister, what are your thoughts on the reasons for this ALN spending trajectory?

speaker: Stephen Senior AS
debate: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language
section: Questions Without Notice from Party Spokespeople
text:
Okay, thank you, Minister. Finally, the national literacy and numeracy assessments are online and personalised to each pupil. So, they're rather like a flow chart, where the next question depends on the answers to the last one. These tests can be taken whenever the school feels it's appropriate. Pupils can take time out during the assessments, and pupils are permitted to repeat the exercise any time. This is not a standardised test where all pupils in a cohort take the same test at the same time of the year so that judgments can be made about pupil and school standards, including progress.

This is what the tests were originally designed to do when Leighton Andrews introduced them, and that is what happened when the tests were introduced in 2014. This adaptive system, as it's called, has been in place for a decade, but has clearly not led to any improvements in the Programme for International Student Assessment results. Minister, will you reintroduce standardised literacy and numeracy tests to be used by all pupils annually at the end of year 2 to year 9?

speaker: Llŷr Powell AS
debate: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Education and the Welsh Language

In September, more than 300 pupils in the Caerphilly borough lost their free school transport because, as the council said, they fall within the two-mile measurement of the Learner Travel (Wales) Measure 2008. Now, the problem with that is that the Measure is looking at distance but not incline. I've walked this route with campaigners and parents and children themselves—I went from Aberbargoed to Bargoed—and it's the incline that is the tricky part. During different weathers, whether it's the heat we experienced in the summer, or even cold winter days, when that road can be slippery, it does become a risk. Will the Government now look at reviewing the Learner Travel (Wales) Measure 2008 and look to include the advice on inclines and the difficult weather paths that this could create?
