speaker: Steve Bayliss AS
text:
Thank you to the Member for raising this. Cabinet Minister, I spent over 20 years with South Wales Fire and Rescue Service, so I recognise the efforts of crews, Natural Resources Wales officers, and everyone containing pollution. But the facts are deeply concerning: kerosene from GE Aerospace's Nantgarw site has affected around 4 km of the Taff. Dead fish have been recovered, residents have been advised to close windows and doors, and fumes are present. GE Aerospace said it isolated the source on Friday, yet on Monday Natural Resources Wales said it was still investigating the drainage system to stop further pollution. Stopping the original leak is not the same as stopping pollution reaching the river. And this is not the first time; in 2024, pollution from PB Gelatins UK in Treforest killed fish. The outcome announced this June was the enforcement undertaking, including a £50,000 donation and nearly £15,000 in costs.

Cabinet Minister, you chaired the committee that reported Natural Resources Wales's own concerns that its fines and sanctions weren't enough to deter polluters. You now oversee Natural Resources Wales. Our Reform manifesto commits us to dismantling and fundamentally restructuring Natural Resources Wales, bringing strategic policy under ministerial oversight while environmental protections continue without interruptions.

The public deserve to know what went wrong, who is accountable and who will pay to put it right. So, Cabinet Minister, will you commit to a written statement to this Senedd within 14 days, setting out how much fuel was released, the damage identified so far, the timetable for Natural Resources Wales's investigation and any enforcement decision, and how all legal recoverable costs will be pursued from those found responsible and not the Welsh taxpayer? Diolch.

speaker: Benjamin Hodge Mckenna AS
debate: 6. Members' Legislative Debate under Standing Order 11.21(iv): An NHS first Bill
text:
Reform UK, we support the NHS. We believe in an NHS that is free at the point of need. And we believe in an NHS that is properly funded and an NHS that puts its patients first. Too many people in Wales are waiting too long for treatment. Roughly a quarter of people are on a waiting list, and two-year waits have not been eradicated as was promised. A&E departments across Wales remain under tremendous pressure, and our planned care capacity is still short of what is required. Everybody who interacts with our NHS can see that the staff are under pressure, the estate needs investment, and the system is not delivering the outcomes that the public deserve.

But we also know that throwing money at a problem doesn't automatically solve it. We cannot fix capacity issues in our NHS if we refuse to look at every practical tool available to us. Therefore, we cannot risk totally excluding independent healthcare providers if they can provide quality care that clears backlogs. I'm not interested in privatisation or charging patients. I'm interested in utilising additional capacity funded by the NHS purse and free to the patient.

Now, I don't believe that the motion before us today seeks to completely exclude the private sector. But I'm concerned that, ultimately, the Bill could result in a set of legal requirements that make it too difficult for us to make use of independent capacity when it is needed. Patients want to be treated in a reasonable time and receive care that is safe and effective. If this Bill leads to a situation in which people are waiting years for NHS care because the system cannot utilise its independent capacity, then it would have failed in achieving the core mission of our NHS: putting patients first.

I'm not opposed to the principle of ensuring that the NHS is properly managed and resourced before seeking alternative solutions. And I'm supportive of the measures that strengthen the NHS, improve the accountability of our health boards and encourage investment into our workforce and estates. But any Bill that effectively rules out practical capacity solutions could, ultimately, end up failing the very people it seeks to protect. Therefore, I will be looking forward to the detail of this Bill, and I will judge it on its ability to get people treated sooner whilst protecting the NHS's founding principle of free care at the point of need. Diolch yn fawr.

speaker: Gareth Beer AS
debate: 6. Members' Legislative Debate under Standing Order 11.21(iv): An NHS first Bill
text:
I believe that the NHS first Bill has worthy ambitions, as long as the NHS is able to deliver the care when required. All my constituents ask for is a local medical centre or a hospital that can treat them quickly, with local expertise.

Gwyn Williams has often talked about how health board boundaries stop the movement of patients, staff and experts. This means that services are fragmented, duplicated and delayed. Patients should not be refused access simply because they live on the wrong side of a health board boundary. There must be no postcode lottery in treatment or outcomes. The ministerial advisory group recognised last year that de facto regional arrangements are already widely established and called for stronger regional working.

To support the Bill, there is clear need for more medical staff. I welcome the Government's announcement of 253 additional graduate nursing jobs recently, but the Royal College of Nursing has said that the uncertainty has caused a huge reduction in people accepting nursing degrees in Wales.

This Bill should also call for greater transparency. Health boards should publish clear information about the use of private providers, including costs, activities and outcomes. That would allow the public to judge whether spending leads to permanent NHS capacity or just short-term solutions. An NHS first approach must have stronger accountability. For too long, the Welsh Government has taken a hands-off approach to NHS management. Ministers must exercise firmer oversight and set clear expectations when performance, decision making or patient safety falls short. Successful practices should be shared across Wales. Our NHS needs management that is results driven, not process driven. We must allow our front-line health professionals to concentrate on what matters most: their patients.

What's needed is faster treatment, safer care and better use of public money. It is about building capacity and resilience within a national health service that belongs to us all. Let us put the NHS first, break down the barriers that delay care, strengthen democratic oversight and ensure that every decision begins and ends with what is best for the patients in Wales. Diolch yn fawr.

speaker: Benjamin Hodge Mckenna AS
debate: 7. Reform UK Debate: Prostate cancer strategy
text:
I stand today to move the motion tabled in the name of my colleague Llŷr Powell calling on the Government to explicitly include prostate cancer in the national cancer strategy for Wales. Prostate cancer is the most common form of cancer amongst men in Wales. Each year, more than 2,500 are diagnosed, and around 640 sadly die from the condition. If it's caught early, the outlook can be more positive. Nearly everybody diagnosed at stage 1 goes on to live for five years or more. But, if it's caught late, the picture is very different. Too many men in Wales are being diagnosed too late, particularly in our most deprived communities. The consequences of this are severe, and they're measured in lower quality of life, unnecessary suffering for patients and their families and too many people losing their lives too soon.

The 'National Prostate Cancer Audit State of the Nation Report 2026' found that prostate cancer diagnoses in Wales rose by 12 per cent between 2023 and 2024. That growth included more stage 1 diagnoses, which is an encouraging sign if it means that the disease is detected early. But it also shows the need for capacity and careful clinical planning in this area. In Wales, 54 per cent of men with high-risk or locally advanced prostate cancer received radical treatment. That's compared to 69 per cent in England. Serious concerns have also been raised regarding higher rates of emergency readmission after surgery and a significant drop in recorded numbers of radical prostatectomies—try saying that after a night out—and radical radiotherapy.

The audit also raises serious questions about data quality in Wales. It highlights problems with incomplete data, data with linkage issues and underrecording. We also know that waiting times for cancer treatment remain a serious problem here. The 62-day target is still missed routinely, and diagnostic capacity needs to be addressed. Across Wales, particularly in north Wales, patients have faced unacceptable delays that have allowed their cancers to progress. If we don't have adequate data systems in place to track treatment and outcomes, it becomes incredibly difficult to make improvements to the system.

Cancer is the leading cause of death in Wales and, for too long, we have lacked a proper cancer action plan as a nation. There is a clear need to implement a strategy that invests in modern diagnostic technologies and treatments and uses evidence-led screening initiatives that improve patient access. That is why I support the principle of the 10-year national cancer strategy. However, I have heard concerns from clinicians, campaigners and the third sector that prostate cancer will not receive the explicit focus, accountability and resources that it needs. So, today's debate is an opportunity for the Government to address those concerns and ensure that people across Wales who are suffering with prostate cancer get the attention and treatment they deserve.

The fact is that there are serious questions that need to be asked with regard to prostate cancer in Wales. What assessment has the Government made of the UK National Screening Committee decision only to recommend a limited screening programme? Alongside that, what discussions has the Government held with the NHS and third sector about the feasibility of implementing a prostate cancer screening programme? And in the absence of a screening programme for all high-risk men, will the Government consider including other early-detection commitments within the cancer strategy to ensure that more men with prostate cancer are diagnosed early?

A strategy that does not contain firm commitments that prostate cancer will be a priority risks leaving men behind. That is why today's motion was both reasonable and necessary. Prostate cancer needs more than a passing mention in the cancer strategy; it needs clear actions, including targets to increase the proportion of men who are diagnosed at an early stage, particularly in our most deprived communities; measurable improvements in the proportion of men with high-risk disease who receive timely radical treatment; urgent action to fix data quality issues so that progress can be monitored; plans to improve diagnostic and treatment capacity; and an integration with a broader men's health approach that encourages men to come forward sooner.

Patients in Wales deserve to be diagnosed before their cancer has spread so that they can receive proper treatment in a timely manner. By explicitly prioritising prostate cancer in the national cancer strategy, the Government can take a practical step towards that goal. It will give clinicians, health boards and patients the clarity that they need, and it will give this Senedd the ability to hold the Government to account against delivery. Prostate cancer deserves a clear place in Wales's cancer strategy, one that is supported by resources, data and delivery. That way more men can be diagnosed early and more lives can be saved. Therefore, I urge Members to support our motion today. Diolch yn fawr.

speaker: James Evans AS
debate: 7. Reform UK Debate: Prostate cancer strategy
text: Thanks for taking the intervention. On top of those things that you've just listed, though, I think you have to recognise that, even through my time in the Senedd, when we were looking at waiting lists, actually cancer waiting lists targets were missed almost every time they were coming out from the centre of Welsh Government. So, do you admit that, actually, that's one thing in Government that you actually got wrong, that you never actually got on top of cancer waiting lists in Wales?

speaker: Adrian Mason AS
debate: 7. Reform UK Debate: Prostate cancer strategy
text:
I'm going to address the men of Wales, and first of all, thank you, Llŷr Powell, for tabling this debate. This is one of those debates where we should be able to put politics to one side. Prostate cancer doesn't care who you vote for, where you live or what you do for a living. When somebody is told they've got cancer, they're not thinking about politics, they're thinking about their family, what happens next and whether they're going to be all right.

This issue is personal to me. My grandfather died from kidney failure caused by prostate cancer, and several other men on my mother's side of the family have been affected by it. That's why it matters to me. I'm thinking about my grandfather and about the families across Wales facing those same worries today. I'm also thinking about the men who may have put off speaking to their GP. I'm 61 now, and because of my family background, I've had the prostate-specific antigen test, and, thankfully, the result was reassuring. But many men don't take that step. Some don't want to make a fuss. Some are worried about what they might be told. Others simply think if they feel fine, there cannot be anything wrong. The reality is that prostate cancer does not always give you a warning. That's why awareness matters and why men need to understand their own risk. But awareness on its own isn't enough. When someone does come forward, the NHS has to be there for them. If they need tests, scans or treatment, they shouldn't be left waiting and worrying about what happens next.

For those of us in rural Wales, there can be additional challenges. A hospital appointment can mean a long journey, time away from work and an entire day spent travelling. If you're already anxious about your health, that only adds to the burden. The latest national prostate cancer audit also raises concerns about variation in treatment in Wales. The figures come with important warnings about data quality, but that itself raises a question: how can we be confident that patients are receiving the right treatment if we cannot reliably measure what is happening?

I also want to say a brief word about the Conservative amendment. I understand the case being made, because I'd like to see more men diagnosed earlier too, particularly given my own family's experience. There is important work taking place around targeted screening for men at particularly high risk, and I believe Wales should continue to follow the evidence and medical advice as that develops.

But today's motion is straightforward. We're asking the Welsh Government to ensure that prostate cancer has a clear place within Wales's national cancer strategy. And inclusion in a strategy must mean more than just a mention in a document. It needs clear commitment on earlier diagnosis, timely treatment and fair access across Wales, with progress that patients and families can actually see—not because prostate cancer is more important than any other cancer, but because it affects so many men and families, and deserves sustained attention.

I'd like to thank organisations such as Prostate Cymru, Prostate Cancer UK, Lingen Davies Cancer Support in my own constituency, and Movember, along with the NHS staff and all the other organisations and individuals who work tirelessly to support patients and their families. Llywydd, I can't change what happened to my grandfather, but I'd like to think we can improve things for the men and families who come after us, because behind every diagnosis is a husband, father, grandfather, brother or friend. And what matters to those families isn't which party brought this debate forward; what matters is what we do next and whether we make the difference. Diolch.

speaker: Helen Jenner AS
debate: 7. Reform UK Debate: Prostate cancer strategy
text:
Nothing can ever prepare a person for receiving a cancer diagnosis, or indeed hearing about the diagnosis of a family member or a friend. It's one of the most terrifying things that anyone can be told, and it's a disease that touches, in effect, so many of us. Therefore, I welcome the Government's 10-year cancer strategy, because it's badly needed.

We're hearing today about why prostate cancer deserves proper attention within the national cancer strategy for Wales, and I'll be building on those points. But I also want to share with you a personal experience. I'd like to thank Paul and Janet for sharing their experiences also. My father was diagnosed with prostate cancer in 2023. It was the most horrendous news to hear and it's been a very tough experience for our family, especially, at one point, we had an agonising wait of seven days to find out whether or not it had actually spread to his bones. I'm relieved to be able to tell the Siambr today that, three years on, he's still in remission. He doesn't like to have a fuss made of him, and he went through the first few weeks of this process alone because he didn't want to worry anybody. Thankfully, we're beginning to turn the page and move on from a very difficult chapter for us.

Early diagnosis and timely treatment were essential for my father, as they are for all men affected by prostate cancer here in Wales. Ensuring that our health service has the ability and the bandwidth to test and treat the thousands of people in Wales being diagnosed annually is crucial. The 'National Prostate Cancer Audit State of the Nation Report 2026' recorded around 2,700 prostate cancer diagnoses in Wales in 2024, as we've heard, and it increased 12 per cent on the previous year. And as we've heard a few times, but it does bear emphasis, just 54 per cent of men in Wales with high-risk or locally advanced prostate cancer received radical treatment, compared with 69 per cent in England. Meanwhile, 11 per cent of men in Wales with low-risk disease received radical treatment, with concerns that this may represent over-treatment, compared with the 7 per cent in England.

These figures raise serious questions about whether patients are consistently receiving the right treatment at the right time. However, the audit itself warns that problems with Welsh data quality and completeness mean that these findings must be interpreted with caution. Reliable data, modern systems and effective accountability are needed to deliver on its commitments. How can the Government properly assess performance, allocate resources or establish whether its policies are working if it cannot reliably measure what is happening? Cancer services need reliable systems that allow clinicians to access accurate information, co-ordinate treatment and identify delays. The Government must explain how it will ensure that the new platform delivers and how it will hold those responsible to account if it does not.

Llywydd, there is a wider lesson here about funding. In its evidence to the Senedd's Public Accounts and Public Administration Committee, the Wales Cancer Alliance argued that increased investment in cancer services has not translated into proportional improvements in performance or patient outcomes. It also highlighted that the national target requiring 75 per cent of patients to begin treatment within 62 days of their first suspicion of cancer has not been met across Wales as a whole, or by any individual health board, since August 2020. Let us consider that. Years of missed targets across every health board in Wales. That should concern every Member of this Senedd.

Of course, cancer services need adequate funding so that the NHS can afford modern diagnostic equipment, effective treatments, reliable digital infrastructure and properly staffed services. They all require investment. But we cannot simply assume that spending more money will automatically produce better outcomes. We need clear lines of responsibility, transparent performance measures and accountability when commitments are repeatedly missed. Prostate cancer must be included in the national strategy and that must mean measurable commitments on earlier diagnosis, timely treatment, reliable data and reducing unwarranted variation between health boards. And it must mean publishing progress, identifying failures and directing resources where they will make the greatest difference to patients. We should not accept a situation in which the Government cannot confidently establish what is happening to patients because its data is incomplete. The forthcoming strategy is an opportunity to put these failures right.

The Government must explicitly recognise prostate cancer as a priority and demonstrate how investment, digital transformation and service reform will work together to improve outcomes, because men diagnosed with prostate cancer do not need another promise, they need to know that their health is considered, understood and included. They need a health service that can provide the right treatment, at the right time, and demonstrate that it is getting better. That is what accountability looks like; that is what our motion will deliver. I therefore urge Members to support it. Diolch, Lywydd.

speaker: Gareth Thomas AS
debate: 7. Reform UK Debate: Prostate cancer strategy
text:
Every Member here will have met a constituent who has lived with prostate cancer or a family who has lost someone to it. A man who put off seeing the GP because he felt fine. A wife who noticed something was wrong before he did. A son who now gets himself checked because his father was diagnosed too late. These are not abstract cases. They are our neighbours, our friends and, for some of us, our own families.

Prostate cancer does not affect all communities equally. In our most deprived communities, most men, or more men, are now diagnosed at a later stage than at an earlier one, while men in more affluent areas are more often caught early. In practice, that means that a man's postcode can decide whether his cancer is found while it can still be treated.

According to the 'National Prostate Cancer Audit State of the Nation Report 2026', diagnoses in Wales rose by 12 per cent between 2023 and 2024 to around 2,500 men. That is 2,500 men in a single year who heard the words, 'You have cancer', and 2,500 families whose lives changed in that moment. The same audit found that only 54 per cent of men in Wales with high-risk or locally advanced disease received radical treatment, compared with 69 per cent in England. Those are the men whose cancer is the most dangerous, and too many of them do not appear to have received the treatment that could have saved their lives.

At the same time, 11 per cent of men in Wales with low-risk disease received radical treatment that may not have been needed, compared with 7 per cent in England, with all the lasting consequences that that can bring. The audit urges caution about the Welsh figures because of problems with data quality. Think about what that means. We cannot even say with confidence how many men with prostate cancer are being treated in Wales. That should trouble every one of us, and should be put right.

We also know how hard it is for many men to come forward. Too many have grown up believing that talking about their health is a weakness, and prostate cancer often gives no warning in its early stages. Members of the Senedd have spoken with real courage about their personal experiences, and I pay tribute to them, Paul. Our party leader in Scotland has done the same. But we cannot ask men to be brave enough to come forward and then fail to have a clear plan waiting for them when they do.

Men account for 54 per cent of cancer deaths in Wales. That is why Reform Wales has called for a 10-year cancer strategy, investment in modern diagnostics, targeted screening where need is greatest, and a men's health framework for Wales. So, I call on the Government to name prostate cancer in the strategy, with clear and measurable objectives included, to fix the data, so that we know what is happening to men diagnosed with prostate cancer, and to close the gap between our richest and poorest communities, so that no man is diagnosed too late because of where he lives. I urge all Members to support this motion. Diolch.

speaker: James Evans AS
debate: 7. Reform UK Debate: Prostate cancer strategy
text:
And then Paul Davies—and thank you, Paul, for giving your own personal experience. You and I have talked a lot about this in the past, about your own personal experience of living with prostate cancer and the need to include it within that cancer strategy. That's something that we need to see, because it is the biggest killer of men in terms of cancer. We do need to make sure that it is included. You also raised the consultation, and we all need to see that, if consultations are had by Government, then the lived experience of people has to come through that consultation. It can't just be a tick-box exercise, as you raised. It actually needs to be considered and thought out. You also raised, and I know you've been a real champion for it, the national screening programme, when it was first discussed, and then the UK screening committee decided not to roll it out. I know that you were deeply disappointed about that, like a lot of others, and I'd just like to thank you for the work you've done, not just in this Parliament but in other Parliaments across the UK, to understand why that screening programme should be happening. You also talked about the advances in medical technology as well, and that men in Wales should have access to that technology and not outdated technology, and that was picked up a little bit by the Cabinet Minister.

Matthew, your commitment to cancer is unmatched, really, in this Chamber. You worked for a number of cancer charities before you even came to this place, and now you're chairman of the cross-party group on cancer. As someone who's been here before, I can say that that cross-party group does an awful lot of very good work, and it's informed a lot of the work of the cancer strategy over the years as well. So thank you for that. You talked about the excitement that there is amongst a number of third sector bodies and our charities about a cancer strategy, something that a number of us have been shouting about for a long time to have, so it's positive that that is coming forward. You raised the cancer pathways as well, and the delays that some people are experiencing through those pathways. I'm sure that's something that the Government will take heed of from your cross-party group as well, to see how we can improve, not just for prostate cancer but all cancers, to improve the pathways.

Ken Skates then opened with his support for the motion. I will give credit to the last Government—I don't give them credit much—for the new Velindre cancer care centre. [Interruption.] You can keep rolling your hand, Ken, but that's as far as it's going. And the work it did with the new cancer centre in Nevill Hall Hospital, the Velindre cancer centre there, and just how that's opened up so many more avenues to get care closer to home. I know the new Cabinet Minister has been there, and I've also been there in a personal capacity with a family member. I know just how important that centre is for so many people. He also talked about the strategy being evidence led by stuff that's going on at a UK level. I think that was really important to highlight.

Adrian, you raised your personal experience, like a lot of others did, with cancer, and that a lot of men don't seek out help. That's something that we do see across men's health across the country. A lot of people don't seek help with their own health problems, they just tend to deal with it quietly, and they don't go to the GP, and they don't go for tests. They just put it in a box somewhere and say, 'We won't talk about it'. I think that's really important. You also raised screening, and that the Welsh Government here should follow the advice as it develops. You also mentioned the support that can be given to patients and their families. I think that's really important.

Janet, thank you very much. I know about your personal experience. As you said, you and I have also talked about that a lot. You raised the point that 40 per cent of people are only caught at stage 3 and 4, which is an absolutely shocking statistic. It's coming well too late. That's probably one of the worst out of all the cancers, actually, except some of our rarer cancers. And you, like others, raised the screening programme as well. So I'm sure the Cabinet Minister has heard that, that a lot of us in this Chamber want that.

Gareth, you said that cancer can affect everyone, and that men in deprived areas are actually more likely to get diagnosed later than those in more affluent areas, and that's something about health inequalities, which the health committee have looked at on a number of occasions, and how we do need to make sure there is that health equality across Wales, without detriment to anyone in any part of the country. And the postcode lottery—I don't know how many times the Cabinet Minister and I have both heard that before, and others in this Chamber, about how where you live across Wales can really decide how your outcomes and prognosis look, which is also shocking.

Elwyn Vaughan talked about people who live in rural areas. You and I and a lot of others share this as well, about the barriers we face to diagnosis. You talked about the farming community especially. Just raising something from my own community, Shearing is Caring raised an awful lot of money for Prostate Cymru, and that's about the farming community and getting men talking more about their health. You talked about the link with the Farming Community Network at Macmillan. I'll give a shameless plug now that I'm running a Hyrox race next week for Macmillan. So if anybody wants to sponsor me, I'm still taking sponsorship. You also talked about the Welsh Government's plan for the rapid diagnostic centre in Powys. I don't agree with Plaid Cymru on much, but I think this could actually be an area where I think it's really positive for the people who live in rural areas, especially in Powys.

Helen Jenner spoke about her own personal experience in her own family, and I think it's very important that people do talk about their personal experience. I think it's something that really shapes a parliamentary democracy, that we've got people in here who actually do understand the issue, that have got family going through it. You also said about your father not wanting to worry people. How many times have we heard that with men who are going through a diagnosis? ‘I'm just not going to tell my family.’ I've even known people who've passed away from cancer, and their own family don't even know why they've passed away until after, because it's been hidden from them, because they just don't want them to worry. So, making sure that men talk more is important. You also raised the data and the years of missed targets, and I think that's something that the Cabinet Minister needs to reflect on, and perhaps other Members in the Chamber who were in Government before, that actually this is a historical issue and a historical injustice that really does need to be sorted.

Then we moved on to our Cabinet Minister, and I do not pretend that you're not showing commitment to this area. I know you and I have worked closely in the past on cancer pathways and improving cancer care across Wales, so I don't doubt your commitment to that. As you said, cancer is the leading cause of death for men in Wales. It's still too high, and it needs to be addressed. As I said earlier, you talked about us wanting to be the best in Europe. I want us to be the best in the world when it comes to addressing cancer, especially prostate cancer. We're a small nation that spends an awful lot of our public money on the health service. For the money we put into it, we actually get a pretty poor return. Making that money work better to get better outcomes for the people of Wales, and especially men struggling with prostate cancer, is really important.

You also talked about the Welsh Government wanting new technologies and tests. I know there are new lung screening tests that are coming through, but there are new tests coming through as well for prostate cancer, and it would be really good if Wales could be a leading partner with charities and with the university institutions to develop these new technologies so people can get seen quicker.

You mentioned screening. Something I haven't heard before, actually, is the commitment from the Government—that they've asked Public Health Wales to look at the screening. It's perhaps not as wide as some Members want, but it's screening for perhaps a portion of the population who are at higher risk of getting prostate cancer.

The clock has now gone red, but I'm going to make another shameless plug. It's something that I've always been very keen on. It was something in our manifesto—a proper men's health strategy for Wales. I think that is something that is needed. Prostate cancer is a leading cause of death in men, but there are also a lot of other health areas that need to be addressed for our men across the country. We don't talk about it often enough, and I think that's something that the Government should take into serious consideration—a proper men's health strategy for Wales to address the health inequalities of a number of men across our country. I urge all Members to support our motion this afternoon. Diolch.

speaker: James Evans AS
debate: 7. Reform UK Debate: Prostate cancer strategy
text:
Diolch, Llywydd. Can I just start by thanking all Members who've contributed to this debate, and also the Members who haven't contributed, but have actually sat through and listened to the debate? Because I think it's very nice that we've got a debate that galvanises the whole Chamber together. With all of the rumpus conversations that we have in here, it is quite nice to have some that do bring us together.

Ben opened the debate and, as you said, it's the most common cause of cancer in men: 2,500 people diagnosed and, as many people, like yourself, said, 640 of those sadly passing away—sadly too young, a lot of them as well, because the diagnosis wasn't caught early. And that only 54 per cent of men in Wales are accessing rapid treatment compared to 69 per cent in England, and that's something that should concern us all. I know the Cabinet Secretary highlighted—I'll come on to it later—about wanting to be the best in Europe, and I share that ambition, I'm sure we all do, but we need to put a laser focus on this area of cancer, because it is preventable if it is caught early enough.

You also raised the issue, as a lot of Members did, around data. It's something that a number of us who've been here a long time have always heard about cancer care, that the data just isn't there to inform decision making, so having more accurate data is very, very important. You also raised early screening. I know a number of Members raised that and that's something that's also very important. I know Prostate Cymru, for example, have gone out doing screening themselves on top of what the NHS is doing, and I think they've done an absolutely phenomenal job in finding a number of people across the country. Sometimes, those are men, as Members have talked about, who wouldn't naturally go and see a doctor, but they've had the sessions in rugby clubs, in gyms, for example, or down the local pub. So, it's actually been really good that they've rolled that out.

speaker: James Evans AS
debate: 7. Reform UK Debate: Prostate cancer strategy
text: Would the Member take an intervention?

speaker: Jason O'Connell AS
debate: 8. Welsh Labour Debate: The M4 around Newport
text:
Oh, have I waited for this one. [Laughter.] Now, we, Reform, will of course support the motion today. It's pretty clear, though, that it's an obvious attempt to cut the strings of Labour's puppet master, Mark Drakeford. Now, we welcome the decision and we congratulate Welsh Labour on taking 27 years to come to the same conclusion that it took us exactly one minute to make. And that one minute was 59 seconds too long, in my opinion.

Now, every day, tens of thousands of motorists sit in queues on the M4. Businesses lose money, workers lose time and families spend more of their lives sitting in traffic than sitting at home with loved ones. And after literally decades of promises, what have they been given? More congestion, more excuses and absolutely no solution. The very politicians responsible for this failure are trying to convince the people of Wales that they have the answer.

Let's start with Labour. Twenty-seven years in Government. Twenty-seven years to deliver a solution to the most important transport problem in recent Welsh history. One hundred and fifty million pounds of taxpayers' money spent on plans, consultations and reviews. And what did the people of Wales receive for that substantial investment? Nothing. Perhaps a few sheets of paper. Mark Drakeford cancelled the M4 relief road, abandoning a project that would have made a real difference. And who was the Government Minister at the time? A gentleman called Ken Skates. [Interruption.] Good timing, sir.

speaker: Jason O'Connell AS
debate: 8. Welsh Labour Debate: The M4 around Newport
text: Well, good news, Ken: I can see straight through you, so no problem there. [Laughter.]

speaker: Jason O'Connell AS
debate: 8. Welsh Labour Debate: The M4 around Newport
text: Didn't know it was coming.

speaker: Jason O'Connell AS
debate: 8. Welsh Labour Debate: The M4 around Newport
text:
Not at all. Reform has been very clear: we will build the M4 relief road. So, that's our position. That's the one we're currently going down, and it will not be a toll road. It will be paid for out of the sovereign wealth fund from the UK Government. Thank you very much.

But continuing, did you stand up and challenge the decision? No. Did you stand up and fight for businesses, commuters and families who desperately need that road? No. You defended the very Government that cancelled it. Now Labour wants to lecture this Chamber about the importance of building a relief road. It is quite funny. The same party that killed the project want to take credit for bringing it back to life. So, here's my question to Labour: if the M4 relief road is so desperately needed today, why didn't you build it when you were in power? The truth is, Labour hasn't changed. They've discovered the political consequences of ignoring it. And now, frightened of losing even more support to Reform UK, they're desperately trying to distance themselves from the anti-motorist legacy of Mark Drakeford and Lee Waters. But the people of Wales won't forget, and neither will we.

So, let me now turn to Plaid Cymru, a party that promised change but are determined to continue the same failed approach. The black route has apparently been ruled out. But good news, stranded motorists, we've been offered more studies, more assessments and even more delays, and astonishingly, proposals to close motorway junctions and divert traffic onto local roads in Newport and the surrounding towns. Now, think about that for a moment. Their answer to congestion on the M4 is to move that congestion into the communities of Newport. How on earth is that supposed to improve the lives of the people we represent?

Now, thanks to resurfaced tweets, we have greater clarity on the mind behind the junction closures. In 2019, the Minister stated he wanted to discourage car use on the M4 because of the climate emergency, and even went so far as to seriously suggest that the way to solve the M4 issue was that workers in Wales, in the public sector, should work a day fewer a week. Now, they call us climate conspiracy theorists, of course, yet they're the ones blocking the relief road as part of their net-zero agenda. That is their design: punish motorists and push them onto public transport. And if you don't believe me, just take a look at the transport Minister's own words for it.

Today is about setting the record straight. Labour had the opportunity to build the road and cancelled it. Plaid Cymru had the opportunity to deliver a solution and is ruling out the very project that would provide one. Now, one party cancelled it, the other refuses to build it, but we all know it was the constant pressure of Reform, our historic election result and our grass-roots campaign that has got us here today. The people of Wales already know how they're going to get this M4 road delivered, and that is with a Reform UK Government.

speaker: Jason O'Connell AS
debate: 8. Welsh Labour Debate: The M4 around Newport
text: Didn't know it was coming.

speaker: Stephen Senior AS
debate: 8. Welsh Labour Debate: The M4 around Newport
text: Will you take an intervention?

speaker: Art Wright AS
debate: 8. Welsh Labour Debate: The M4 around Newport
text:
Diolch, Lywydd. I have been asked to shorten this debate, so I'll take no interventions, please, because I'm going to have to cut out as I go, because some people like to talk more than they should need to. [Laughter.]

For more than 30 years, the Welsh Government has wrestled with M4 congestion around Newport, yet we are still here facing the same question today: the problem at Brynglas. The Welsh Government review considers several options, but says none alone or combined would fully resolve the M4 problem.

Despite previous Governments spending £136.5 million already, the review estimates currently that around 25 per cent of peak-time traffic would need to be removed to avoid congestion unless road capacity is increased. Yet the package considered could only achieve 17 per cent, with planning to fail instead of planning to fix things. Take the proposed junction changes: £14 million could be spent closing junctions 27, 26, 25 for an estimated 3 per cent reduction. These are direct questions from residents. So, where does that traffic go? How much moves into Newport local roads? Which communities take that additional traffic? What happens to congestions on routes such as Queensway and the southern distributor road? And what happens to the journey times for drivers that live around those junctions?

These questions matter even more with the housing growth that is coming to the area. Research supplied to me already estimates between 7,100 and 7,400 homes have been built across the four former Gwent authorities since 2019. Most of the councils are now sending out their regional development plans. Newport plans just shy of 400 homes; Monmouth to provide between 5,400 and 6,200 homes. Caerphilly identifies 7,400 new homes by 2035. Torfaen and Blaenau Gwent are still developing theirs, so their numbers will be added at a later date.

Now, Minister, not every home puts another car on the M4, but more homes mean more people, more journeys in the long run. The review says that benefits are uncertain because of future growth and that latent demand could take up capacity over time. It also says that no new transport modelling was undertaken in the review. So, Minister, how long will these proposals work? How quickly could the growing demand wipe out the 3 per cent reduction? Where is the modelling that includes thousands of new homes? The review reflects a greater emphasis on sustainable travel and carbon reduction, but the Minister must answer this: is the primary objective to solve the M4 capacity problem or to get people out of their cars in the pursuit of wider net-zero objectives? They are not necessarily the same thing. The review says public transport improvements will help, but to a limited extent.

I'm going to have to skip over some, because I'm aware you want me to keep the time down.

When Welsh Labour, the Government, cancelled the black route, it was estimated that the cost at the time was £1.4 billion. I'm not suggesting that £1.4 billion would still be today's price, but it would need recalculating. That is precisely the point—why exclude it before the calculation is made? The review says a new motorway was excluded primarily because of likely affordability and environmental and planning challenges. Surely, those must be assessed and compared so that we can compare apples with apples.

So, why not give us today's cost of the black route? Give us the full cost of the alternative packages. Show us the congestion reduction that each would achieve. Show us the additional capacity that each would provide. Include future housing growth in every model. And then tell us how long each option's benefits are expected to last. Show us where the displaced traffic goes. Show us what happens to the 1,000 more homes built. Show us what every option costs and delivers, and give the black route the same test. If the Government alternative provides the best long-term answer, let the evidence demonstrate it. But if it costs more, delivers less, and leaves Newport with a capacity problem, the black route should be put back on the table.

Finally, Minister, a few weeks ago, when we discussed the M4 before, I asked you if you would listen to the residents of Newport. Two petitions have been raised: one by Labour, which has achieved 5,846 signatures as of yesterday morning, and one sponsored by Reform Members, which has reached 13,713. Will you now listen to their voices?

speaker: Sarah Pochin
debate: Rough Sleeping and Good Growth Funds
text: While the Minister’s statement is laudable, it seems that her Department is working against the Ministry of Justice by moving in what is clearly a different direction. speaker: Robert Jenrick
text: The Foreign Secretary and I represent communities 15 miles apart—decent, hard-working people who are finding life very tough at the moment. In that context, how would he justify to working people and pensioners spending £6 billion on foreign aid while freezing the tax-free personal allowance and cutting the state pension? [Interruption.]

speaker: Richard Tice
text: It is bad enough that dangerous criminals are being released early, but my constituents are frankly terrified that these prisoners are being released without tags—the world has gone mad, Minister. Will this Government commit not to release prisoners without tags?

speaker: Lee Anderson
text: Will the Minister please tell the House how many people who should be wearing an electronic tag are wandering around our communities with no electronic device fitted at all? That should be a simple question.

speaker: Lee Anderson
text: Ashfield district council is being run by criminals—criminals such as Councillor Tom Hollis, who is the vice-chairman of the council. Councillor Hollis, along with his family, keep putting in planning applications that are recommended for refusal by the planning officers, and then, as if by magic, they go to committee and they are planned, netting Councillor Hollis tens—if not hundreds— of thousands of pounds for him and his family. Will the Prime Minister please send in the commissioners to root out that corruption and put those people where they belong?

speaker: Danny Kruger
text: Can the Prime Minister confirm that the Budget calculations assume the approval of the Rosebank gasfield, and, if so, has he told the Energy Secretary of this important development? If he is now taking back control of energy policy, will he approve more North sea exploration and, while he is at it, speed up the roll-out of nuclear as well?

speaker: Richard Tice
text: The hon. Lady may not have read the Budget Red Book, but GDP growth is forecast to reduce from 1.6% back in March to just 1% in 2027, and indeed GDP per capita is also forecast to reduce from 1.3% to 0.9%, so the numbers in the forecasts are actually getting worse, not better.

speaker: Richard Tice
text: I’m here!

speaker: Richard Tice
text:
Poorer—that is what every household in the country is, including in my constituency of Boston and Skegness. This year alone, real household disposable income is down 0.8%, and every single year between now and the end of this parliamentary term, the average household’s real disposable income is down compared to what the OBR forecast just six months ago. Let us look at the other main economic data: GDP growth for 2027 is forecast to be down once again—from 1.6% to 1%—under this failing Labour Government; and GDP growth per capita is forecast to be down from 1.3% to 0.9%.

And let us just look at what is up, shall we? Government borrowing in this financial year alone is up almost £20 billion compared to what the OBR forecast just six months ago. Over the lifetime of this Budget book for the next five years, Government borrowing will be over £65 billion more than the OBR forecast just six months ago. This is a Government who are completely out of control in terms of spending. That is why the bond markets are applying what is known internationally as “the moron premium” to the United Kingdom under this Labour Government.

Credit where credit is due, this Chancellor does know where the real problems are and he has tried to do a little bit. He understands that there is a crisis with energy bills, which are now forecast to go up by an extra £466 per household in January, and then by another £200 per household in April—all because of the madness of net zero and the rush to renewables, which is happening as we speak. Every single day, NESO is having to tweak and twiddle the dials and add balancing costs to the tune of some £50 million. That is ten times what it was just a few years ago. Next year, it will cost £200 per household for the balancing costs on the grid alone. This is completely out of control. The Chancellor has shuffled the cards in the pack. He has moved a bit from bills to general taxation, but he has not dealt with the real crux of the crisis, which is that the rush to renewables is driving up all our household energy bills at a catastrophically high rate.

Now, I am constructive sort of guy, so I want to give credit where credit is due, so let me say that the Government have done the right thing in approving Jackdaw—but they need to go further. Ministers know in their heart of hearts that they need to approve the oilfield at Rosebank—the Prime Minister was tempted to confirm it at question time today—and grant many more licences in the North sea, because that is our energy treasure; that is where the jobs are and where the growth is. This Government are completely failing on growth. The energy crisis is getting worse, and everybody needs to understand that. If we use our energy treasure, the bills will come down.

If we look at property and housing—again, credit where credit is due—the Chancellor has eased regulations to try to build more homes on brownfield sites. I think he might have read the teal paper I released in September on how to reduce the cost of construction and get more things built. He is right to remove the need for biodiversity requirements on brownfield sites, but there is so much more to do to reduce the construction cost of the new homes that I think we all agree we need to build. There is a £15,000 to £20,000 increase in the cost of homes because of unnecessary regulations, but again the Chancellor has not grasped the real opportunities to go for it and reduce the cost of building. That is what we need. We all agree that we need more affordable social housing, but to do that we have to reduce and remove unnecessary restrictions and the delays in getting planning consents.

We now know that the Secretary of State for Housing, Communities and Local Government has given up on her 1.5 million target. In reality, we will be lucky to get to half that number—750,000 homes instead of 1.5 million. These are the lost opportunities from a Government obsessed with regulation, obsessed with process and obsessed with bureaucracy. They cannot do the right thing to deregulate and get some growth.

speaker: Richard Tice
text:
Far from it—we are actually trying to build more houses on brownfield sites, because that is what we should do all over the country, including in the great town of Tunbridge Wells. We need to make it easier to build on brownfield sites. At the moment, house builders are giving up all over the country because the costs are too high.

I think the Chancellor has been looking at some of our excellent Reform policies, but while he is right to lift the income tax threshold for pensioners, he could have gone much further and lifted it for everybody—up to our recommended level of £15,000—by being more dramatic about cutting the vast amount of wasteful spending on welfare and cutting foreign aid to overseas nations that do not need it. Those are the differences between the right things to do and the lost opportunities of this Government.

I think the Chancellor has listened to another Reform policy, which is to lift the threshold on business rates, but he has not gone far enough. While the £18,000 threshold is better than £12,000, it needs to be much higher. That is another lost opportunity.

We have a nation of voters, and every household who looks at this Budget book and listens to the Budget will say, “No, thanks. Every single year between now and 2030-31 we’re all getting poorer than the OBR forecast just six months ago.” People feel it and they sense it. They know that their money is being wasted on bureaucracy and unnecessary quangos—more taskforces and quangos have been set up during this Budget. It could have been so much better. I feel that this Chancellor has just not had the courage or the strength. He has not risen to the occasion. He has tried, but it is not good enough. We are facing a financial crisis and an energy crisis, and we need a Government who do the right thing—a Government who cut our bills. This Budget is a lost opportunity.

speaker: Andrew Rosindell
text: Will the Leader of the House join me in celebrating Essex Day, which was on Monday this week, and thanking Mr Speaker for flying the flag of the county of Essex from New Palace Yard here in Parliament? speaker: Nigel Farage
text: I am pleased that my party’s legal challenge has bought us a stay in Essex and elsewhere, but to re-emphasise: district councils matter to remote, rural and coastal communities. In Clacton, planning decisions—big decisions that matter—are taken in Clacton town hall. Under your proposals, those decisions will be made in a large population centre.

speaker: Nigel Farage
text: Under these proposals, big planning decisions that are currently taken locally will be taken miles away, in a big population centre with no understanding of the local ground. speaker: Richard Tice
text: The reason this local government reorganisation has been so appalling shambolic is that the Government made political decisions, as opposed to the right decisions. Reform in Lincolnshire welcomes the decision to pause there, but does the Minister understand that Reform in Warwickshire is concerned that the two-unitary proposal he is minded to accept will lead to the bankruptcy of both unitaries within a matter of years?

speaker: Andrew Rosindell
text: The Minister knows, because we have discussed this many times, that the boundaries of historical counties and cities are very different from local government boundaries, and I am pleased that he has said today that city status is preserved, as are ceremonial matters. Will he finally allow historical and ceremonial counties to be as one, in order to avoid confusion, and so that we in Romford can have our Essex identity, regardless of local government boundaries? speaker: Lee Anderson
text: Kinver Business Solutions has secured more than £1 million in project management fees from Ashfield district council. speaker: Suella Braverman
text: The Prime Minister has made it clear that Labour councils should end their power-sharing agreements with local Green parties, following the disgracefully antisemitic motion passed by the national Green party that Zionism is racism. Does the Minister agree that that is a breach of the Nolan principles, and will he clarify who is right: the Prime Minister, or the Labour leader of Havant borough council?

speaker: Danny Kruger
text: Swindon and Wiltshire councils are building a lot of new housing, which is excellent, but the Government have now abolished an essential safeguard for communities against inappropriate planning, which is the power of councillors to call in applications. What steps are the Government taking to review that particular measure, and will they reconsider if it turns out that it is not working?

speaker: Robert Jenrick
text: Summer was a difficult time for Nottinghamshire fire service; it battled with wildfires and a lot of heat-related incidents. The firemen and women had to wear protective equipment and clothing in which it was simply unbearable to work in that type of heat. I know that the Secretary of State has made some funding available for this, but will she work to ensure that by next summer, if we have the same hot weather and wildfires, brave firemen and women will have the clothing and protective equipment that they need to work in those conditions?

speaker: Robert Jenrick
text: I respect the Home Secretary, but these are not the reforms that she wanted. When she said that the Boris wave was destabilising and unprecedented, and that it would cause incalculable damage, she was absolutely right. The Boris wave was the worst public policy failure of the 21st century, and now she risks locking it in for generations to come. When the last Conservative Prime Minister—my Prime Minister—ignored my advice on immigration, I resigned. Her Prime Minister has ignored her advice on immigration, and the damage is going to be disastrous for this country. Why has she not considered her position?

speaker: Sarah Pochin
text: In August last year the Government admitted that they had no idea how many people who came in on care worker visas were still working in the care sector. How can the Home Secretary make an informed decision on their earned settlement when she has no idea whether they are still here doing the jobs they came in to do?

speaker: Andrew Rosindell
text: What assessment he has made of the potential impact of levels of Government borrowing on the economy.

speaker: Andrew Rosindell
text: Does the Minister understand just how devastating the effects of his Government’s spending, taxing and borrowing policies are for my constituents in Romford? Does he recall that the last time we had a Prime Minister who understood that we need low taxes, a smaller state and lower borrowing was in 1990? Then the national debt was 21% of GDP; now it is heading for 100%. Will he please reduce the size of the state, cut taxes for hard-working people and start to live within our means?

speaker: Richard Tice
text: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Treasury, the hon. Member for Swansea West (Torsten Bell), and the Chancellor have both inadvertently misled the House by saying that Government borrowing is coming down. It is not: in the Budget, borrowing for this year will be almost £20 billion higher than at the March OBR forecast; and for the lifetime of the Budget book, it will be £65 billion higher.

speaker: Richard Tice
text: Today the Tory party has shamefully said that it does not give two hoots about 12,000 workers, including dozens in my constituency. What is going on here is that the management of Poundland are very concerned that the owners of Poundland are looking to abuse the insolvency process to maximise their financial returns, not giving two hoots about 12,000 workers. Will the Minister confirm that the Government will do everything they can to ensure that Gordon Brothers will not act as a rogue owner by abusing the insolvency process?

speaker: Suella Braverman
text: Will my right hon. Friend give way?

speaker: Suella Braverman
text: My right hon. Friend is making a very powerful speech. Does he share my disappointment and dismay with this fact—that, for every young Brit who is hired today, 27 young foreign workers are hired? Young people are being locked out of the labour market because of mass immigration.

speaker: Suella Braverman
text:
One million—that is the number of young people who are not in education, employment or training. Youth unemployment stands at 14%. That is a scandal and a crisis. Far from giving young people hope, this Budget throws them under a bus, frankly, because it is fundamentally unfair. We are losing a generation.

This Budget is unfair to the 16-year-old who has finished their GCSEs and wants to start working, but who faces zero opportunities to find an apprenticeship or learn a skill. It is unfair and offers no hope to the 21-year-old who has done the right thing and studied for a degree, but who has come out with a qualification that is not opening any doors and has instead saddled them with crippling debt and directed them to the welfare office to claim out-of-work benefits.

This Budget is also unfair to the British taxpayer, who currently lays out £22 billion a year in student loan payments. That is a taxpayer who will see hundreds of billions of pounds never repaid; a taxpayer who faces chronic shortages in our labour market, particularly in the NHS, construction and hospitality. We have a lost generation, and this Budget does nothing for our young people.

speaker: Suella Braverman
text:
The right hon. Gentleman is absolutely right. That is exactly the point that I am about to make.

How did we get to this youth unemployment crisis? For the past 30 years, starting with Tony Blair, we have sold one promise to young people: that they need to get a degree, regardless of what it is or where it is from, and they will be set up for life. However, for so many young people today, that has been exposed as a lie. We have 700,000 graduates currently unemployed, some 400,000 of whom are claiming welfare. Average graduate debt stands at £50,000, average graduate salaries are falling, and graduate hiring is disappearing.

For many of those young people, it is not so much that they have taken out a student loan; they have been saddled with a life sentence. It is no wonder they cannot start saving, buy a house, get married or think of starting a family. They are being crippled by the system, and this Budget does nothing to support them.

speaker: Suella Braverman
text:
I am afraid that is just a drop in the ocean compared with the enormity of the challenge we face. I will come on to skills and apprenticeships in one minute, but I will dwell on how we got to this great university scam, as I call it.

We have some of the best universities in the country, and I will always defend them, but our universities are failing many of our young people and offering awful value for money. Some of the courses are not worth the paper they are written on. Is it really right that vice-chancellors are earning huge salaries but offering awful job prospects? Do some of them really deserve their £200,000 or £300,000 salaries when their institutions are offering job prospects for only 40% of their graduates? No. Do we really need courses in politics, sexuality and gender, with a vice-chancellor on more than £200,000? No. That is all while we have gaps in our NHS, construction and hospitality. That is why a Reform Government would deal with this issue. We would reduce the student loan budget by 20% and invest the billions saved into helping our country. We would train up British doctors and nurses and scrap the arbitrary cap on medical training places.

Let me say a word about immigration, because it has been a big factor. Many universities have got fat on foreign students. I am afraid that I have to say it: the last Conservative Government opened the floodgates to international students. It is something that I started to reverse when I was Home Secretary. As a result, universities have been selling immigration, not education. As a consequence—as I said earlier—for every young Brit who is employed in this country, 27 young foreign workers are also employed.

speaker: Suella Braverman
text:
I am sorry, but I do not have much time. I will try to come back to the hon. Lady.

What I have described is locking our young people out of the labour market. A Reform Government would put British workers at the front of the queue for British jobs. That used to be common sense, but today it is controversial.

Moving on to apprenticeships and skills, I am afraid that this Budget is conspicuously silent on investing in skills, apprenticeships and the vocational trades. The number of apprenticeships has almost halved over the past decade, particularly among small and medium-sized businesses and for entry-level positions.

speaker: Suella Braverman
text: The reality is that £100 million is a small amount compared to the enormity of the challenge that we are required to face, as I said to the hon. Gentleman’s colleague, the hon. Member for Mid Derbyshire (Jonathan Davies). Employers are not taking on young people—that is a fact and it is borne out by the statistics. Employers are not taking on apprentices, because it has become too expensive for them. It has become heavily regulated and bureaucratic, and the training requirements are now too rigid.

speaker: Suella Braverman
text:
The hon. Lady is on a weak point there, because it was the last Conservative Government who started the apprenticeship movement, and apprenticeships peaked at around 600,000 in 2016. I was very pleased to champion apprenticeships in my constituency, and thousands of young people in Fareham and Waterlooville have taken them up, but that number has been halved—we are now at about 300,000 apprentices.

A Reform UK Government would introduce an apprenticeship wage credit. We would pay small and medium-sized enterprises 30% of an apprentice’s salary to help them with the cost of taking on a new person, investing in our future and in young people. I want to live in a country where a young person is able to enjoy opportunities to prosper, work hard and thrive in their life, regardless of where they come from, what their parents did or the kind of school they went to.

I am afraid that this Budget offers precious little to our young people and zero hope to the next generation, and is a real disappointment for our young people, who are crying out for hope and opportunity. That is why I will be voting against it tonight.

speaker: Steve Bayliss AS
section: Cwm Taf Morgannwg University Local Health Board
text: 1. What assurances has the Welsh Government sought from Cwm Taf Morgannwg University Health Board about their safeguarding arrangements and health visiting capacity? OQ64801 [R]

speaker: Steve Bayliss AS
section: Cwm Taf Morgannwg University Local Health Board
text: Diolch, First Minister. I accept that the health board is the employer, but holding it to account on child safety is your responsibility. On 16 September, your Cabinet Minister for health told this Chamber that he had sought and received detailed assurances on safeguarding. Eight days later, the board's own nursing director proposed only qualified assurance on safeguarding, and limited assurance on capacity, warning that reduced contact diminishes opportunities to identify hidden harm. That is the child nobody yet knows is at risk. When the First Minister was first told about the safeguarding and capacity concerns, its quality committee's paper records 'ministerial requirements'. On 13 October, you spoke of full transparency. Then let families see the evidence. Within seven days, will you publish what Ministers required, what the board replied and the number of child health contacts missed or deferred—totals, not names? Diolch.

speaker: Louise Emery AS
text: 2. What assessment has the Welsh Government made of the impact of the UK Government’s autumn budget on small retail, hospitality and leisure businesses in Wales? OQ64842

speaker: Louise Emery AS
text: So, you've probably guessed, First Minister, that I'm going to talk about the threshold, which has been increased to £18,000 for small retail, hospitality and leisure premises in England. In Wales, if we just remind the Chamber, it's £6,000, with tapered relief up to £12,000. Will your Government assess how many Welsh businesses would actually benefit if the threshold matched over in England and publish that estimated cost ahead of the Welsh budget? Diolch.

speaker: Helen Jenner AS
section: Questions Without Notice from the Party Leaders
text:
First Minister, these were your commitments, not mine, not Reform's, and I'm simply holding you to account by asking you why you haven't kept to them. And I'll say once again, the question is: will witnesses be compelled to give evidence under oath? And the answer is 'no'. And that's simply not good enough for these families.

First Minister, a leaked letter to Betsi Cadwaladr University Health Board staff has revealed that the health board has approved a formal consultation on proposals to cease its urgent primary care centre services across north Wales by 31 March next year. These centres were established to relieve pressure on GP surgeries and emergency departments. And you know as well as anyone in this Chamber what that pressure looks like, especially at hospital emergency departments. Penrhos Stanley hospital in Holyhead has already lost the St David's Hospice ward. The award-winning specialist leg ulcer and complex wound service has been reduced to just one member of staff, while the minor injuries unit has, on occasion, operated on reduced hours. Where does this end, First Minister? What next? Are we eventually going to see somewhere like Penrhos Stanley hospital close altogether? Betsi Cadwaladr remains in special measures, and I don't want to hear that these decisions are simply a matter for the health board. Your Government has responsibility for overseeing this health board, and your health Minister, sitting right there, has statutory powers of intervention. So, will you ask your health Minister to urgently examine the use of those powers to prevent these proposed cuts? speaker: Helen Jenner AS

speaker: Iain McIntosh AS
debate: 3. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution: Wales Covid-19 Review
text:
still some very serious questions that need to be answered. Why did the Welsh Government wait until 23 October 2020 to introduce the firebreak, despite receiving advice weeks earlier? Why were more than 1,000 patients reportedly discharged into Welsh care homes without being tested? Why were there delays in vaccinating some of our most vulnerable care home residents? And why did the Welsh Government have PPE stockpiles containing equipment that had expired years earlier? These weren't just administrative decisions. They potentially affect people's lives, and the families deserve to know why those decisions were made and who was responsible.

So, here's my first concern. Nowhere in your statement do you confirm that this panel will have legal powers to compel witnesses to give evidence or require documents to be handed over. And that matters, because if a former Minister or senior official refuses to co-operate, what can this panel actually do about it? Can it compel them to attend? Can it demand the evidence, or will it simply have to accept whatever information people choose to provide? Because surely we cannot have a process where the people responsible for making decisions can decide for themselves whether they want to answer questions about them or not.

And there's another issue. You say the panel will consider how best to involve bereaved families. I'd like to thank the Cabinet Minister for his—sorry. Sorry, let me start again. You say the panel will consider how best to involve bereaved families, but why is that still something to be considered? That's the point I'm making. Surely those families should be guaranteed a meaningful role from the very beginning. They've waited long enough, and they've already made it clear what they want. They want a process that can establish the truth and hold decision makers accountable. I understand the Government doesn't want to duplicate the UK COVID inquiry, and I agree that we shouldn't waste tax moneys unnecessarily, but the families themselves have suggested a focused Wales inquiry, using evidence already gathered by the UK inquiry, while retaining the powers needed to obtain further evidence where necessary. So, why has that option not been taken forward? And what evidence does the Government have that the panel announced today will deliver the same level of scrutiny?

Dirprwy Lywydd, I also notice that the Minister hasn't given us a budget or a reported deadline. We're told that the panel will meet for the first time in the new year, but how long will it take? How long will it cost? And when will the families finally get some answers?

So, I want to finish with four straightforward questions. First, will this panel have the legal powers to compel witnesses and to obtain documents? If not, why not? Secondly, will bereaved families be guaranteed a meaningful role in this work? Third, what is the budget, and when will the panel report? And fourth, will it investigate the decisions made by Welsh Ministers during the pandemic, or will it only examine whether we're better prepared for the next one?

speaker: Iain McIntosh AS
debate: 3. Statement by the Cabinet Minister for Government Effectiveness and the Constitution: Wales Covid-19 Review
text:
Diolch, Dirprwy Lywydd. I'd like to thank the Cabinet Minister for his statement and acknowledge the fact that the Welsh Government is finally taking steps to establish a Wales-specific COVID review. But, having listened to what we've just heard, I have to say, I am concerned that this isn't going to deliver what the bereaved families have actually been asking for. Because there's a big difference between looking at whether we're better prepared for the next pandemic and properly investigating what went wrong during the last one, and that's the distinction I want to focus on today.

Dirprwy Lywydd, more than 13,000 people in Wales lost their lives to COVID. Behind every one of those deaths is a family. Families who have waited years for answers about what happened to their loved ones. Last week, Members received the voices of the Welsh COVID bereaved, and some of those accounts were absolutely heartbreaking. One daughter described watching her mother die through a care home window because she wasn't allowed inside. Another account described a care home losing 26 of its 52 residents after untested hospital patients were transferred in. And one family lost their father after he caught COVID in hospital, only to receive a letter inviting him for his vaccination the following week. Now, these are the people this process must deliver answers for.

Now, Cabinet Minister, you've announced an independent review panel, and I acknowledge the appointment of an independent chair, but your statement makes it very clear that the panel's main purpose is to assess whether Wales is better prepared for a future pandemic. That's important, of course it is, but what about accountability for the decisions made during the last pandemic? Because there are still some very serious questions

speaker: Iain McIntosh AS

speaker: Iain McIntosh AS

Minister, following on from that, I need to talk about human sewage, or black water as it's sometimes euphemistically known. As you know, much of Wales is covered by a combined sewer system where human waste and rainwater all goes, effectively, into the same pipe. When it was originally built, that wasn't a problem because it just went into the nearest river or into the sea. However, today, that pipe network just can't cope at times, and the water treatment plants can't cope during very heavy rain. We know that there are overflows, which either put the water into the river or into the sea, and even those can't cope sometimes, and it gets backed up, and some of these places that are flooded end up with a very stressful situation where we have human waste in that flood water. That's the harsh reality of our water system.

Now, to separate out those two different systems at a UK level would cost anything between an estimated £300 billion and £1 trillion. The fact we can't put a figure on it shows the problem. We actually don't even know or have an accurate map of where some of those pipes are. So, Minister, my question is: does the Welsh Government, having worked with the water industry in Wales—which is, obviously, more than one company—have any estimate for how much it might cost to solve the problem of combined sewers and combined sewer overflows?

Having previously farmed in France, I saw first-hand a much more structured system of support for people wanting to enter the industry. In France, young farmers were able to access substantial establishment grants averaging €32,000 under the previous national scheme, alongside lots of additional financial incentives.

Here in Wales, the barriers are considerable, and the cost of acquiring land is probably the worst thing—machinery, livestock. It just makes it prohibitively expensive, particularly for someone without a farming family behind them. The figures speak for themselves. According to the FUW in Wales, just 3 per cent of farmers are under 35, and the median age of the principal decision maker in Wales is 61. What consideration is the Welsh Government giving to more ambitious—. Well, you've just sort of covered this, really, but it's something we really need to look at, and find a way of dealing with it.

speaker: Tom Montgomery AS
debate: 2. Questions to the Cabinet Minister for Rural Resilience and Sustainability
section: Spreading Slurry and Other High Readily Available Nitrogen Organic Manures
text:
Thank you, Minister. In March five years ago, a Member of this Chamber brought forward a motion calling for this Parliament to annul the Wales-wide nitrate vulnerable zones. As you said in this very Chamber, ‘the regulations are disproportionate’. I agree. They cover all of Wales when NRW's own advice was only for a small proportion of Wales to be covered. And again, Minister, in your words, you called the approach ‘absurd’ because it uses the calendar rather than weather conditions for when slurry can be spread.

Whilst I welcome the extension of the spreading season to 15 November, that doesn't address the underlying issue. The approach is wrong. We need an approach that is targeted and not Wales-wide. We need an approach that recognises that we farm by weather. Minister, you were content then to annul the regulations. Will you now work cross-party to scrap them now so farmers can farm by weather and not by calendar this winter? Diolch.

text:

Welsh Water's supply interruption figure was one hour, 23 minutes against a five-minute target. Serious pollution incidents rose by half and the average household bill is £683.

When you chaired the environment committee, Minister, you told Welsh Water to up its game. In June, you told this Chamber that you'd asked to meet with the chief executive.
